saltinanatomy.c: SALT, in Anatomy, is one of the three Processes made by the doubling of the Dura Mater; it rises by a narrow Beginning from the Chrifta GalU, to which it is fastned; and as it approaches the Hinder part of the Head, it grows broader and broader, till it terminate where the Longitudinal Sinus ends. It divides the Cerebrum into two Hemispheres, near as deep as the Corpus Callofum. Tis called Falx from its resembling a Sickle.

salcon.c: SAL CON, a fort of Cannon, whose Diameter at the Bore is Inches, Weight Pound, Length Foot, Load a Pound, Shot i Diame - ter, and T Weight.

sailingofrecord.c: SAILING of Record, is when an Adion is brought against one who pleads any Matter or Re - cord, ' and avers to prove it by Record; and the Plaintiff faith, Nul till Record, whereupon the De - fendant hath a Day given him to bring it in, at which Day he fails, or brings jn such a one as is no bar to this Adion; this is said to be sailer of Record.

saint.c: SAINT - PLEADER, in Law, signifies a False, Covenous, or Collufary Manner of Pleading, to the Deceit of a third Party.

self.c: SELF des, is he that commit Felony by Mtir - shewing of himself.

sights.c: SIGHTS, in a Ship, are the waste Cloths which hang round about her in a Fight, to hinder the Men from being seen by the Enemy j and they call those Bulkheads afore or abaft the Ship which are put up for Men to Hand secure behind and Fire on the Ene - my in case of Boarding, Cl. ose Sights.

FIGURE, in Geometry, is a Space compassed round on all Sides, and are either Rettilineal, Cur - r vilineal or Mixt.

slie.c: SLIE, that Part of the Mariner ’ s Compass on which the Winds are drawn, and to which the Needle is fattened underneath, they call the Slie.

slower.c: SLOWER - DE LIS, the Mark of Difference in Heraldry for the Sixth Brother of any Family: Tis also often born as Coat Ar - mour.

socleminus.c: SOCLE Minus, is the letter Bone of the Cu bit called Radius; or the lesser Bone of the Leg called Tibia.

soulaword.c: SOUL, a Word uled - at Sea in two Senles ' when a Ship has been long untrimmed, so that Grass, Weeds, Barnacles, or Periwincles, slick or grow to her Sides under Water, she is then laid to be soul. They fay also a Rope is soul, when it is either tangled in it self, or hindred by another, so that it cannot run or be haled.

soul.c: SOUL - WATER: A Ship is laid to mak e. soul Water, when being under Sail, she comes into such Shole or shallow Water, that though her Keel do not touch the Ground, yet she comes so near it, that the Motion, of the Water under her ariseth the Mud from the Bottom, and so pullet or fouleth the Water.

sugavacui.c: SUG A Vacui; it is a Notion of the Peripateticks, and some other Ancient Philosophers, that there is an Abhorrence in Nature of a Vacuum; and this in Latin they call Fuga Vacui, or Nature ’ s endeavour to avoid a Vacuum.

sutileanimposthume.c: SUTILE, an Imposthume in the Ears. Blan - chard. '

suretheseaword.c: SURE, the Sea Word for wrapping up and binding any Sail close to the Yard, which is done first by haling up the Braces, and then wrapping the Sail close together, and fq binding it fast to the Yard with the Caskets, and Furling - lines. This was formerly written Farther, because the Sail is thus made up in a Bundle or Farther; but tis now every where corrupted into the Word Furle.

soaring.c: SOARING j the Seamen fay a Sail is cut Godr - ing, when tis cut doing by degrees, and is broad - der at the Clew than at the Baring, as all Tog - fails and Tog - gallant Sails are.

steady.c: STEADY, is a Word common to both these ways of Sailing, either on a Wind, or Large, and fignifi. es that the Man at Helm should keep the Ship straight o her Course, and not let her go in and out, ormake Tawes, as they call it.

sable.c: SABLE; the Heralds Word for a Black Colour in the Arms of Gentlemen but in those of the Nobility, they call it Diamond, and in the Coats ’ of Soveraign Princes, ’ tis called Saturn. Tis expressed in engraving by strokes drawn perpendicularly a - cross each other, thus.

sacculimedicinales.c: SACCULI Medicinales, are when several Sim - ples, according to the Nature of the Disease, are compounded and beaten together, and tied up in a little Bag, to be applied to the Part affected. This Bag is to be sewed or quilted down in several pla - ces, that the Ingredients run not altogether in a Lump. Blanchard.

sacculuschyliferusorbpriferus.c: SACCULUS Chyliferus or Bpriferus, is what We usually call the peceptaculum Chyli, or the com - mon Receptacle of the Chyle; and sometimes Re - ccptaculum Pecquettianum, from Pecquet, who first found out both it and the Ductus Thoraciciis ( whole beginning it is ) in the Year,. I mean he was the first that assigned the true ule unto them, but both were observed in Horses by Bartholomaus Eufiacius, above Years ago, as appears in a Book he writ,. fag.. of the Vena fine pari, Wherein he has these Words, ( as cited. by Dr. What - ton. ) From this not aft e left Trunk: of the Throat, ( viz. the Subclavian Vein ) there Springs a great Branch, which besides that it has a Semi - circular Door, ( or Valve ) in its Origin, is moreover white, and full of watry Humour; and not far from its rije it is divi - ded into two, that after a little J pace, unite again in - to one, which fending forth no Branches, defends by the left side of the Vertebra;; and having passed thro ’ ' the Midriff, runs down the middle of the Loins: Where becoming larger, and folding about the great Artery, it has an obscure ending, which I have not as yet well d if covered. Here we have a clear Description of them, only that it is the beginning which he takes for the end: And contrarily, it is called the common Receptacle, because it receives both the Chyle and Lymph a pro - mifcuoufly, tho ’ some call it the Receptacle of the Chyle, in particular, but without region for it. might as well be called, Rpceptaculum Lymph a, as Chyli; for that the Lympha passes not only with the Chyle, but after this is all distributed, the Lympha still continues to glide into ir, and to ascend by the Ductus Chyliferus Thoracicus, which might as well be called Lymphaticus for the fame reason. It is seated under the Celiack Artery, and Emul - gent Veins, about the middle Distance between the Kidneys and Capsula atrabilarix, upon the Ver - terra: of the Loins, but for the moll part, rather toward the left side. Pecquet and Cafp. Bartholin lay, ' Tis seated be - twixt the Tendons ( or Appendices ) of the Dia - phragma; by the Motion whereof, ir is pressed and milked, as it were and its Contents propel - led. It is of a Membranous, but thicker Substance in Men than in Brutes, but not so capacious, ie dom being so large as to admit ones Fingers end. Out of it there springs a Dud: that presently af - ends up into the Thorax ( behind the defending Trunk of the Artcria magna ) where it begins to be called, Ductus Thofacicus; but according to Sylvius it might more fitly be called, Spinalis, fee - ing it runs along the inside of the Spina Dorsi ] This Dud having past the Abdomen and the Mid - riff, marches farther upward under the great Arte - ry, till about the fifth or sixth Vertebra of the Tho - rax, where it turns a little aside from under it ter the left Hand; and so underneath the Intercofta ! Arteries and Veins, and the Gland Thymus, it af - ends to the left Subclavian Vein, into whose lower side it opens, just there where the left Ju - gular Vein enters into it on the upper side, so that their Mouths face one another. But it opens not into this Vein with any large Orifice, but by fix or seven little ones, which are all cover ’ d in the Cavity of the Subclavia with one broad Valve, looking towards the Cava from the Shoulder, whereby there is granted to the Chyle and Lympha a free Passage out of the Ductus Chyliferus into the Subclavia, but their return ( or of Blood with them ) out of the Vein into the Dud, is prevented. This Dud ending thus in the Subclavian Vein, the Chyle that it conveys into it, passes with the; Blood ( returning by the Cava ) into the right Ven - triple of the Heart, where we will leave it to fop - ply the Defed of the depauperated Blood; having only observed, that this Dud has many Semilunar Valves that hinder the ascending Chyle and Lympha from gliding back again; which Valves are mani - sest by this, that the Chyle contained in the Dud may easily by the Finger be pressed upwards, but by no means downwards; or if one make a hole in it, the Liquor tending from beneath upwards, will flow out at it; but that which is above it, is so stopt by the Valves, that it cannot be made to descend by it.

saccus.c: SACCUS, is with r - me Writers the Gut called ReBum.

sacerignis.c: SACER Ignis. See Herpes Exedens. SAC'ER Morbus. See Epilepfa.

sacer.c: SACER ( Muf cuius ) which may be also called Tranfverfalis Lumborum. It lies under the Tendi - nous part of the Longiffmus Dorsi it ariseth fleshy not only from the Os Sacrum, but also from all the transverse Precedes of all the Vertebra of the Loins, and is inferred to their Superior Spines. We have sometimes observed, ( faith Mr. Cowper ) a Spinalis Lumborum, like the Spinalis Colli, which arising from the Superior Spines of the Os Sacrum, and marching with dired fleshy Fibres, is so inferred to the Superior Spines of the Vertebra of the Loins: The Tranfverfalis Lumborum lying under it, helps to move the whole Spine, or Vertebra of the Neck, Back and Loins, obliquely backwards, as in look - ing behind us,

sacksofearth.c: SACKS of Earth, used in Fortification, are made of course Cloath, the largest of them being about a Cubick - foot wide, and the lesser sore - what v what more than half a Foot. They are serviceable upon several occasions, more especially for making Retrenchments in haste, to place on Parapets, or the Head of the Breaches, &c. or to repair them when beaten down. They are of good use also when the Ground is rocky, ' and affords hot Earth to carry on Approaches, because they can be easily brought on and carried off: The fame Bags on oe - casion, are used to carry Powder in of which they hold about c Pound a piece.

sacramento.c: SACRAMENTO recipiendo, quod vidual Regis fe, non mar it obit fine licentia Regis, is a Writ or Commifiion to one, for taking of an Oath of the King ’ s Widow, that she may not Marry without the King ’ s Licence.

sacrilegiumsacrilege.c: SACRILEGIUM, Sacrilege, or an Alienation to Lay - men, and to profane or common purposes, of what was given to Religious Persons, and to Pious Uses. Our honest Forefathers were very tender of - incurring the Guilt and Scandal of this Crime. And therefore when the Order of the Knight - Templers was dissolved, their Lands, &c. were all given ro the Knights Hofipitallers of Je - rufalem, for this sacred Reason: Ne in fins ufus erogate contra donatorum voluntatem in alios ufus diflraherentur.

sacrolumbalis.c: SACROLUMBALIS, is a Muscles theThoraXj which with the Dorsi Longijfmus, have their Origi - nation in Common: Externally they are Tendinous as they spring from the Posts rior part of the Spine of the Os Ilium, and Superior Spine of the Sacrum, and all the Spines of the Vertebra of the Loins: In - ternally it arises fleshy, not only from those parts, but from the Transverse Processes of the last na - med Vertebra; whence with direCt Fibres amend - ing before it marches over the last Rib, its divided into z fleshy Bodies; the outermost of which is cal - led Sacrolumbus, whose Fibres ascend directly, and make so many thin Tendons as there are Ribs to whom they are inferred, which are joined with so many Accessory Muscles, arising from each Rib, and united with them, before their Insertions, as they pass over the Superior: And this Order or muitiformed Disposition of it, is continued the whole length of the Thorax, to the third, fourth, fifth and sixth Vertebra of the Neck; which superior part is by Diemerbroeci made a distinct Muscle, and called, Cervicalis defcendens.

sacrumos.c: SACRUM Os: The Os Sacrum is the broadeft of all the Bones of the Back and doth sustain all the other Vertebra: On the inside it is smooth and hollow, on the outside convex and uneven, being of something a triangular shape. In its upper part on each side it is knit firmly to the OJfa Ilia, by an inverting Cartilage. It consists of five or fix Bones, plainly distinguishable in Infants, but more obscurely in grown Persons. These Bones have the Refem - balance of ( and are usually called ) Vertebral for each of them have a Body and Processes, and a large hole to receive the Spinalis Medulla. The Bo - dies of thele differ from those of the other Vcrte - Ira in this rested:; that whereas in those the lower part is always bigger, in these it is the less by which means the uppermost is the biggest, and the - lowest the least.. Their smaller holes which serve for the ingress and egress of the Vessels, differ also from those of the other, in that they are not in their sides, but before and behind -; of which those before are much the larger. As for their Processes, the Oblique can hardly be discerned, except in the first. The Transverse are pretty long, but so uni - ted, that all seem but one. The hinder, or Spines are like those of the Loins, but less, and still the lower the lesser; insomuch that the lowest hath nO Process, but only a round Protuberance. SAFFRON of Gold. See Aurutn Fulminhnsi

saffronofsteelyormars.c: SAFFRON of Steely or Mars. See Crocus Mari tis.

sagittaaconfcllation.c: SAGITTA, a Confcllation in the Northern He - mifphere, confiding of S Stars.

sagittainbotany.c: SAGITTA, in Botany, signifies the upper part of any small Twig, Cyon, or Graft of a Tree.

sagittainmathematicks.c: SAGITTA, in Mathematicks, is the fame as the Versed Sine of any Ark, and is so called by some Writers, because ’ tis like a Dart or Arrow hanging on the Chord of the Ark. See Versed Sind.

sagittalissutura.c: SAGITTALIS Sutura, or Veruculata, is that Su - ture of the Scull, which begins at the Coronal Su - ture, and ends in the Lambdoidal Suture.

sagittarius.c: SAGITTARIUS, is the Ninth, in the Order of the iz Signs of the Tfdiack.. To SIGNER a Moat, is to drain the Water by Subterraneous Conveyances, to the end that Hur - dles laden with Earth, or a Bridge of Buirufhes, may be afterward laid upon the Mud that remains, and the Passage thereby consolidated.

sail.c: SAIL: Every Yard in a Ship hath its proper Sail to it, and it takes its Name from the Yard As the Main - fail, is that which belongs to the Main - yard: The Fore - top Sail, is that which be - longs to the Fore - top - mast Yard, & c. Head Sails, are such as belong to the Fore - mast and Boltfprit: These are used to keep a Ship from the Wind, and to fiat her After Sails, as the Main - mast and Mijfen Sails do keep a Ship to the Wind. Few Ships can steer on a quarter Wind with one Sail, but require a Head Sail and an After Sail both, one to countermand the other: Tho ’ some Ships can Steer with their Main - top Sail only. The Mijfen Sail is cut by the Leech twice as deep as the Mast is long, from the Hounds to the Deck: And the Sprit Sail is of the Depth of the Fore - Sail.

sailing.c: SAILING. See Plain, and Mercator ’ s Sailing.

saker.c: SAKER, a fort of Cannon, is either Extraordi - nary, Ordinary, or leaf Si e.

sakerextraordinary.c: SAKER Extraordinary, is Inches Diameter at the Bore, Pound Weight, Foot long, its Load Pounds, Shot Inches i Diameter, and something more than Pound Weight; its level Range is Paces.

sakerordinary.c: SAKER Ordinary, is a size lesser, Inches and Bore, Foot long, weight, its Charge Pounds of Powder, Bullets Diameter ' Inches, Weight Tounds; level Range c Paces.

sake.c: SAKE K the leaf Si e, is Inches Diameter at the Bore, Pound weight, Foot long, its Load near Pound, Shot Pound weight, and Inches - Diameter.

salamandersblood.c: SALAMANDERS Blood, is a foolish Term that the Chymifts give to the red Vapours, which in Di - stellation of Spirit of Nitre, towards she latter end, do fill the Receiver with red Clouds theyjare the most fix ’ d and strongest part of the Spirit and no - thing but Nitre yields a red Vapouf in Diftilla - tion... '

salarm.c: SAL Arm niacJ, is either Natural, which is found in some Parts of Africa, near the Line; or Artificial, which is made thus: Five parts of Urine, one of Sea Salt, or Sal Gem - ma ?, and half an one of Chimney Soot arc boiled toge together into a Mass, which Mass, being after this put into subliming Pots, over a gradual Fire, it sublimed into the Form of that Salt, which is the common Sal Armoniack. It is purified by Dissolution in Water, Evaporation, ( c. As other Salts. Equal Parts of this Salt, and common Salt de - crepitated, are mingled, and then the Armoniack is fublimedfrom the Mass, which is called, Flowers cf Sal Armoniack - If Instead of Sea Salt, you should use Filings of Steel, the Flowers would be yellow, and they are a little more penetrating than the former.

sal.c: SAL circulatus Paracelf, the fame with the AI - kaheft.

SAL P olychrejlum, is a Preparation of Salt - petre. made by burning equal Parts of it with Sulphur in a Crucible, whereby ’ tis deprived of its Volatile Parts. They give it this Name from the Greeks to u'xj - r -, as being good for many Uses. Tho ’ tis in - deed no very good Medicine, and unless it be very white, ought not to be used. They give it as a Purge, from half a Dram to fix Drams; but there are so many other good Pur - native Medicines, that there is no need of using this.
SAL L of Steel, See Vitriol of Mars.

salprunella.c: SAL Prunella, is only purified Salt - petre, having some of its molt Volatile Parts separated from it, by burning upon it when melted in a Crucible over the Fire, about a th part of its weight of Flour of Brimstone. ’ Tis given to cool and provoke U rine in Fevers and Quinsies; but Salt petre purist - ed three or four Times, is certainly a much better Medicine; for this burning of Sulphur upon it, carries off a good part of the fine and volatile Parts, and instead of opening it, renders it mote fix ’ d. They often adulterate Sal Prunella with Alum, but you may distinguish it by its over whiteness, and glittering too much. This is sometimes cal - led, Lapis, Prunella and Chrystal Mineral.

salvolatileoleofum.c: SAL Volatile Oleofum, or an Aromatic k Volatile Salt is made, by putting to every Ounce of Vola - tile Salt of Sal Armoniack,, distilled with Salt of Tartar, and dulcified with Spirit of Wine, about a Dram and an half of some Aromatick Oil or Ef - fence, drawn from one or more noble odoriferous Vegetables; as Cinnamon, Cloves, Rosemary, Balm, ( c. and after the Spirit and Oil are well stirred and incorporated together, the Volatile Salt and Spirit is drawn off in a Cucurbit. Some mingle all together, vi. the Sal Armoni - ack, Sal Tartari, Spirit of Wine, and the Powder of Cinamon, Cloves, ( c. at first, andjhen distill off the Volatile Salt and Spirit all at once; but the former is the best way. The Sal Volatile Oleofum, is a well known and noble Medicine; ’ twas first invented by Sllvius de la Bee: ’ Tis a great Cephalick and Cordial, and is much beyond any of the Volatile Parts that are not Aromatized.

saliantangle.c: SALIANT Angle, a Term in Fortification. See Angle.

salienttheterminheraldry.c: SALIENT, the Term in Heraldry for a Lion in a leaping Posture, and standing so that his right Fore - foot is in the Dexter chief Point, and his hin - der left Foot in the Sinister base Point of the Ef - scutcheon, by which ’ tis diftinguifhedfrom Rampa ? it. , SILIQUE Law, De terra Salica null portio FI - ' editatis mullcri venial, fed ad virllem Sexttm tot a terra hcereditas perveniat, &c. was an ancient I. aW made by Pharamond King of the Franks; part of which seems to have been borrowed by our Henry the First, in compiling his Laws, as cap.. Qiui hoc secant fecundum Legem Salicam moriatur. S ALI V A, or Spittle, is a Liquor separated by proper Duds ( which they call the Duchts Saliva - les ) from the Glands of the Mouth, as the Part - tides, the Glandule NuSUdna, the Maxillares, this Suhlinguales. ’ Tis probable that the Origin of the Saliva, is from the Arterious Blood; for as the Arteries pour Nutritious Blood into ali other parts, so they do into the Glands also; part of which they convert into their own Nourishment, part is returned by the Veins in the circulation, and part ( vi. of what is serous ) they separate, and bellowing a subacid quality thereupon, make Saliva ( or Spit - tle ) of it. To the Composition whereof ( if not for the Se - pacation of it ) some think a Nervous Juice is con - tributed, the rather because larger and more nu - merous Twigs of Nerves are communicated to the Glands, than to more other parts, which yet have a more exquisite sense than these. But in refutation of this Opinion, the above -, mentioned Dr. Neck alledges this Experiment. That if the Nerve that runs to any Gland, be either hard tied or cut in sunder, yet the Secretion of the Saliva will not thereupon cease, but will on - ly proceed more slowly; which slowness may be attributed not to the want of any constitutive Prin - cipe of the Saliva, so much as to the want of that Motion in the Gland ( that to be sure depends as well upon the Nerves as upon the Pulsation of the Artery ) which is necessary for the quicker dispatch of the Saliva, through or out of the Gland. The manner of the Secretion of the Saliva, is like that of the Liquor of, all other Glands, and proceeds from the Conformity of the Particles of the Liquor to the Pores in the Gland, or the Mouths of the Excretory Vessel. After its Separation, its Motion into and along the Salival Dudts, is much farthered by the Mufcu - lar Motion of each part respectively. Now the Saliva is not to be reputed a meer Ex - cement, for it is believed by all Modern Anato - mists, that it serves for the fathering of the Fer - tentation of Meats in the Stomach, if it be not the main Ferment of it. That it has a fermentative Quality Diemerbroeck, proves by this Experiment: That if a piece of white Bread be chewed and moisten ’ d with much Spittle, and then be mixed with Wheat - paste kneed - ed with warm Water, it will make it ferment. Dr. Neck thinks it is an Universal Ferment for Meats and Drinks, partaking of Divers Qualities ( or Particles ) but of none in any excessive Degree. That it is Acid he demonstrates by this familiar Ob - serration. “ That if when Milk is a boiling, one take a “ Spoonful to taste of, and then presently whilst it “ is moist with the Saliva, put it into the Milk a - “ gain ( Till a boiling ) the Milk will break as if “ some Acid Liquor were mixed with it. That it is endued with a Volatile Salt, he thinks is evident from its curing the Itch, Tetters, ( c. That Oleous Particles are mixed with the acid, he supposes must be concluded from its killing Quick - silver: And whereas it usually becomes frothy in the Mouth, upon its being agitated by the Motion of of the Muscles of the Tongue, and those which move the lower Jaw, and that he thinks proceeds from its being endued with lixivial Salt and Spi - iitous, Oleous and acid Particles ( while the Vo - latine Spirit vanishes. )

salivation.c: SALIVATION, is an Evacuation of Spittle by Salivating Medicines, of which fort principally are Mercurial Preparations.

sally.c: SALLY, in the Art of W ar, is the Term for the i sling out of the Belieged from their Works, and falling upon the Besiegers to cut them off, and to destroy their Works.

salt.c: SALT, the first of the three Hypostatical, but the third of the five Chymical Principles: Its two Effen - till Properties seem to be, Dijfolubility in Water, and a pretty Pungent Sapor, being an alive income - buftible Substance; they fay it gives all Bodies their Confidence, and preserves them from Corrup - tion, and occasions all the Variety of Tasts. There are three Kinds of Salts: Fix ’ d, Volatile, and EJfential. The Fix ’ d Salt is thus drawn: The Matter is first calcined, and then the Ashes are boil ’ d in a good deal of Water, that the Salt may be the bet - ter dissolved: After this the Solution is filtrated, and all the Moisture evaporated, and then the Salt remains in a dry form at the bottom of the Vessel. This Fix ’ d Salt so drawn, is called a Lixivious Salt, because a kind of Lixivium, or Lye, was made of the Allies of the Body calcined. Volatile Salt, is that which is drawn from the Bodies or Parts ( chiefly ) of Animals, and from some fermented, or rather purified parts of Vege - tables: It rises quick and easily, and is the most Volatile of any Bodies so called. The EJfential Salt is drawn from the Juice of Plants by Chrystallization: How, fee EJfential Salt. Mr. Boyle reckons three other Kinds of Salts, viz. Acid, Vrinous, and Lixiviate: See those Words. And he discovers whether any Liquor contains an Acid Salt, or no, by dropping some of it on Sy - up of Violets, for then it will turn it red; but if it turn it green, it is either of an ‘ Urinous or Lixi - piate Nature: To distinguish which, he drops some of it into a Solution of Sublimate, made in common Water j then if a white or milky colour be produced, he concludes it to belong to the Tribe of Vrinous Salts; but if it produce a yellow or orange colour, he judges it to be of a Lixiviate Nature.
SALT; a Ship is Walt, when file hath not her due Ballast, i. e. not enough to enable her to bear her Sails.

SALT, Sir If. Newton ( hews that Salt is com - pounded of a dry Earth, and an Aqueous Acid ] on - ed together by Attraction, and that Earth can ’ t be turned into Salt, unless by the mixture of so much of an Acid, as may make it capable of a Diffoliati - on in Water. And as it is owing to the Force of Gravity, that the Sea flows round the more denie and ponderous Globe of the Earth, so will the Principle of Attraction ( fee that word ) occasions that the Aqueous Acid may flow round the more compass Terrestrial Particles, andfocompofe the Particle of Salt. For by no other way ( faith he ) can we account for Acid, being in place of a Mean, between Earth and common Water, in order to ren - der Salt dissolvable in the latter. And as in the great Terraqueous Globe, the most Denie Bodies will by their Gravity subside in Water, and do al - ways tend towards the Centre of the Globe, so in the Particles of Salt, the most Dense Matter al ways endeavours to get to the Centre of the Par - ticle. So that a Particle of Salt is a kind of Cha - os, dertfe, hard, dry, and Earthy at the Centre, but rare, moist, soft, and watery at the Surface. And hence it appears, Salts are of so durable and lading a nature as they are; for they can scarce be destroy ’ d, unless the Aqueous Parts be either drawn off by a great force, or by Putrefa & ion and a moderate Heat, permitted to get down into. the Occult Meatus, or Pores of the Central Earthy Parts, and at last dissolve them by cutting them into small pieces. If Salt in a small quantity be dissolved in a great deal of Water, the Saline Particles, tho ’ fpecifi - cally heavier, will not subside, but diffuse them - selves equally throughout ail the Water, and ren - der it equally Salt in all places; which seems to shew that the Parts of the Salt do mutually recede one from another, and endeavour to expand rhem - selves all manner of ways, and to part and sea - rate rate as far as the space will, permit: And this En - devour ihews that they have some kind of Bf sel - ling Force, by which they fly from one another, or at least are more strongly attraRed by the Farts of; the Water, than by one another. For as all Bo - dies ascend in Water, which do gravitate less to - wards the Earths Centre than the Parts of the Wa - ter; so all the Particles of Salt which sworn iri ( Water, and are less attracted by any one Particle of Salt, than they are by the Water it self, must necessarily recede from that Particle, and give place to the Water, which is more forcibly attrap - d: ed. When a Liquor impregnated with Salt, hath its Moisture so far Evaporated by Heat, that a Pelli - cle,. Cuticle, or little Skin appears upon its Sur - face, if thenitbe fet to cool, the Salt will shoot in - to Chrystals, which will be of some regular Fi - gure From whence it appears, that the Saline Particles before their Concretion, were placed in the Liquor in some certain Order, and at equal Di - stances or Intervals; and consequently that they did aR one upon another by some kind of Force, which is equal at equal Intervals, and unequal at un - equal Distances. For the Supposition of some such Force will occasion rheir being disposed every where into such Orders; but without it they would ramble about and be dispersed, perfectly ir - regularly in the Fluid. In the French Memoirs of the Academy of Sci - ences for the Year, there is a Method, by Mr. Homberg, of finding the exadfc quantity of the Volatile Acid Salt that any Liquor contains. ( z. ) Their way of making Salt at Nant - vtyche in Chefkire, is thus ( faith Mi. fity ) The Sait - spring, or as they call it the Brine - it is near the River, and is so plentiful, that were all the W ater boiled out that it will afford, it is thought it would yield Salt enough for all England. The Brine - pits belong not all to one Lord; but some have one Lead - walling some two, three, four, &c. A Lead - walling, is the Brine of Hours boiling for one House: Two hundred and sixteen Lead - wallings, or thereabouts, belong to all the Owners of the Pits; No Tradesman, Batchellor, or Widower, can Rent more than Lead - wallings. They have Sworn Officers chosen Annually, which they call Occupiers of PVallingj whose Du - ty it is to fee equal Dealing between Lord and Tenant, and all Persons concerned, to appoint how many Houses shall work at a time ( which is at most to appoint a Crier ( when Salt is to be made; ) to make Proclamation so, that all Parties concerned may put to their Fires at the fame time, and so also when they shall cease; which is at a determinate Hour: And he that doth not leave off then hath his Salt spoiled, by throwing Dirt, &c. into it. In the Town are about Houses, and every House hath Pans, which the Officers are to fee must be allexadly of the fame Measure. The Salt Water taken out of the Brine - pit, in boiling Hours will be Evaporated, and boiled, up into Salt. When the Liquor is more than like - warm, they take Strong - ale, BuilockVblood, an Egg - shell full, the White of one Egg, and of Ale a Pint i This Mixture is put into a Pan of Gallons, or there - abouts; the Whites of Eggs, and the Blood serve to Clarlfie the Brine, by railing the Scum which S A L they take off just. upon the boiling of the Pans, - otherwise it boils in apd spoils the Salt. The order the Blood is the better, c & teris paribus, when the Liquor boils too fast, they don't put in, any Blood, but allay it with Brine that hath been before boil - ed and drain ’ d from its Sait. Crude Brine, they fay, will diminiffi their Salt; and they fay, the Ale serves to harden the Cor of the Salt - After one hours boiling, the Brine will begin to Com, or Granulate. Then they take a fmallquan tity of clear Ale, of which they sprinkle about an Egg - shell full into the Pan, but if you put in too much Ale, it will make the Liquor boil over the Pan; a little while before they put in the last Ale, they cause the Pfan to boil as fast as they can; but ' after that Very gently, till the Salt be almost dry. For they do not Evaporate quite, adficcitatem, but leave,, or,., Quarts of Brine in the Pan, left the Salt should burn, and stick to its sides. The Brine thus sufficiently Boiled and Evapo - rated, they take out the Salt and pour it into Co - nical Baskets ( which they call Barrows ) and in them let the Water drain from it an hour, more or less, and then fet it to dry in the Hot - house be - hind the Furnace. A Barrow containing Pecks, is fold there for Pence. ' Out of Pans of Gallons they expe & y Pecks of Salt, Winchefler Measure. The House in which the Salt is boiled, they call the lijtcbe - house - the Vessel whereinto theBrine is by Troughs conveyed from the Brine - pit, is cal - led the Ship. ’ Tis raised out of the Pit by a Pump. Between the Furnace and the Chimney - tunnels, which convey the Smoak, is their Hot - house, where they fet their Salt to dry; along the Floor where - of run Funnels from the Furnaces, almost Parallel to the Horizon, and then they arise Perpendicularly; in these the Flame and Smoak running a - long from the Furnaces, heat the Room by the way. At Droitwyche in Warcejlerfhire ] the Salt is boi - led in HialldW Leaden - pans. They first put in the Salt - water out of the Brine - pits, and theft after an hours boiling they fillip the Pan with the Water that drains from: the Salt let to dry in the Barrows, and after a second hours boiling, they fill up the Pans again with the fame. In five hours boiling the Pan grows dry, and then they take out the Salt - In hours they boil out Pans, and then draw out the Ashes; after which they put in the White of an Egg to make the Scum arise ( which is partly Dust and Ashes, falling into the Pan when they are taking out the Ashes. j The Scum they takeoff with a Scummer, and after hours they begin to take out the Salt, and once in hours they take out a Cake which sticks to the bottom of the Pan, and which they call Clod - Salt, o - otherwise the Pan would melt. They use there new - ther Blood nor Ale, and the Salt made there is ex - traordinary fine and white. In Lancafoire they make Salt of Sea - Sand, thus. They pare off in dry Summer - weather, the upper part of the Sand in the Flats and Wallies / which are cover ’ d at Full - Sea, and bate when the Tide is out ) and lay it up on great heaps. Of this Sand they put into Troughs, bored with holes at the bottom, a sufficient quantity, and then - pouring Water upon it, they make a Lee or Lixivium, and the Water draining thro ’ the Sand, A z carries carries the Salt with it down into Veffeis placed SALT - SILVER, was one Penny, formerly underneath. As long as this Liquor is strong e - j paid at the Feast of St. Martin, by the Servile Te - nought bear an Egg, they keep pouring more nants to their Lord, by way of Commutation, for the Service of carrying their Lord ’ s Salt from Mar - ket to his Lardar. saltcommon.c: SALT Common, its Spirit how drawn, fee Spi - rit of Salt. Mr. Boyle proves this Principle producible by Art, as well as other. See Sceptical Chymist, Part ult. p. i.

saltofsaturn.c: SALT of Saturn, Saccharuni Saturni, or Sugar of Lead, is the Body of that Metal opened and red - ced to the Form of a Salt by distilled Vinegar. ' Thus any of the Calxes of Lead, as suppose Ce - ruse, is powdered, and distilled Vinegar is poured upon it to four Fingers height above the Matter, an Ebullition will follow, but without ' sensible heat it must be digested in a Sand - heat, two or three Days, and stirred often: Then pour off the Liquor bv Inclination, and digest more distilled Vinegar with the Ceruse, and more after that, till you have dis - solved about half the Matter, mix all the Impreg - nations together in an Earthen or Glass Vessel; evaporate the Matter in a Sand - heat, till a small Skin or Pellicle, begin to arise upon the Surface - after which, place the Vessel in a cool place, there will appear white Chrystals: Take them oat, and evaporate again as before, and let the Vessel to cool to gain the reft of the Salt: Continue this till you have gotten ail; then dry the Chrystals in the Sun and keep them in a Glass, ’ Tis chiefly used out - wardly for Diseases of the Skin; but sometimes ’ tis given inwardly, from two to four Grains at a Dole in Quinsies, &c.

saltofsulphur.c: SALT of Sulphur, a Preparation in Chymistry improperly so called, since it is only a Sal Poly cbm stum impregnated with Spirit of Sulphur, and then reduced to an Acid Salt by Evaporation of all the Moisture. Some fay this is a great Febrifuges

saltoftartar.c: SALT of Tartar, is made either by powdering what remains in the Retort after the Distillation of Tartar; or else by calcining bruited Tartar wrap - ed up in a Paper, till it turn white. Either of these must have a great deal of hot Water poured upon them to make a Lixivium, then the Liquor is fil - trated and evaporated in a Sand - heat ", till the Fix ’ d Salt remain at the bottom of the Vessel. This is the Alkali, or Fix ’ d Salt of Tartar. If it be ex - posed to the Air a few Days in an open Vessel in a Cellar, or some such moist place, if will melt or run into a Liquor; and this the Chymist s call Oyl of Tartar per Deliquum. SA. LTIER, the Name of one of the Ordina - ries in Heraldry, of the Form of St. Andrews Cross. They tell you, that anciently ’ twas the Figure of an Engine, Which being stuck full of Pins, was used in the Scaling of the Walls of a Besieged Place. Pearl a Saltier Puby, the Coat of my Lord Macclesfield. The Saltier is often counter - changed with the Field and some - times quarterly quartered, c. SA. LV A guardian, is a Security given by the King to a Stranger, bearing the Violence of some of his Subjects, for seeking his Right by Course of Law. r SALVATELLA, is that Vein which from the Veins of the Arm is terminated in the little Fin - ger.

sanativewaters.c: SANATIVE Waters, are the Mineral Waters of any kind, such as the Chalybiate ones of Tunbridge, the Vitriolic Ig ones of Epfom, c.

sandaracha.c: SANDARACHA, is by some Chymifts the Term for red Arfenick; ’ tis called also pe argal. X

sanguification.c: SANGUIFICATION, is the turning of the Chyle into Blood; which is performed in all the parts of the Body, and not as the Ancients image - ned in some particular parts, as the Heart, Li - ver, &c.

sanguinetheheralds.c: SANGUINE, the Heralds term for the Colouf usually called Murry, being made of Lake, with a little Spanijlo Brown; ’ tis represented in Engraving by Hatches like Purpure t ’ Tis mostly used in the Coats of Knights of the Bath. When ’ tis born by Nobles, ’ tis called Sardonyx; and in the ' Coats of Soveraign Princes they call it Dragons Tail.

sanies.c: SANIES, is a thick and bloody Pus, or Matter issuing out of a Wound or Sore.

saphena.c: SAPH ENA, is the Vein of the Leg, of Crural Vein, it goes down under the Skin of the Thigh and Leg, accompanied with a Nerve which loses it self at the inner Ankle; it turns towards the up - per part of the Foot, where it gives several Bran - ches, of which some go to the great Toe. SCAPHA - S A R

saphatum.c: SAPHATUM, is a dry Scurf in the Head. See j Achor. Blanchard.

saponea.c: SAPONEA, is a Lambitive made of Almonds. Blanchard.

saporificparticles.c: SAPORIFIC Particles, are such as by their Action on the Tongue occasion that Sensation which We call Taste or Sapor. The manner of which, see in Table.

saporous.c: SAPOROUS, are such Bodies as are capable of yielding sore kind of Taste when touch ’ d with our Tongue; but those that afford no Taste, are called Insipid.

sarcocele.c: SARCOCELE, is a kind of Rupture, which consists in a fleshy Excrefence of the Testicles. Blanchard.

sarcolpiplocele.c: SARCOLPIPLOCELE, a fleshy Rupture, or Promberancy of the Omentum, either about the Navel, or in the Cods.

sarcoma.c: SARCOMA, is a fleshy Excrescence in the No - ftrils, and chiefly in the lowest part of the Nose, where it is fleshy, without any shape, but like the proud Flesh of an Ulcer. Blanchard.

sarcomphalum.c: SARCOMPHALUM, is a fleshy Excrefence of the Navel. Blanchard.

sarcoticks.c: SARCOTICKS, are those Medicines which fill up Wounds with Flesh, such as by their moderate Heats, and cleansing Qualities keep Wounds and Ulcers free from Filth, and preserve the Natural Temper of the Parts, so that the Aliment easily supplies the Solution of the Parts. Blanchard.

sardonianorsardoniclaughter.c: SARDONIAN, or Sardonic Laughter, is an Involuntary Laughter, or rather a Convuldve Di - ftortion of the Muscles of the Mouth, in which the Patient appears to Laugh.

sarrasininfortification.c: SARRASIN, in Fortification, is a kind of Port - cullice, otherwise called a Herse, which is hung with a Cord over the Gate of a Town, or For - tress, and let fall in case of a Surprize.

sartoriusamuscle.c: SARTORIUS, a Muscle of the Leg, which receives this Denomination from the Use Taylors make of it, in bringing one Leg and Thigh over the other, to fit cross - leg ’ d. It is also called Lon - gifiimus Femora, it exceeding the reft of the Muf - cles of that Part in length; and Fafcialis from its palling over the Muscles of the Thigh and Leg like a Swathe. It ariseth sharp and fleshy from the fore - part of the Spine of the Os Ilium, close by the Mem - branofus, and descending obliquely inwards above the Mujculus Rectus, and Vastus Interims, and over part of the Tibiceps, of an equal breadth or Thick - ness, meets with the Gracialis below the middle of the Thigh internally, and descending with it be - comes Tendinous in its Passage over the Internal and Inferior Head of the Thigh - bone, ( under a strict Inclosure of the Fascia Lata ) and is inserted four Fingers breadth below the superior part of the Tibia internally: Its Use is declared above.

satellitesbyastronomers.c: SATELLITES, by Astronomers, are taken for those Planets who are continually, as it were waiting upon, or revolving about other Planets as the Moon may be called the Satellite of the Earth and the reft of the Planets, Satellites of the Sun. But the Word is chiefly used for the new discovered small Planets, which make their Revolution about Saturn and Jupiter.

They were first discovered by Gallilaus, by the help of the Telescope. And the Distance of this Satellite from the Centre of Saturn, to be about Diameters of the king, or of th q Globe and the place where it moves, to differ little or nothing from that of the king; that is to fay, interfering the Orb of Saturn with an Angle t Degrees, so as to be nearly Parallel to the Earths Equator. The Periodical Times of the Satellites of Saturn, ac - cording to Mr. Caffini, are of the First Days. i Hours. Minutes l Second il Third Fourth l n Fifth SATURN; The Proportion of the Body of Saturn to our Earth, is about to. The Periodical Time of Saturn ’ s Revolution a - bout the Sun, is in the space of Years or Days. The Semi - diameter of Saturn s Orbit, is almost ten times as big as that of the Magnus Orhis, and therefore is of English Miles. According to Mr. Caffini, Saturn ’ s greatest Di - stance from the Earth is, his mean Di - stance, and his least Distance Se - mi - diameters of the Earth. Mr. Hugens found the Inclination of the Ring of Saturn to the Ecliptick, to be an Angle of De - grees. Mr. A out asserts, That the remote Distance of Saturn from the Sun doth not hinder but that there is Light enough to fee clear there, and more than in our Earth in Cloudy Weather. In an Observation which Caffini made June, of a precise Conjunction between a Fixt Star, and one of Saturn ’ s Satellites, he faith, That with his Foot Glass, he could plainly see the Shadow of Saturn ’ s Globe to be in part oval upon the hinder part of his Ring. The Diameter of Saturn at the time of this Observation, appear - ed to be Seconds. The Diameter of Saturn to that of his Ring is as to. And the Diameter of the Ring seen from the Sun, would be but ". and therefore the Diame - ter of Saturn seen from thence would be but ". as Mr. Flamftead found by measuring it. But Mr. Fiemon thinks it ought rather to be accounted but as " or ". because he supposes the Globe of Saturn to be a little dilated by the unequal Re - frangibility of Light. Capt. Halley, in his, Preface to the Catalogue of the Southern Stars, says, He found Saturn to move flower than the Astronomical Tables rere - sent him. The Distance of Saturn from the Sun, is about times as great as that of our Earth from him; and therefore that Planet will not have above the both part of the Influence of the Sun which we have; and consequently cannot be Habitable by such Creatures as live on our Globe, unless there J ome utlknow way of communicating Meat to L Dr Greg / y in his Astronomy, makes the Semi - j diameter of the Ring of Saturn to that of the'Pia - net, as to. and the Interstice between the Plain - ner and the Ring, is the Breadth of the Ring. Howthe Ring of Saturn will appear in all parts of the Orbit of the Planet, to an Eye placed at the Sun, or at the Earth, the fame Learned Aftrono - mer mews in his Aflron. Phy. & Geometr. LiR IV. Prop.,. If an Eye were placed in Saturn, the Diameter of the Sun would appear times less than it doth t jULa m anc conCequendy, his Disk, Light and Heat will be there times less. Saturn s Year is almost of ours, but the length of his Day is yet uncertain, because the time of his Revolution round his Axis is not yet known; But Mr. Hugens judges they are not longer than the Days in Jupiter. That great Astronomer supposed the Axis of Sal turn to be perpendicular to the Plane of his Ring, and of the Orbits of the Satellites: If so, then there will be the fame Position of the Equator and Poles, fas to the Fixt Stars ) as there is in our Earth. The lame Pole Star and the Fixt Stars will appear to Rife and Set after the fame manner, in the lame Latitudes. There is a vast Inequality in the Length of the Day in several parts of this Pla - net; and as great a diversity of Summer and Win - ter j which depends on the Quantity of the Incli - nation of the Plane cf the Equator, to the Plane of the Orbit of Saturn round the Sun j which Hugens makes to be Degr. which is almost - f more than in our Earth; where yet the differences and va - piety of Seasons and Weather are very sensible. For in Saturn, in the Latitude of Degr. the longest Day will have no Night at all, and the longest Night will have no Day. And the two Frigid Zones will be each of them gri broad, at least to times as large as the whole Surface of our Earth. The. Eye thus placed, will be able to dis - corn none of the Planets but Jupiter, which will appear always to accompany the Sun, and never to be from him above gr. The Parallax of the Sun in Saturn, is but ", and therefore Insensible but the Parallaxes of all his Moons or Satellites, are very considerable, and therefore their Distant - ices from him will be easily computable. But what an Eye placed in Saturn would most admire, is the Ring of that Planet the only thing of that nature that is discovered. in any of the Pla - nets. T ho. Kfpler in his Epitome Aflr on. Coper nic. Lib.. p., and after him Capt. Halley in his Enquiry into the Causes of Variation of the Nee - dles Variation j Phil. Trans N, do suppose our Earth may be composed of several Crufts or Shells one within another, and concentrical to each other. And if. so, then ftis pofljble the Ring of Sa - turn may be the Fragment or remaining Ruins of his formerly exterior Shell, the reft of which is broken and fallen down upon the Body of the Pla - net. ’ And if Saturn ever had such a Shell round it, its Diameter would then have appeared as big to an Eye at the Sun, as that of Jupiter doth now, when seen from thence. Since the outward Margin of the Ring is distant from Saturn of Saturn ’ s Semi - diameter, this can - not be seen at the distance of Degr. from Sa - turn ’ s Equator fin whose Plane the Ring is placed, ) Therefore a Spectator placed in a Latitude higher than that, can never see the Ring at all; so that there S A U s c there is a Zone of almost broad toward either Pole, to whom this famous Ring can never appear. And as the Spe & tor flail move nearer the Pole, first one, then the second Satellite, next the third and fourth; and when he is come within one De - gree of the Pole, even the fifth Satellite cannot be seen, unless by Refraction; and in the Wintertime, neither Sun, Moon, nor any Planet, will be there visible, unless perhaps a Comet, If the Eye be supposed to be placed in the Equa - tor of Saturn, or in the Zone nearly adjoining, it can never fee those Stars that are in or very near the Equator, nor any one of the Satellites; because the Ring will always hide them; and then at the Equinoxes it cannot see the Sun; and if it were any where else placed, it could not then see the Ring; because neither of its Faces will then appear ill - minated by the Sun. The Breadth of this Ring his hard to determine from our Earth, because its Thickness is lo frnall: But Mr. Hugens makes it to be about six hundred German Miles. For one half of Saturn's Year, vig. Y ars of ours ) only one Face of the Ring Will be en - lightened by the Sun: Whence the Inhabitants which may be supposed to live in that Hemisphere, to which this Face of the Ring is turned, or to whom it is Summer, will fee that part of the Ring which is above their Horizon, shining faintly by Day, ( a. our Moon doth when the Sun is above out Horizon ) but brighter and stronger by Night, as our Moon doth in the Sun ’ s absence: And af - ter Sun - let, the Eastern part of this enlightened Arch will fall within the Shadow of Saturn; which Shade will ascend as Night comes cn, and at Mid - night will be at the highest; and then will descend again towards the Western part of the Ring, ac - cording as the Sun comes more and more to the Eastward. This enlightened Ark will always hew how to describe a Meridian Line; for a Plane perpend - cular to the Horizon, and palling thorough the Vertex of the Ark, will be in the true Meridian, To an Eye placed any where without, and at less than distance from the Equator, this en - lightened Ark of the Ring will appear Concave as well as Convex, like a kind of Furnace or Vault, riling above the Horizon: But to an Eye at more than ', and less than Degrees distant from the Equator, the hollow or concave Part will not be visible; but there will appear a brightilh Body arising as it were out of the Ground, and contigu - ous to the Horizon. For the other half of Saturn s Year, while the Sun declines towards the depressed Pole, or during the Years Winter, the Ring will not be visible, as having not that Face Illuminated which is ob - verted to the Spectator ’ s Eye; but however will render it self sensible, by covering from the Sight, such Stars and Parts of the Heavens as are oppo - site to it, or apparently behind it. The Shade of the Ring alio will be extended more and more to - wards the nearer Po'e; so that to an Eye placed any where within the aforesaid space, the Sun, when he attains such a certain Declination, will, appear to be covered or eclipsed just at Noon, and then strait to emerge out of the Shadow. The next Day, the like Phenomenon iii happen, but the Eclipse will begin sooner, and will be over la - ter: And these Meridian Eclipses will daily en - creale in their duration, until the middle of Win ter and then they will decrease again gradually till at last they will come to nothing again - vi When the Sun returning from the Tropick, hath the fame Declination as he had when these MerL dional Eclipses began. And this will happen, if any Eye be placed ins any Latitude greater than or Degrees; but if in a Latitude less than this, when the Meridian Darkness is of the greatest duration, the Sun will suddenly appear just in the Meridian, and then I ftraitway will be Eclipsed again. The next Day, there will appear the like lort of Light, but it will last longer; and this Meridian Light ni grow still longer and longer induration, till Midwinter, and then ( like the Darkness above - mentioned ) it will be continually decreasing, untfi it quite dilap pear. And from hence ’ ris plain, that there is the greatest difference between Summer and Winter in the Globe of Saturn, of all the other Planets; and this both on the account of the long duration of each, and the great declination of the Sun from the Equator; and - also, by reason of these Meridio - nal Darknefles in the Winter, arising from the Rings Eclipsing the Sun. Gregor. Aftr. Phy. Geom. Lib.. Prop.. p..

sausage.c: SAUSAGE, is a long piece of Cloth, the sides whereof are iewed in form of a Gut, as large as to contain a Tennis Bali, It is dipt in Pitch or Tar, and filled with Powder, on purpose to serve as a Train to fet Fire to Mines, Fougades, or Bomb - Chests. Two of these S aufages are com - monly applied to every Mine, to the end that if one Ihould fail, the other may take effeCt,

saucissons.c: SAUCISSONS, are a fort of Faggots made of great Boughs of Trees bound together in the mid - dle and at both ends. Their use is much the fame with the Bavins or frnall Faggots, vi. to console - date the Way for Carriages, to make Traverses or Parapets in Ditches full of Water,

saver.c: SAVER default, in Law, is Word for Word to excuse a Default in Court, comes afterwards and alledges a good Cause why he did it, as Imprison - ment at the fame time, or such like.

scaladoe.c: SCALADOE, is the mounting of the Wall of a Fortify ’ d Town or Castle, with Scaling Ladders.

scale.c: SCALE of the Gamut, or Afufical Scalet is a kind of Diagram, confiding of certain Lines and Spaces drawn to shew the several Degrees, whereby a Na tural or Artificial Voice or found may either ascend or descend. The Name thereof is taken from the Greek. Let - ter Gamma, which Guido Aretinus, who reduced the Greek. Scale into this Form, plac ’ d at the bot - tom, to signifie from whence it was derived; so that ever since, this Scale or Gamut, hath been taken for the Ground - work or first Foundation of all Musick, both Vocal and Instrumental. But there were three different Scales in use a - long the Ancients which had their Denominati - ons from the three several forts of Musick, vi. The Diatonical, Chromatical, and Enharmonical. Which fee.

scaleni.c: SCALENI, are three Muscles of the Thorax, so called from their Figure, having three, unequal Sides. . Scalenus Primus, which arises fleshy from the Fore - part of the second, third, and fourth Trans - verse Processes of the Vertebrae of the Neck; and j descending obliquely forwards, becomes Tendi - nous at its Insertion to the first Rib: The Axil - lay Nerves pass between this and the following Muscles. Its Use is to draw the Superior Rib, to gether with the reft, upwards in Inspiration. . Scalenus Secundus, this ( firings fiefhy from the second, third, fourth, and fifth Transverse Pro - ceases of the Vertebra of the Neck, laterally, ( like the former, ) in its descent, it becomes thin and tendinous, marching over the first Rib to its In - ferticn in the second, and sometimes to the third. S G A . Scalenus fertius, this has its beginning neaf the former, from the fame Tranverfe Processes of the Vertebra of the Neck; as also from the fifth and sixth of those Processes, and is soon Inferred to the first Rib.

scalprum.c: SCALPRUM; a Surgeon ’ s Rafping and Scra - king Iron, with which he scrape rotten Bones.

scamilliimpares.c: SCAMILLI Impares, in Architecture, are cer - tain Blocks or occ ’ s which serve to elevate the reft of the Members oflmy Column or Statue, which was placed before the Horizon, ( i. e. ) be - death the Projedtures of the Stylobata Cornices, and, other Saillies and will easily be conceived by con - sideling the Pedestals of Statues, which do well represent them. SG AMNUM Hippocratis, Hippocrates ’ s Bench, is an Instrument of fix Ells long: ' Tis used in setting of Bones.

scan.c: SCAN D ALU M " Magnatum, in Law, is the special Name of a Wrong done to any high Per - nonage of the Land, as Prelates, Dukes, Earls, Barons, and other Nobles; as alio of the Chan - cellar, Treasurer, Clerk of the Privy - Seal, Steward of the Houle, Justice of one Bench or ocher, and other great Officers of the Realm, by falle News or Meffages, whereby Debates and Discords be - twixt them and the Commons, or any Scandal to their Persons might arise; and hath given Name to a Writ granted to recover Damage there - upon.

scapha.c: SCAPHA feu Linter, is the Inner Rim of the Ear.

scaphoides.c: SCAPHOIDES, is the third Os Tarfi in the Foot; ’ ns joined to the Ancle - Bone, and the three - hinder Bones. Tis called alio Os Naviculare, from some resemblance it has to a Boat.

scapulatheshoulder.c: SCAPULA, the Shoulder - blade, a broad train - gular Bone, with Processes; ’ tis very thin in the middle, but grows thicker about the Processes.

scapularisexternalandinternal.c: SCAPULARIS, External and Internal, are two little Veins so called, of which the former arises from the Alufcles covering the Scapulae. and the latter, from the Alufcles which possess the cavity of the Scapula:.

scapus.c: SCAPUS, is the term in Botany for the strait Stalk or Shaft of a Plant, ( landing upright like a Pillar or Column.

scarfed.c: SCARFED, in the Sea - Carpenters Language, is the fame as Pieced, or fastened or joined in: Thus they fay the Stem of a Ship is Scarfed into her Keel; and they imply by it, That the two Pieces are shaped away flantmg, so as to join with one another close and even; which they call Wood and Wood.

scarification.c: SCARIFICATION; ’ tis an Xncifibn of the Skin with a Pen knife or Lancet. This is done either with or without Cupping - Glasses without Cupping Gaffes, sf there beany Mortification or Gangrene, because the separation is by no means to be hastened i with Cupping - Glasses, if there be a necessity to take away Blood.

scarpinfortification.c: SCARP, in Fortification, is the Foot of the Rampart - Wall, or the sloping of the Wall from the bottom of the Work, to the Cordon on the side of the Moat SCARPS, I S c I

scarpe.c: SCARPE, a term in Heraldry, probably derived from the French EJcharpe, Signifying the Scarfe which Military Commanders wear for Ornament. It is born some thing like a Battoon sinister, but is broader than it, and is continue - ed out to the Edges of - the Field; whereas the Battoon is cut off at each end. He beareth Argent a Scarpe Azure.

scelotyrbe.c: SCELOTYRBE, is a wand ring Pain in the Legs, proceeding chiefly from the Scurvy. Hence the Water proper for this Distemper, is called Aqua, Scelotyrbitis. Blanchard.

scenography.c: SCENOGRAPHY, in PerftpeSliv e, the Sceno - graphicli appearance of any Figure, Body, or Build - ing, is that Side that declines from, or makes Am gles with that strait Line imagined to pass through the two outward convex Points of the Eyes, gent - rally called by Workmen, the Return of a fore - right Sidej and differs from the Orthographic ] Ap - pearance in this, That the latter represents the Side of a Body or Building as it is seen, when the Plain of theGIals Hands parallel to that Side: ButScewo - grapy represents it as it seems through a Glass, not parallel to that Side. In Architecture and Fortification, Scenography is the manner of delineating the several parts of a Building or Fortress, as they are represented in Perspective.

sceptick.c: SCEPTICK, is the term for a Person who main - tains there is nothing Certain, and no real Know - ledge at all to be had; but that a Man ought to Doubt of, and Disbelieve every thing.

scheme.c: SCHEME, is the Representation of any Geometrical or Astronomical Figure or Problem, by Lines sensibly to the Eye; and these are otherwise called Diagrams.

scetica.c: SCETICA fehris, is opposed to the HeCtick Fever, becauSe. it is Seated mostly in the Blood, and is easily cured; but the Hedtick Fever is fixed in the, very Habit of the Body, and not to be remove ’ d without great difficulty. Blanchard -

schirrusandschirroma.c: SCHIRRUS, and Schirroma, is a hard, livid Swelling, that refills the touch, and is without Pain. Blanchard.

sciaticathegout.c: SCIATICA, the Gout in or about the Hip Bone.

science.c: SCIENCE, is Knowledge founded upon, or ac - quir ’ d by clear, certain, and Self - evident Princi - ples.

sciography.c: SCIOGRAPHY, is the Art of Shadows or Dyal - ing. AlSo in Architecture, this Word is Sometimes taken for the Draught of a Building cut in its Length or Breadth, to shew the Inside of it; as also the Thickness of the Walls, Vaults, Floors, Timber - works, &c.

sciothericumtelefcopium.c: SCIOTHERICUM Telefcopium, is an Horizontal Dyal, with a Telescope adapted for observing the true Time both by Day and Night, to regulate and adjust Pendulum Clocks, Watches, and other Time - keepers; Invented by the Ingenious Mr. Mo - lyneux, who hath published a Book with this Title, which contains an Accurate Description of this In - strument, and all its Uses and Applications.

scire.c: SCIRE facias, is a Writ Judicial, most com - monly to call a Man to shew cause to the Court whence it Issues, why Execution of a Judgment palled, should not be made out. This Writ is not granted until a Year and a Day be elapsed after a Judgment given. Scire facias, upon a Fine, lies not but within the fame time after the Fine levied, otherwise it is the fame with the Writ of Habere fa - cias feijinam.

sclerophthalmy.c: SCLEROPHTHALMY, it is hard Blearedness of the Eyes, accompanied with Pain; a flow mo - tion of the Eyes, with redness and dryness. Blan - chard.

sclerotica.c: SCLEROTICA, or hardening Medicines, are Such as unite the Parts more firmly amongst themselves; and that either by dissipating the thin and Soft Pans, or else Sometimes by retaining them; the first by hardening the Matter into a Schirrus by too hot Medicines; the latter is done when the Part affected acquires a Hardness, by cooling and astringent Medicines, Such are Scngrcen, Night - Jhade, Purflane, and heater - Leiitils. Therefore these Sclerotic / Medicines are either Healing, orelfe Cooling and Astringent. Blanchard.

scoliasis.c: SCOLIASIS, is a distortion of the Back - Bone to one or t ’ other side.

scloopomach.c: SCLOOPOMACH / ORION, is a Chirurgeon ’ s Knife, with which Wounds of the Thorax are wi - dened; ’ ris used also in opening larger Swellings; as also in opening the Abdomen.

sconces.c: SCONCES, are small Forts built for Defence of fomePafs, River, or other Place. Sometimes they are made regular of four, five, or fix Bastions; others of Smaller Dimensions fit for Passes, or Rivers, and likewise for the Field, which are . Triangles with half Bastions, which may be all of equal Sides, or they may be Something un - equal. However it be, divide the Sides of the Triangle into two equal Parts, one of these three Parts will fet off the Capitals, and the Gorges, and the Flanks being at Right Angles with the Sides, make half of the Gorge. . Square with half Bastions, whose Sides may be betwixt ioo and Feet; and let. one third of the Side let off the Capital and the Gorges; but the Flank ( which raise at Right - Angles to the Side ) rust be but one half of the Gorge or Capital,, that is on the sixth part of the side of the Square. . Square with half Bastions and Tong. . Long Squares. . Star Redoubt of four Points. . Star Redoubt of five or fix Points. . Plain Redoubts, which are either small or great: The small are fit for Court of Guards in the Trenches, and may be a Square of Foot to. The middle fort of Redoubts may have their Sides from to Feet the Great ones from to Feet square. The Profile ( that is, the Thickness and Height of the Brest - works ) to be let on these leveral Works, and the Ditches, are alterable and under - tain: for Sometimes they are uSed in Approaches, and then the WideneSs of the Brest - work at the Bottom may be or Foot, Inward Height and Outward Foot; the Ditch may be or Feet, and Sometime; and for the Sioaps to be wrought according to the nature of the Earth; Sumenmes they may be made or Feet Wide at the Bottom, and the Height of,, or Feet, and Said to have two or three Ascents to rife to the Pa - tapet j the Ditch may be or Feet Wide, and or Deep and sometimes they may come hear the smallest fort of Ramparts, and have a Brest - work Cannon Proof, with a Ditch of or So Feet Wide, and are thus made to let upon Passes or Rivers to endure.

scopek.c: SCOPEK - Ho / es, in a Ship, are Holes made through the Sides, close to the Deck, to carry off the Wafer that comes from the Pump, or any - ther way. These Holes in the lowed Deck, and in the Manniger, have round Leathers nail ’ d over them, to keep the Sea - water from coming up into the Ship, which are called S coper Leathers; and the short Nails with broad Heads, whicfffaften these Leathers down, are called Scoper - Nails.

scorbutusthescurvy.c: SCORBUTUS, the Scurvy, is a Disease that is Epidemical to the Hollanders. The symptoms of it are generally livid Spots on the Hands and Feet, weakness of the Legs, linking Breath,, loose - iiefs of the Teeth, bleeding of the Gunis, Com vulfions, Pains, running Gout, Cholick, &c. Blan. chard.

scoreinmusick.c: SCORE, in Musick, is the Original Draught of the whole Composition, wherein the several Parts, vi. Treble, Second Treble, Base, ( c. are distinctly scored or marked.

scorpio.c: SCORPIO, is the th Sign of the odiacl be - ing usually marked thus ( ii ).

scotapartorportion.c: SCOT, a Part Or Portion, according to Bast all, is a certain Custom, or common Tallage made to the Use of the Sheriff, or his Bailiffs; but now signifies a customary Contribution laid upon all Subjects, according to their Ability; for who - ever are AfTeffed to any Contribution, are gent - rally said to pay Scot and Lot.

scotia.c: SCOTIA, a term in Architecture, the fame with Trochile; which lee.

SCOTIA, is Architecture, in a certain Member hollowed in form of a Demi - channel, which is placed between the Torus and the Ajlragal in the Safes of Pillars as also sometimes under the Lar - mer or Drip, in the Cornice of the Dorick Order.

scotomydizzinessorswimming.c: SCOTOMY, Dizziness or Swimming of the Head, is when the Animal Spirits are so whirl ’ d about, that the external Objects seem to run round. Blanchard.

scrobiculuscordis.c: SCROBICULUS Cordis, or Anticar dium, the Heart Pit, formerly called Cardia, the Pit of the Bread, or, as ’ tis usually called, the Sto - mach.

sckophula.c: SCKOPHULA, are preternatural hard Glan - rules, or preternatural Swellings of the Glandules of the Neck and Ears they are contained in a proper Tunick. Blanchard.

scrotum.c: SCROTUM, is that Rag which contains the Testicles of the Male: It consists of a Skin, a fleshy Panniculus, and the two Tunics; of which, the outermod is called Elytroidcs or Vaginalis the innermod Tunic is called Albuginea. In the middle of it is a Line extended in the length, which divides the right part from the left, which they call the Septum. For its more easie Diften - tion or Contraction, ’ tis generally supposed to be void of Fat. See more under the Word Tejles and Tediculi.

scrotumcordis.c: SCROTUM Cordis, so some are plea fed to call the Pericardium; which fee.

scrowlesorvolutes.c: SCROWLES, or Volutes, a term in Architecture. See Valuta,

scutiformeos.c: SCUTIFORME Os. See Mola Genu. SCUTIFORMIS Cartilago. See Enjlforttiih SCUTTLES in a Ship, are square Holes, big enough to let in the Body of. a Man, cut in the Deck, to let People down on occasion into any Room below. They are generally before the Main - Mad, before the Knight in the Fore - Cadle: In the Gun - Room to go down to the Stern Sheets. In the Round - House to go down into the Captain ’ s Cab - bin, when forced by the Enemy in a Fight aloft. There are also some smaller Scuttles, which have Gratings over them and all of them have covers to them, that Men may not tumble in at Night, when ’ tis dark. Also, t - hose little Windows and long Holes which are cut out in Cabbins to let in Light, are called Scuttles.

scyphos.c: SCYPHOS, is the Infundibulum in the Brain likewise those Passages which convey the Spittle from the Os Cribriforme to the Pallat, are so called by some Writers. Blanchard,

sea.c: SEA - Gate, when two Ships are aboard one a nother, by means of a Wave or Billow The Sea - men fay, They lie aboard one another in a Sea Gate.

SEA - Take, when the Sea is so rough, that they cannot govern the Helm with their Hands, then the Seamen seize two Blocks to the end of the Helm / one on each side, and then reeking two small Ropes through them, Which they call Falls, and which are fastned to the sides of the Ship by ha - ving some Men at each Tackle, they govern the Helm according to Direction. This they call & / Yoke to deer by. ' Sometimes they make a Yoke by taking a double turn about the end of the Helm by a single Rope, the ends being laid to the Ship - sides j and by this means they guide the Helm but this is not so good a Yoke as the other.

seams.c: SEAMS of a Ship are Places where her Planks meet and join together. There is also a kind of peculiar Seam in the sowing of Sails, which they call a Monks Seani j which fee.

secant.c: SECANT, is the Right Line drawn from the Centre of a Circle cutting it, and meeting with the Tangent without. See under Trigonometry.

second.c: SECOND, is the Sixtieth part of z Minute.

seconddeliverance.c: SECOND Deliverance, is a Writ that lies for him, who after a return of Cattle Replevied; Ad - judged to him that didrained them, by reason of a default in the Party that Replevied for the Re - levying of the fame Cattle again, upon Security put in for the re - delivery of them in case the Di - stress be Juilified.

secondarycircles.c: SECONDARY Circles, in reference ro the E - ecliptick, or Circles of Longitude of the Stars, are such as pa fling through the Poles of the Ecliptick, ate at Right Angles to the Ecliptick ( as the Meri - dian and Hour Circles are to the Bquinodlial. ) By the help of thele ( Infinitely many Circles, all Points in the Heavens are referred ) to the Ecliptic: That is, Any Star, Plane, or other Phcenome non, is understood to be in that Point of the EclipJ tick which is cut by the Secondary Semicircle which passes through such Star or Phenomenon. And if two Stars, &c. are thus referred to the fame Point of the Ecliptick they are said to be in Conjunction j if in opposite Points, they are aid to be in Oppo - sition: If they are referred to two Points at a Qua - drants distance, they are faick to be in a Quartile AfpeSl f Afpeci if the Points differ a sixth part of the E - ecliptick, the Stars are said to be in a Sextile A - fpeCl, &c. And in general, jail Circles which Interfecft one of the fix greater Circles of the Sphere at Right Angles, may be called Secondary Circles as the Azimuths or Vertical Circles in refpedfc of the Horizon, &c.

secondaryplanets.c: SECONDARY Planets, are such as move round others, whom they rested: as the Centre of their [ Motion; tho ’ they move also along with the Pri - mary Planets in the Annual Orbit round the Sun. And these are otherwise called the Satellites: Such is the Moon to the Earth and Jupiter hath four moving round him as Saturn, according to Cajjini, hath five Mars, Venus, and Mercury, have no Se - condary Planets moving round them, that have been yet discovered. The Learned Dr. Gregory in his AJlronomia Com. Physica, Lib. IV. shews and proves at large, That tho ’ the Motion of the Primary Planets be sufficiently Ample and uniform, as being compound - ded only of a projectile M'otion forward in a right Line, which is a Tangent to the Orbit, and a Gra - vitiation toward the Sun at the Centre and also being at such vast distances from each other, that the effects of their mutual Gravitation towards one another are insensible yet is the matter far otherwise in reference to the Secondary Planets. For every one of these ( altho ? it chiefly gravitate toward its respective Primary one, as towards its Centre, ) at equal distances from the Sun, is attrap - sted towards him with equal accelerated Gravity, as the Primary one is tcrward him but at a great - ter distance with less, at a nearer distance with greater. From which double Tendency towards the Sun, and towards its own Primary Planet, the motion of the Satellites or Secondary Planets comes to be mightily compounded and asserted with ma - ny Inequalities. As for Instance, he Proves, . That the Satellite shall be continually accede - rated in its Motion from the time of its Quadrature with the Sun, to the next following Con jundfci - on or Opposition, but that contrariwil'e, from the Syzygys to the Quadratures, it shall be retarded, and therefore will not always moveSwifter in or near the Syzygys, and Slower near the Quadratures. From whence will follow, a. That the Orbits of these Secondary Planets will be of a Figure more circular in the Quadratures, than in the Syzygys, where the swiftness of the Motion will make the Figure of the Orbit more Re & linear. And therefore the Satellite will run farther from its Primary Planet in the Quadratures, than at the Syzygys; so that the Orbit will be a little Eliptical, having the Primary Planet for its Centre; and the longer Diameter will coincide with the Line of the Quadratures, and the Shorter with that of the Syzygys. And these Irregularities will arise, if the Sun ’ s power of perturbing the motion of the Satellite be excluded and the Orbit be concentrick with that of the Primary Planet. For, if the Orbit be eccen - trical, it may happen that the Satellite shall be far - ther off from the Primary one in the Syzygys, and so move flower, than it shall do at the Qua - dratures. And when this is the case, that the Satellite ’ s Orbit is not a Circle concentrick to the Primary Orbit, but an Elipiis in one of whole Focus ’ s the Primary Planet is placed then the motion of the Satellite will be so disturbed by the Sun, that as it runs into its Orbit, the Apfes of the Orbit shall be moved sometimes in Cohjequcntia, and sometimes in Antecedentia ( whereas he proves before, that the Nodes and Apfes of the Primary Planets are at reft. ) . When the Plane of the Satellite ’ s Orbit, is inclined to the Plane of the Primary Orbit, the Line of the Nodes of the Secondary Orbit will be moved in Antecedentia, with an angular motion, and an unequal Velocity for it will recede molt swiftly when the Nodes are in Quadrature to the Sun after which, it will move flower and at the time of the Nodes being in the Syzygys, it will be perfectly at reft. . The Inclination also of the Plane of the Se - condary Orbit to the Primary one, will be conti - nually varying, and will be greatest when the Nodes are in the Syzygys with the Sun; and less ( cxteris paribus ) when they are in the Quadratures and from the time of the Nodes being in the Sy - zygys to the Quadratures, it will be always de - ceasing and from the time of their being in the Quadratures to the Syzygys, continually eri - ceasing. And he proves, that all these Irregularities, whe - ther in any excentrick or concentrick Orbit, will always be something greater when the Satellites is in Conjunction with the Sun, than when he is in Op - position to him. After this, he proceeds to shew, what Errors or Irregularities in the motion of these Secondary Pla - nets will be produced by the Sun, supposing the Primary Planet to move in an excentrick Orbit round the Sun. Of which, Secft. IV. of the said Book IV.

secretion.c: SECRETION, is the separation of one Fluid from another in the Body of an Animal or Vegeta - ble, by the means of Glands or something anglo - gous to them. Dr. Havers in his Ojleologia, explains Glandular Secretion, by observing, first, That all Motion in its proper Tendency is direct, ( which is exadfly right ) and that the Glands which are seated on the sides of the Arteries all over the Body, are so pla - ced, as to favour the motion of any Particles that strike againftthem in a Right Line, more than the Veins and having Pores adapted to the Figure of the Particles which they separate, the Particles en - devour in their motion to get into those Glandules and being there received, are separated and distil - guilhed from the reft of the mass of Blood, and lo assume the form of that Liquor which we find separated by every Gland. And that the Glands are so situated as to favour the motion ' of a Particle in a Right Line more than the Veins, he faith, is apparent from Observation of the gradual construe - bion of the Arterial Channel. See Vol. II. SECT A. ad Curiam, is a Writ that lies against him who refutes to perform Suit either to the County or Court - Baron.

secta.c: SECTA facienda per illam qua: habet ceniciam partem, is a Writ to compel the Heir that hath the Elder ’ s part of the Co - heirs to perform Service for all the Coparceners.

SECTA unicatantum facienda pro pluribus hcere - ditatibus, is a Writ that lies for that Heir that is distrained by the Lord to more Suits than one, in relpedt of the Land of divers Heirs defended un - to him, ' SECTION SECTlO Ccefaria. See Hyfieratomotocia. SECTION Conickj is the Figure made by the solidity of a Cone ’ s being supposed to be cut by a Plane. If the Section be made by the Axis, or through the Vertex, the Figure arising is a I riangle. If by a Plane, parallel to the Base of the Corner, or fubcontrarily posited, the Figure produced is a Cir - cle. If the Section be made parallel to one side of the Cone, the Figure produced is a Parabola. - If thro ’ both sides of the Cone, ’ tis an Ellipsis; and if thro ’ one side of the Cone, thro ’ the Bale, and not parallel to the other side of the Cohe, ' tis an Hyper - bola, Archimedes, Euclid and other ancient Mathe - maticians, called that only a Conicl Section, when the Plane cutting the Cone was at right Angles to the side of the Cone; and according as the Angle made by the sides of the Cone meeting in the V er - tex, as it was a right, obtuse, or acute one, they called it the Section of Right - angled, Obtuse - angled, or Acute Angled Cone. By which Words they un - derftood what we now call the Parabola, the Hy - pergola, and the Ellipsis: Which three Sections, ( as also the Circle ) Apolonius Pergaus ( justly called Magnus Geometry ) found out to be / producible in any Cone, according to the four ways of cutting it, as above - mentioned. SECTION, in Mathematicks, signifies the cut - ting of one Plane by another, or a Solid by a Plane. The common Seliion of two Planes is always a right Line, being the Line supposed to be drawn on one Plane by the Section of the other, or by its Entrance into it. ' SECTION of a Building, in Architecture, is understood of the Perfile or Delineation of its Heights and Depths raised on the Plane as if the Fabrick were cut asunder to discover the Inside.

sectis.c: SECTIS non faciendis, is a Writ that lies for a Woman, who, for her Dower, ought not to per - form Suit of Court.

sector.c: SECTOR, is an Instrument made of Wood, Ivory, Brass, &c. with a Joint, and sometimes a piece to turn out to make a true Square, with Lines of Sines, Tangents, Secants, Equal Parts, Rumbs, Polygons, Hours, Latitudes, Metals, So - lids, ( c. and is generally useful in all the Practi - cal Parts of the Mathematicks, and particularly contrived for Navigation, Surveying, Astronomy, Dyaling, Projection of the Sphere, &c. By Gunter, Poster, Collins, and others. There are like wife Sectors for Fortification and Gunnery, by Sir Jonas Moor. The great Advantage of the Sector above any other Rule or Plain - scale, is that all its Lines can be accommodated to any Radius; which is done by taking off all Divisions Parallelwife, and not Lengthwise - The ground of which Pradiceis this, That Parallels to ' the Base of any Plain Triangle, bear the fame Proportion to it:: as the Parts of the Legs above the Parallel do to the whole Legs.
