On the contrary, if the Setter be opened to an Angle at a venture, you may find the quantity of that Angle, thus: Take the Parallel Chord of o. and rneafuie it in the Lateral Chord, and it shall there give the Angle, i. e. the Angle that those Lines of Chords are opened to: But that will be different from the Angle of the Edges of the Se - dor. N. B. If you can apply the Centre of a Pro - traitor to the Centre of the Sector, you may easily and readily find the Quantity of any of these An - gles.

secunda.c: SECUNDA superoneratione paflura, is a Writ that lies where Admeasurement of Paflure hath been made; and he that first surcharged the Com - mon, doth again surcharge it, notwithstanding the Admeasurement.

secondans.c: SECOND ANS, in Mathematicks, is an infinite series of Numbers, beginning from Nothing, and proceeding as the squares of Numbers in Arithme - tical Proportion. As for In fiance, o,,,,,,,,, ( c.

secondary.c: SECONDARY; that Officer who is the second or next to the chief Officer; as the Secondaries of the Fine Office; the Secondaries of the Compters, who is next to the Sheriff of London in each of the two Compters; Secondary of the Office of the Privy - Seal; Secondaries of the Pipe two; Second day to the Remembrancers, which are two Offi - cers in the Exchequer. SitCUNDINE, the Secunding or After - Birth, are the three Membranes, Chorion, Alantois, and Amnion, which with the Placenta, are excluded after the Birth.

securitate.c: SECURITATE pads, is a Writ that lies for one who is threatened Death or Danger, against him that so threatneth, and is taken out of the Chancery, and directed to the Sheriff.

securitatem.c: SECURITATEM inveniendi quod fe non di - vertat ad partes exteras fine licentia Regis, is a Writ that lies for the King against, any of his Subjeds, to stay them from going out of his Kingdom: The, ground of which is, That every Mantis bound to ferveand defend the Common - wealth, as the King ( hall think meet. SE defendendo, is a Plea for him that is charged with the Death of another, saying, he was necks - situated to do that which he did in his own defence; the other so Assaulting him, That if he had not done as he did, he must have been in hazard of his own Life: But this Danger ought to be so - great, that it seems inevitable; and tho ’ he justifie it to be done in his own Defence, yet he is driven G t S - S E J to procure his Pardon of course from the Lord - Ghancellor, and forfeits his Goods to the King.

sediment.c: SEDIMENT f UM ' Urmce, the sediment os - rine, are parts of the nutritious Juice, which being separated from the Blood, with the Serum, because of their Gravity, sink to the bottom of the U - rine.

seelaseaword.c: SEEL, a Sea Word much of the fame Sense with Heel for as they call it feeling, when a Ship lies down constantly or steadily on one side; so they call it feeling, when file tumbles on one side violently and suddenly, by reason of the Sea for la - king her, as they call it; i. e. the Waves leaving of her for a time in a rowling Sea: When a Ship thus tumbles to Lee - vonrd, they call it Lee - feel; and in this there is not much danger, even in a Storm, be - cause the Sea will presently right her up again; but if file Rowls pr Seels to Windward, there is fear of her coming over toofhort or suddenly, and so by having the Sea break right into her, be ei - ther sounded, or else have some of her upper Works carried away.

segment.c: SEGMENT of a Circle, is a Figure contain ’ d between a Chord and an Ark of the fame Circle. To find the Superficial Content of any Segment of a Circle, fee Area, N.. - SEGMENT of a Skerc, is a part of it cut off by a Plane; and therefore the Base of such Segment must always be a Circle, and its Superficies a part of the Surface of the Sphere. Its solid Content is found by multiplying the Surface of the whole Sphere, by the Altitude of the Segment, and then dividing the Project by the Diameter of the Sphere ', and to the Quotient, ad - ding the Area of the Base of the Segment, Or if it is less than an Hemisphere thus: Take the Altitude of the Segment from the Radius of the Sphere, and by the Difference multiply the Area of the Base of the Segment; and Sub - firatfi this Product from that which will arise from multiplying the Semi - Axis of the Sphere into the Convex surface of the Segment; then divide the Remainder by, and the Quotient is the Solidity fought. This latter Method supposes the Axis of the Sphere to be given; if not, it may be found thus. Let the Altitude of the Segment be called a, and its Semi - diameter s. Then will s s s s a. s:: s. -; add to a, and that shall. a. a, give the Axis lought.. e Euclid.

segmoidalesorsemilunares.c: SEGMOIDALES, or Semilunares, are Valves of the Arteria Pulmoharia, and are so called, because they referable a Half - moon, or Segment of a Cir - cle; their Substance is Membranous; When they separate, they give passage to the Blood, from the Ventricle into the Artery; but they shut the Pas - sage, and are thrust together by the Blood, if it endeavours to return.

segreianttheheraldswordforgriffins.h: SEGREIANT the Heralds Word for Griffins
segreianttheheraldswordforgriffins.c: SEGREIANT, the Heralds Word for Griffins, when drawn in a leaping or saliant Posture.

sejant.c: SEJANT, ( i. e. fitting ) the Term is used in He - raldry for a Lyon, or other Beast, when it is drawn S E M in an Escutcheon fitting like a Cat, with his Fore - feet strait.

seisin.c: SEISIN, from the French Seifine, pojfeffio So grimier Seisin, is the first Possession; and to Seif, is to take Possession. Seisin, according to the Common Law, is two - fold; Seisin in fact, and Seisin in Law. Seisin in Fact, is when a Corporal Poflefficn is taken. M Seisin in Law, when something is done which the Law accounteth a Seisin, as an Inrolment i And this Seisin in Law, is as much as a Right to Lands and Tenements, tho ’ the Owner be by Wrong disseised of them: And he who hath had an Hours Possession quietly taken, hath Seisin de droit & de claime, whereof no Man may difieife him by his own force or subtilty, but muff be driven to his Adion; and ’ tis called by Coke y Seisin in Law or Actual Seisin. The civilians call the one Civilem PoJJeJfionem, the other Naturalem.

sesina.c: SESINA habenda, quia six habit annum, diem & vafium, is a Writ that lies for Delivery of Seisin to the Lord of his Lands or Tenements, after the King, in the Right of his Prerogative, hath had the Years, Day, and Waste.

seizingorseafing.c: SEIZING, or Seafing, in the Sea Language, is the fame as fafiening, ( vfi. ) of two Ropes toge - ther with some Rope - yarn, &c. Also the fafiening of a Block at the end of a Pendant or Tackle, Garnet, &c. is called Seizing. The Boats sealing, is a Rope by which a Ring, or little Chain is made fast in the Foreship of the Boat, whereby, in a Harbour, the Boat is fattened to the Ship ’ s side.

sellaequina.c: SELLA Equina, feu Turcica, or Sphcenoides, a part of the Brain, is compounded of four Processes of the Bone Sphancides, or the Wedge - like Bone; it contains the Pituitanan Glandule; and in Brutes, the site Mirabile.

semeiotica.c: SEMEIOTICA, is that part of Physick, or the Art of Medicine, which treats of the Signs of Health and Sickness; assisting tse Physician to make probable Guefles and Conjedures of the Constitution and State of his Patient.

semees.c: SEME ES, according, to Dr. Grew, are the Apices of the Attire of a Plant. See Apices.

semi.c: SEMI - BREVE, a Term in Musick. See Notes and Time.

SEMI - CIRCLE, is the Figure contained be - tween the Diameter of a Circle, and half the Cir - cumference. Also an Instrument for Surveying, made of Brass, and divided into Degrees, being half the The - polite.
SEMI - COLON, is a Stop, or Point in a Sen - tence, between a Comma and a Colon, and mark ’ d thus (; ) and expresses a Pause greater than the former, and less than the latter.

SEMI - CUBICAL Paraboloid, is a Curve whole Ordinates are in Subtriplicate of the Duplicate pro - portion of the Diameter: That is, the Cubes of the Ordinates are as the Squares of the Diame - ters. In this Paraboloid, the Segments of the Curve, cut by Ordinates ( at equal Distances ) are as the Ordinates in a Parabola; and therefore their Squares increased by Equals in Arithmetical Pro - grefifion; and consequently that Curve to a Right Line, as the Trunk of a Parabola to a Parabola. SEMI - V I , ' s EM s E N t
SEMI - CUPXUM, is a Bath, in which the Pa - tient is only up to the Navel in Water;
SEMI - DIAMETER, or Radius, is that Line that is drawn from the Center to the Circumference of a Circle.

SEMI - DIAMETER / in Fortification, is two - fold, vi. the Greater and Letter.: The former be - ing a Line cotnpofed of the Capital, and the Small Semi - diameter of the Polygon; And the other, a Line drawn to the Circumference from the Centre thro ’ the Gorges.
SEMI - DIAPASON, a Term in Musick, signify - ing a Defective or Imperfect Obtave.
SEMI - DIAPENTE, a Term in Musick signify - ing an Imperfect Fifth.

SEMI - MEM BRANOSUS, is a Muscle of the Leg, so called from its being half Tendinous and Membrane - like, lying immediately under the Semi - nervofus: It ariseth broad and tendinous from the Protuberance of the Os lfchium, and in its descent becomes broader; and in less than half its Progress begins to grow fleshy, and is dilated into a large and fleshy Belly, lying under the long round Ten - don of the S & mi - nervofus, becoming a ( hort thick Tendon inferred to the superior part of the upper Appendix of the Tibia backwards. Its Ule is to help to bend the Tibia.

SEMI - N ER V OSUS, feu Semi - tendinosus, a Muf - cle of the Thigh, which is so called from its be - ing half Tendinous, and Nerve - like. It ariseth partly Tendinous and partly Fleshy from the Enter - nal part of the Protuberance of the Os lfchium, and presently being dilated to a large fleshy Belly, be - comes a round Tendon in half its Progress, which descending over the fleshy Belly, of the Semi - mem - branofus, marcheth close by the Gaflerocnemius, on the posterior part of the Superior Appendix of the Tibia; from whence it passes forwards to its In - section in the said Bone immediately below the termination of the Gracilis: This with the Gracilis adding, bend the Tibia directly backwards. Its Tendon, together with the Sartorius, Gracilis, - Se - mi - membrancfus and Biceps, make the inward Ham - strings, as they are commonly called.
SEMI - QUADRATE, the fame with Semi - quar - til'e.
SEMI - QUARTILE, an Afpedt of the Planets ? when distant from each other Degrees, or one Sign and a half.
SEMI - QUAVER, a Term in Musick. See Notes and Time.
SEMI - QUINTILE, an Afpedt of the Planets when at the Distance of Degrees, from one a - nother.
SEMI - SEXTILE, an - Afpedt of the Planets, when distant from one another Degrees, or Sign, and is noted thus, SS.

SEMI - SPIN ATUS, is a Muscle which seem. s r. o be a Continuation of the Sacer - and therefore may not improperly be called Tranfverfalis Dorji fit a - ? rifeth fleshy from all the T transverse Processes of the Vertebra of the Thorax, and marching obliquely upwards, is inferred, to the superior Spines of the said Vertebra These with the Quadratus Lumbo - rum Sacer, and Tranfverfales Colli adding, move the whole Spine, or Vertebra of the Neck, Back, and Loins, obliquely backwards, as when we end - vour to look ' very much behind us: If they all at together on each side, they assist in crediting the Trunk of the Body.
SEMI - TONE, a Term in Musick, of which there are two forts, vi. a Greater and a Lesser the Enharmonical Deifis, being the Difference be tween them.

semlditoneinmusick.c: SEMLDITONE, in Musick, is the Lesser Third having its Terms as fix to five. SEMI - LUNARES Vahula. SeeSegmoidales.

seminalleaves.c: SEMINAL Leaves: much the greatest part of all Seeds which are sown in the Earth, come up, or shoot forth at first with too little, plain, soft, and undivided Leaves; which because they are usually very different from the Leaves of the succeeding Plant in Magnitude, Figure, Surface and Position, are called very properly by this Name Seminal Leaves: As the little embrionated Plant which lies in Minaturein every Seed, is called, the Plantula Seminalis.

semitaluminosa.c: SEMITA Luminosa, is a Name given by Mr. Childrey in his Britannia Baconica, p., to a kind of Lucid Track in the Heavens, which, a little before the Vernal Equinox, ( he faith ) may be seen about a Clock at Night, extending from the Western edge of the Horizon up towards the Pleiades. After this, the Phenomenon was taken notice of by Cafjini and Fatioi who both evince. That this Light comes diffused from each side of the Sun: Its brightness is much the fame with that of the Via Lactea, or the Tail of a Comet. ’ Tis seen plainest with us about the beginning of Qbtobers and towards the end of February. S. Ratio conjectures, That the Body, or rather the Congeries or Aggregate of those Bodies which occasion the Light, doth conform to the Sun like a Lens; and takes it to have ever been the fame t But Cajfini thinks it arises from a vast Number of small Planets which encompass the Sun, and give this Light by Reflection, esteeming it also not to have exifted long before he observed it: But this latter is overthrown by Childrey s Observations, whose Book was Printed in and he faith there he had taken notice of it for many Years.

send.c: SEND, when a Ship is either at an Achor, or under Sail, falls with her Head or Stern deep into the Trough of the Sea ( i. e. ’ into a Hollow made between two Waves or Billows ) they fay ftm - fends much that way, whether it be A - head, of A - jlern.

senescall.c: SENES CALL if Marejhallo quod non teneant placit de liber tenemento, ike. is a Writ dire died to the Steward, or Marlhal of England, inhibiting them to take Cognisance of any Action in their Court that concerns either Freehold, Debt, or Co venant.

sensation.c: SENSATION is the perceiving of things by our Senses j and is the Original of moll of the Ideas which we have, which by our Senses are derived to our Understanding. The Cartcfidtis assert Senfarion to be only a sim pie Perception, whereby the Motions of external Objedls asserting the Extremities of the Nerves in the Organs of the Body, are communicated all a long those Nerves to the Glandula Pinealis, where the Soul residing receives her Informations, and ac - cordingly makes Jugdments upon them. In which, ( except as to that Whim of the Sours residing in the Glandula Pinealis ) they are certain - ly much in the right: For Senfarion is properly and ultimately made in or by the Mind, or discerning Faculty, which probably, from the different Mori " G V ' s E S E R. ons of the internal parts of the Brain, is excited and determined to differing Perceptions; and to these we give differing Names, as Heat, Cold, and other Qualities.

sensitiveplants.c: SENSITIVE Plants, are i ’ uch whose Frame and Constitution is so nice and tender, that at the touch, or at the least pressure of ones Hand, they will con - trail their Leaves or Flowers, as if they really felt pain by such a Conradl. Of these the Botanick Writers mention many Kinds, some of which contrail with Heat, others with Cold.

sensoriumcommune.c: SENSORIUM Commune, or the Seat of the common Sense, is that part of the Brain in which the Nerves, from the Organs of all the Senses, are terminated, which is the beginning of the Medulla Oblongata.

sensorytheorganorinstrumentofsence.h: SENSORY the Organ or Instrument of Sence
sensorytheorganorinstrumentofsence.c: SENSORY, the Organ or Instrument of Sence, as the Eye. of Seeing, the Ear of Hearing, &c.

sensljssense.c: SENSLJS, Sense, is when the Motion impressed by the outward Objeils upon the Fibres of the Nerves, is conveyed by the help of the Animal Spirits in the Nerves, to the common Sensory, cr Adedulla Oblongata.

separation.c: SEPARATION, with some Writers of Navi - gation, is the fame with what is more usually cal - led, the Departure; that is, a Ships difference ot Longitude from any place, or from another Ship. Our Seamen commonly call it Eajling or Westing according as the Difference of Longitude isEaft or Weft.

sephyros.c: SEPHYROS fin some Authors ) is a hard In - flammation of the Womb.

septanfevers.c: SEPTAN Fevers, intermitting Fevers that return every seventh Day.

septangular.c: SEPTANGULAR, the fame with Hept an - gular.

sectentariusaconstellation.c: SECTENTARIUS, a Constellation in the Nor - thern Hemisphere, consisting of Stars.

septentrionalsigns.c: SEPTENTRIONAL Signs, are thefirft Signs of the Zodiac !, lo called, because they decline to - wards the North from the Equinodlial, and are the fame with Boreal Signs.

septica.c: SEPTICA, five Putrcfacientia are those things, which by a Malignant fliarpnefs, rot and corrupt the FJefh.

septumcordis.c: SEPTUM Cordis, the fleshy part that divides the Right Ventricle of the Heart from the Left.

septumlucidum.c: SEPTUM Lucidum, is a Partition, which is di - aphanous, upon the account of its thinness, it di - ftinguifh. es the Ventricles of the Brain.

sequatur.c: SEQUATUR fub suo per iculo, is a Writ that lies where a Summons ad Warrrantifandum is a - warded, and the Sheriff returns, That he hath no - thing whereby he may be summoned; then goes out an Alias and Pluries; and if he come not at the Pluries, then goes out this Writ.

sequester.c: SEQUESTER, is a Termufed in the CivilLaw for renouncing, as when a Widow comes into Court, and disclaim to have any thing to do, or to intermeddle with her Husband ’ s Estate, who is Deceased; she is said to Sequefler.

sequestration.c: SEQUESTRATION, is the separating of a thing in Controversie from the Possession of both those that contend for it: And it is of two forts; Voluntary, or Necessary. Voluntary, is that which is done by Consent of each Party. Necessary, is that which the Judge doth of his Authority, whether the Parties will or not. It is used alio for the A ft of the Ordinary, dise poling of Goods and Chattels of one Deceased whose Estate no Man will meddle with. Also for the gathering of the Fruits of a Benefice void to the Use of the next Incumbent.

sequestro.c: SEQUESTRO habendo, is a Writ Judicial, for the dissolving a Sequestration of the Fruits of a Be - nefice made by bishop at the King ’ s Command, thereby to compel the Parson to appear to the Suit of another: For the Parson, upon his Appearance, may have this Writ for the Discharge of the Se - queftration.

series.c: SERIES, properly speaking, is an orderly Pro - ofs or continuation of things one after another. Tis commonly in Algebra connected with the Word Infinite, and there, by Infinite Series, is meant certain Progression, or Ranks of Quantities order - ly proceeding, which make continual Approaches to, and if infinitely continued, would become equal to what is inquired after. This Method took its Rife from the Learned Dr. Wallis ’ s Arithmetic of Infinites, and has been of late so pursued by several Worthy Persons of our own Nation, especially the Incomparable Sir Isaac Nexvton, that it is now one of the greatest Improvements of Algebra.

serosities.c: SEROSITIES, are serous Humours abounding in the Body.

serpentine.c: SERPENTINE, so the Chymifts ( from its Fi - gure ) call that long winding Worm, which is pla - ced in a Tub of Water in the Diftillatlon of Spi - rits. See Worm.

serpentineline.c: SERPENTINE Line, the fame with Spiral which fee.

serratusmajoranticus.c: SERRATUS Major Anticus, is a Muscle which arises fleshy from the whole Basis Scapula, and pas - sing under the Subfcapularis, it becomes broader and thicker, still running somewhat forwards till it ’ s inserted to the eight superior Ribs laterally, by so many diftindl fleshy Portions, or Dlgituli, re - presenting the Teeth of a Saw the two, and some - times three inferior of which, are indented with the Musculus Obliquus Defcendens of the Abdomen. This like the Serratus Minor Anticus, dilates the Thorax, or moves the Scapula forwards and down - wards, when its Muscles are relax ’ d.

serratusminoranticus.c: SERRATUS Minor Anticus, is a Muscle, by Anatomists generally reckoned a Muscle amongst those of the Scapula: but we are persuaded ( says Cowper ) from its Pofidon that it may be equally fer - viceable to the Thorax, in elevating those Ribs it is inserted to: It arises fleshy from the Processus Co - ra co ides Scapula, and descends obliquely forwards, becomes broader and thinner, and is inserted fleshy to the bony part of the second, third, fourth, and fifth Ribs. If the Scapula are elevated by their proper Muscles, this with its Partner, are then ca - table of dilating the Breast in large Infpirations. But if they aredepreft, it may be easily conceived with what Difficulty that Adlion muff be per - formed.

serratus.c: SERRATUS inferior prfticus, is a Muscle of the Thorax, much larger than Authors generally af - sign it; “ In a Robust Man we observed its Conti - “ nation, ( says Cowper ) not only from the Spines of “ the Vertebra ’ s of the Loins, but from all thole of “ the Thorax, as well underneath as below the for - “ mer Muscle its superior and inferior Parrs be - “ ing S E F ei ing entirely Tendinous, its Middle growing fleftiy near its serrated Termination at the Cur - nature of the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and Extre - ' mii; y of the twelfth Ribs. The Ductus of the Fi -, ' bres of this putting transverse, and those of the “ precedent descending obliquely, do decussate each other in Acute Angles which Riolan has “ well observed, and contrary to the Opinion of Authors, assigns it with its Partner, a different “ Use in depressing the Thorax; both performing “ the Office of a Bandage in binding together and constringing the Posterior Muscles of the Spine, not unlike, the Constructive Inclofures of the e Thigh and Cubit.

SERRATUS superior poflicus, is a Muscle of the Thorax, which lies immediately under the Bfom - loides: It arises with a thin Tendon from two in - senior Spines of the Vertebra of the Neck, and three superior of the Thorax, from thence descending ob - liquefy over th e Splenius Capitis, and - under parts of the Sacrolumbalis, and Dcrji Longijfmus, it be - comes fleshy, marching over the Scapula, to its Insertion at the Curvature of the second, third, and fourth Ribs, by so many distend fleshy endings, representing the Teeth of a Saw, whence its Name. This assists in elevating the Ribs or Thorax.

serve.c: SERVE, to serve a Rope ( in the Sea Phrase ) is to lay upon it Spun - yarn, Rope - yarn, Sinnet, a piece of Canvas, or the like, which is there rowled fast round about the Rope, to keep it from fretting or galling in any place.

servientibus.c: SERVIENTIBUS, are certain Writs touching Servants and their Matters violating the Statutes made against their Abufes.

servitiis.c: SERVITIIS acquittandis, is a Writ Judicial, that lies for one distrained for Services to F. who owes and performs to R. for the Acquittal of such Services.

serum.c: SERUM, is. watery, thin, fellowship, and saltish Humour, which consists chiefly of Water, with a moderate quantity of Salt, and a little Sul - pour: The Use of it is to be a Vehicle to the Blood: And this is that Watery part that separates from the Blood in theVeflel, after anyPerfonis let Blood. A small Heat will Coagulate it.

sesamoeidea.c: SESAMOEIDEA OJfa, are,,, and sometimes more little ones, so Called from the likeneis they have to Sesamum Seeds, which are found in the Joints of the Hands and Feet. StSQUIALTER, in Musick. See Time.

sesquialteralproportion.c: SESQUIALTERAL Proportion, is when any Number or Quantity contains another once and an half, and the Number so contain ’ d in the Greater, is said to be to it in Subfelaquiteral Proportion.

sesquiquadrateanafpedorposition.c: SESQUIQUADRATE, an Afped or Position of the Planets, when at the Distance of Signs and an half, or Degrees from each other.

sesquiquintileanafped.c: SESQUIQUINTILE, an Afped of the Pla - nets, when Degrees Distant from each - ther.

sesquitertianalproportion.c: SESQUITERTIANAL Proportion, is when any Number or Quantity contains another once and one third.

sessions.c: SESSIONS, is a fitting of Justices in Court upon Commission, as the Sejjions of Oyer and Terminer, Quarter - ft ejfions, otherwise called General - feffwns, opposite whereto, are Especial, otherwise called Privy - fejfwns which are procured upon some fpeci - al occasion, for the more speedy dispatch of Justice. sex Sejjions of Parliament, is a Sejjions which conti - nues till it be prorogued or difiblved.

setaceum.c: SETACEUM, is when the Skin of the Neck is taken up and run through with a Needle and the Wound afterward kept open by Briftles, a Skean of Silk, ( c, which is after moved to and fro., to give vent to the Humours that are ill disposed in that Part. ’ Tis also called Retort and Setum, '

sett.c: SETT, when the Seamen observe on what Point of the Compass, the Sun, Land, c. bears,, they call it, Setting the Sun, or Land, by their Compass.

settleadeck.c: SETTLE a Deck., is the Word at Sea for ta - king a Deck lower than it was at first, which they call settling a Deck.

several.c: SEVERAL taile, is that whereby Land is given or entailed severally, to two Men and their Wives, and to the Heirs of their Bodies begotten j the Donees have joint Estate for their two Lives, and yet they have fever al Inheritance, because the llfue of the one hall have his Moiety, and the Ilttte of the other, the other Moiety.

severaltenancy.c: SEVERAL Tenancy, is a Plea or Exception ta - ken to a Writ that is laid against two as joint, - which are several.

severance.c: SEVERANCE, is the finglinghr revering of two, or more, that are joined in one Writ. For Example: If two join in a Writ de libertatem probanda, and the one afterward be Non - fun: i Here Severance is permitted; so that notwithftand - ing the Non - suit of the one, the other may see - rally proceed. There is also Severance of the Tenants in an Af fixe, when as one or two, or more Difleifors ap - pear upon the Writ, and not the other. As also Severance in Attaints, and Severance in Debt, where two or more Executors are named Plaintiffs, and the one refuses to prosecute. Severance of Corn, is the cutting and carrying it off from the Ground and sometimes the setting out the Tythe from the reft of the Corn, is called Severance.

sew.c: SEW, when a Ship at Low - water comes to lie on the Ground, and to lie dry, they fay Jhe Js fever - ed; and if site be not quite left dry, they lay, he Jews to such a part.

sexagesimalfractions.c: SEXAGESIMAL Fractions, or Sexagenaries, are such as have always for their Denominator There were anciently no others used in Astronomy - cal Operations; and they are still retained in many Cafes; tho Decimal Arithmetics begins to grow in Use now in Astronomical Calculations. In these Fractions, which some call Ajlroncmi W cals ) the Denominator is usually omitted, and the Numerator only written down: Thus,. ,,, Is to be read, Degrees, Minutes, Seconds of a Degree, or th parts of a Minute, - Thirds, Fourths, ( c. The Ancients, before the introducing of Also - rifm by the Numeral Figures now in use, ( finding M it troublefoine to express and manage Fractions of divers Denominators, especially when they are to be expressed by great Numbers; and troublesome also to express and manage Integers, when they happen to be great Numbers ) thought fit to divide an Integer into Parts, which they call ’ d Xz r, which now we call Minutes, or Scruples; and each of these into Parts, which they called Se - conds, and ( if there were yet need of greater Ex - madness ) each of these into Thirds; and each of these into as many Fourths; and so onward, as far as there was occasion, which they called Sexagefms, or Sexagesimal parts. And ( to avoid great Numbers ) a Colledion of sixty Integers they called a Sexagene; and sixty of such, a Second Sexagene; and sixty of these, a Third; and so onward, as there was occasion. Thus, for - f, the fourth part of an Integer, ( be it Hour, Day, Degree, or whatever else ) they put ' ( that is, i Minutes ); for they put '. ' ' ( that is, Minutes and Seconds ); which is ex - actly the fame in Value: And for, ( because this cannot be exactly express ’ d in a Sexagefms ) they would put ', ( which is pretty near, but somewhat too little ) or ' ( which is yet nearer, but somewhat too much ) or ( if these be not ead enough for the present purpose ) ", or ' ' " " '; or yet more accurately, if need be, till they come to so much exadnefs, as that the ( mail remaining dise - rence might safely be negleded. And such Sexagefms were used not only by To - levy, ( by whom they seem to have been first intro - duced ) and other Greeks Writers, but by the Arabs also, ( in imitation of Ptolemy ) and are continued in Use with us to this Day. So for x, ( which is the Number of Days, whereby the Arabic Yearsof the Hegira begin later than our Account by the Years of our Lord ) they put T " ' '; that is, Third Sexagene, fecondsSexagenes, first Sexagenes, and Days. And this Account we meet with in the Alfhonfine Tables, and ( of later Times ) in those of Lansber - giiis. Now, if I were to Work it by the Sexagesimal Tables of Multiplication, the Work would be so perplex, that I will not here repeat it; and there - fore it is thought better to reduce the first and third Numbers to the lowest Denomination, that is ( here ) to third Scruples, D. Where Multiplying the third Number by the second, and dividing by the first, I shall have the Number of Degrees fought in Integers, with the common Fraction annexed; which being reduced to Sexagefimals, will give the answer in Degrees, Minutes, Seconds, &c. Or I might have reduced the Degrees into Thirds also, ( which must have been done, if to these Degrees there had been an - need first, second, and third Minutes ) and then the Answer had been in third Minutes; and these to be reduced to Degrees, Minutes, &c. Which Operation, thos it be troublesome enough, is yet more expedite, than by the Sexagesimal Multiplication and Division, fin e the time that we have learned, ( by help of the Numerical Fi - gure ) to manage great Numbers, which in Ptolemy ’ s time were not in use. And in like manner, whatever other come to bs so Multiplied. According to this Sexagesimal Method, Ptolemy divides the Radius or Semidiameter of a Circle into Parts, ( and consequently, the whole Diameter ito ) and each of those Parts into Minutes, and each of those into Seconds, and so forward, as far is occasion requires. And accordingly, the Arch answering to such a Chord; ( that is, the sixth part of the Circumference, whose Chord Equals the Radius ) into Degr. and consequently the whole Circumference into & and each of these Degrees into Minutes, Seconds, by a continual Sexagenary Division. And cohfonant hereunto, he makes his Table of Chords or Subtenfes ( in such Parts, Minutes, and Seconds ) answering the several Arches in a Circle, Instead r S H A Instead of which, the Arabs or Saracens have in - produced ( as more Expedient ) their Table of Sines, ( or half Chords of the double Arch ) expressed in like manner by sexagesimal Parts. Which they did in imitation of Ptoldmy, than that they were necessitated so to do, having the use of Numeral Figures as We have, which Ptolemy and others of the Ancients had not. But Ar sachel therein differs thus far from To - levy, that he divides his Diameter into Parts which Ptolemy divides but into, and hath there - fore less need of Subdivisions. The reason why the Ancients did thus reduce their ordinary Fractions all to one kind of Denomi - nation, was, to avoid the trouble which would arise from the different Denomination of Fradlions, which ( when they had not the helps that now we have ) would be very great; and therefore chose to admit of Approximations, many times, instead of accurate Equalities. And why they chose the Number, rather than any other Number, was, because if they had made use of, or such other small Number, they would be put upon a necessity of the more Subdi - vision, and a Number much greater than this they could not well manage; ( there being / even in this, trouble enough ) and of Numbers about this bigness, this was thought most convenient, as being most capable of exact Divisions, without be - ing put to the necessity of Approximations or Sub - divisions; admitting, for Divisors, the fix first Numbers,,,,,,, ( which none less than it can do / and as many more answering to them,,,, o,, ( that is Twelve in all ) there being no Number less than it, admitting of so many Divisors; nor can any, greater than it, admit of more, which is not at least twice as great; which cannot be said again of any greater Number, till we come to. And this is that which is Made the Number of Degrees in the whole Circle. And this Division of Integers into Sexagefms ( Minutes, Seconds, Thirds, Sc. ) especially in the Parts of Arches, Angles, Time, and Motion; the Arabs have retained, in imitation of the Greeks ( or Egyptians ) and we from them, even to this Day. sexangleingeometry.c: SEXANGLE, in Geometry, is a Figure con - siding of fix Angles.

sextans.c: SEXTANS, is the sixth part of any thing, thus: There is an Astronomical Instrument called a Sex - tant, as being the th part of a Circle. This hath a graduated Limb, and is used like a Quadrant.

sextilethepofidonorafpedl.c: SEXTILE, the Pofidon or Afpedl of the Planets, when at Degrees distant, or at the distance of two Signsfrom one another; and is marked thus,.

shackles.c: SHACKLES, aboard a Ship, are those oblong Iron Rings, and bigger at one end than at the other, with which the Ports are shut fast, by thrusting the Wooden Bar of the Port through them. There are also a fort of Shackles to lift the Hatches up with, of the former Figure, butfmaller; they are fastened at the Corners of the Hatches.

shallop.c: SHALLOP, is a small light Vessel with only a small Main - Mail and Fore - Mad, and Lugg - Sails, j to hale up and let down on occasion: They common - j ly are good Sailers, especially the French Cbaboups; and are used often as Tenders upon a Man of War.

shame.c: SHAME, is an uneasiness of the Mind, upon the thought of having done something which is Inde - cent, or will lessen the valued Esteem which others have of us.

shankorshank.c: SHANK, or Shank. Painter, in a Ship, is a Ihort Chain fastned under theFore - Mast Shrowds, by a Bolt to the Ships - side; having at the other end a Rope fastned to it. On this Shank - Painter, the whole Weight of the Aft - part of the Anchor rests, when it lies by the Ships - side. The Rope by which it is haled up, is made fast about a Timber - head.

shapournftt.c: SHAPOURNFTT: The Heralds call a kind of Cap which is born in some Coats of Arms by this Name.

sheerorsheering.c: SHEER, or Sheering; the Sea phrase for the going of a Ship when Ihe is not steered steadily then they fay Ihe sheers or goes Jheering; as they dp also when she goes in and out by means of the swift running of a Tide - Gate, for then being at an Anchor, they fay there is danger, left she should Jheer home her Anchor, or steer a - shore.

sheer.c: SHEER - Hoo x, aboard a Ship; are great Hooks of Iron sometimes uled when a Ship designs to board another. They are like a Sickle, and are let into the Main - Yard - Arms andFore - Yard - Arms, in order to spoil, cut or tear the Enemy's Shrouds, Sails, or Rigging.

SHEER - S / wtz x, at Sea, is the term for a kind of Knot, by which they tye up or shorten a Run - ner when ' tis too long, so that they cannot hoise in the Goods by it over the Ship - sides. ' This Knot can be let loose again when they please -

sheers.c: SHEERS, so the Seamen call two Mails Yards, or Poles fet up and seized a cross - each other aloft, near the top. This Pair of Sheers, as they call it, is placed below on the Chain - Wales of the shrouds: and lashed fast to the Ship ’ s - sides to keep them Hea - dy aloft. Their use is to fet in or take out a Mali; for which end, there is fastned at the place where they cross one another, a strong double Block with a strap. They serve also to hoise in or out of Boats that have Malls, such Goods as are wanted to be taken in or out

sheathing.c: SHEATHING of a Ship, is casing that Parc of her which is to be under Water, with some - thing to keep the Worms from eating into her Planks. ’ Tis usually done by laying Tar and Hair mixt together all over the old Plank, and then nailing on thin new Boards: But this hinders a Ship ’ s Sailing; and therefore of late some have been Iheathed with milled Lead. ' Tis very well worth trying what the New - alone Pitch will do in this case; if it will defend from the Worm, as perhaps. it will, a Ship might be Paid with it heaper than with the Crowjf - Pitch; and it will not crack nor scale off as, fiat will do, but keep always soft and fiqcbth. I have seen where it hath been on x Mohths, and yet it was very black and soft.

sheats.c: SHEATS in a hip, are Ropes bent to the Clews of the Sails; serving in the Lower - fails to Hale - aft or Bound - off the Clew of the Sail: But in Top - fails they serve to Hale - home as the Word is, or to hale she Clew of the Sale dole to the Yard - Arm. If the Main - fail Shears are haled - aft, ’ tis in or - der to make the Ship keep by a Wind; but when the Fore - sheats are haled aft, ’ tis that the Ship may fall off from the Wind: And if site will not do it readily, they then hale the Fore - fail ( by the Heat ) flat. in, as near the Ship ’ s - sides as they can; and this they call Flatting i ? i the Fore - fail. When they fay, Ease the Sheat, they mean Veer it, or let it go out gently; but when the Word is, Let fly the the. Sheat, they mean, let if go all at once, and tun out as fail as it can; and then the Sail will hang loose, and hold no Wind. In a very great Gale or Gad: of Wind, there is another Rope Bent to the Clews of the Main - fail and Fore - fail, above the sheat Block, to succour and ease the Sheat, and this they call a False - Heat. Sheats in a Ship, also, are those Planks under Water which come along her Hun, and are closed into the fern Pofl So also that Part within Board in the Hun of the Ship, is called the Stem - Jheats. The Seamen fay when they would have the [ heats of the Main or Fore - fail haled aft, Tally the [ heats.

shewinginlaw.c: SHEWING, in Law, is to be quit of Attach - ments in any Court, and before whomsoever in Plaints hewed, and not avow ’ d,

shifters.c: SHIFTERS, certain Men aboard a Man of War, who are ' employed by the Cooks to ftiift or change the Water in which the Flefli or Fish is put and laid for some time, in order to fit it for the Ket - tle.

shivers.c: SHIVERS, so the Seamen call those little round Wheels in which the Rope of a Pulley or Block runs. They turn - with the Rope, and have pieces of Brafsin their Centres, ( which they call the Cock ) with Holes in them, into which the Pin of the Block goes, and on which they turn. These Shi - vers are usually of Wood; but some are of Brass, as those in the Heels of the Top - mafls.

short.c: SHORT - Accent, in Grammar, hews that the time of Pronunciation ought - to be short, and Is marked thus ( ).

shot.c: SHOT of a Cable, is the fplicirig of two Cables together, that a Ship may Ride safe in deep Wa - ters, and in great Roads: For, a Ship will Ride easier by one shot of a Cable, than by three short Cables out a - head.

shotforordnance.c: SHOT, for Ordnance, are of several forts, as Hound - foot, which are round Bullets fitted in proportion to the Bore of the Piece. Cross - bar - Jhot, are round hot, with a Iongfpike of ' Iron call in it, as if it did go through the mid - dle of it., Trundle - foot, being only a Bolt of Iron or Inches long, harp - pointed at both ends, and about a Hand ’ s breadth from each end, having a round broad Bowl of Lead call upon it, according to the Bore of the Piece. ' Langrel - Jhot, which runs loose with a hackle to be horned when it is put into the Piece; and when it says out, it spreads it self. At each end of the Bar it has half a Bullet, either of Lead or Iron. Chain - foot, is two Bullets with a Chain betwixt them, foftie being contrived round, yet so that they will spread in dying their full Length and Breadth. Case - foot, is any thing of small Bullets, Nails, old Iron, and the like,, to put into tip Case, to hoot out of Ordnance.

shoulderinginfortification.c: SHOULDERING, in Fortification, is a Re - trenchment opposed to the Enemies, or a Work cast up for a Dfence on one side, whether it be made of heaps of Earth cast up, or of Gabions and Facines. A foouldring also is aiquare Orillon sometimes made in the Bastions on the Flank near the fhoukler, to cover the Cannon of a Casemate. Again, it is ta - ken for a Demi - bastion or Work consisting of one Face, and one Flank, which ends in a Point at the head of a Horn - or, or Crown - work.: Neither is it to be understood only of a small Flank added to the sides of the Horn - work, to defend them when they are too long, but also of the Redents which are raised on a trait Line.

shrowds.c: SHROWDS, are great Ropes in a Ship, which come from either side of all Masts.. They are fa fi - ned below by Chains to the Ship's sides, and aloft over the Head of the Mast, their Pendants, Fore - tockje, and Sw. inters being first put under them: They areulfo served there, to prevent their galling the Mast. The Top - mast - shrowds are fastned to the Puttockj. by Plates, of Iron; and by Dead - mens Eyes and Lanniers also as the others are. The terms are, Ease thejhrowds; that is, flackenthem: Set Taught the shrowds; that is, fee them differ The Boft - sprit hath no shrowds. S CUT ' alias, is a second Writ lent out, when the first was not executed.

sidemenorqueflmen.c: SIDEMEN, or Queflmen, be those that are Yearly Chosen, according to the Custom of every Parifli, to Aiiift the Church - wardens in the Enquiry and Presenting such Offenders to the Ordinary, as are Punishable. in Cat ' Court Chrifiian.

siege.c: SIEGE, is the encamping or fitting down of an Army before a Place, in order to take it, either by Force or by Famine.

sigmoide.c: SIGMOIDE, are the Apophyfes of the Bones, representing the Letter C of the ancient Greeks. Afifo the Valves of the great Artery that hinder the Blood from returning back to the Heart.

significabit.c: SIGNIFICABIT, is a Writ de Excommunicato capiendo, which iffueth out of the Chancery upon a Certificate given by the Ordinary, of a Man that Bands obstinately Excommunicate, by the space of forty Days, for the laying him up in Prison with - out Bail or Mainprise, until he submit himself to the Authority of the Church. And ’ tis facalled, because the Word Slgnificavit is an Emphatical Word in the Writ. There is also another V rit in the Hegifler, Sol.. dire & ed to the Justices of the Bench, commanding them to stay any Suit de - pending between such and such, by reason of an Excommunication alledged against the Plaintiff because the sentence of the Ordinary that did Ex - communicate him, is appealed from, and the Ap - peal yet depends undecided.

siliquainbotany.c: SILIQUA, in Botany, is the Seed - vessel, Husf Cod, or Pod, of such Plants as are of the Legumi - nous kind.

silloninfortification.c: SILLON, in Fortification, is an elevation of Earth, made in the middle of a Moat, to Fortifte it when too broad: It is otherwise galled Envelope f which is the more common Name. A '

similararks.c: SIMILAR Arks of a Circle, are such as are like Parts of their wdiole Circumference. - SIMILAR Bodies, in Natural Philosophy, are called such as have their Particles of the fame Kind and Nature one with another. '

similar.c: SIMILAR, of simple Parts, by Anatomists are called such as are throughout of the fame nature and texture, as all the Parts of the Bone are Bony, ( fc.
SIMILAR PeP angles -, are those which have their sides about the equal Angles Proportional that is, as a b: eh:: ad: ef.
SIMILAR pight - lind Figures, are such as have equal Angles, and the sides about those equal An - gles proportional.
SIMILAR solid Numbers, are those, whose little Cubes may be so ranged as to make similar and rectangular Parallelopipeds.

SIMILAR SeBions in Conicks, are such whose Diameters make equal Angles with their Ordi - nates; and also where the Triangles A D E, A B C, are Sirqilar to the Triangles ad e, a be, and the Bales DE to BC; asde, be. Their Diame - ters also, as A F, and / are called Similar.

similarplanenumbers.c: SIMILAR Plane Numbers, are those Numbers which may be ranged into the form of similar Rc'd - H angles S I M S I M i - r angles; that is, into Rectangles, whose sides are Proportional, such are i z and; for the ( ides of are and z ( as in Fig. BJ and the sides of are and ( as in Fig. C. ) But.::, and therefore those Numbers are similar.

All Squares mu ft be similar PeP angles for since they have all their Sides equal, and all their Angles right ) whatever Proportion the side a m hath to the side h of the other Peel angle, the fame must also the other side a b have to the side e h j because they are equal to a m, and to h i. And that also a b hath the fame Proportion to be:: as d e hath to ef Then those two Polygons are similar. Hence all similar pePangles are to each other as the squares of their Homologous - sides. For the pep angle A, is to B:: as the Square bm is to the Square n '; since as well Squares zs - PeP angles are in a duplicate Ratio to that of their sides.

similarsegments.c: SIMILAR Segments of a Circle are such as con - tain equal Angles.

simony.c: SIMONY, is an unlawful Contract made to have a Man presented to a Redtory or Vicarage: It was agreed by all the Justices, that if the Patron present any Person to a Benefice with Cure, for Money, that such Presentation, &c: is void, tho ’ the Presentee were not Privy to it, and the Statute gives Presentation to the King: But this is now repealed.

simpleplace.c: SIMPLE Place, a Term in Geometry. See Place Simple.

simpleproblem.c: SIMPLE Problem, in Mathematicks. See a Li - near One.

simplequantitiesinalgebra.c: SIMPLE Quantities in Algebra, are such as have but one Sign, whether Positive or Negative: Thus. a a, and b, are Simple Quantities. But a - f b, and d c - p h are compound ones.

sinapismus.c: SINAPISMUS, is a Medicine applied to the Head, and is prepared of Mustard, Wild Raddifh, and Leven. Blanchard.

sinciputthefore.c: SINCIPUT, the Fore - part of the Head, reach - ing from the Fore - head to the Coronal Suture.

sine.c: SINE, or pight Sine, is a right Line drawn from one end of an Arch, perpendicularly upon the Diameter drawn from the other end of that Arch; or it is half the Chord of twice the Arch, See more under the Word Trigonometry.
SINE ajsensu capital, is a Writ against him that alienates Lands without consent of his Chap - ter or Covent.
SINE die, in Law, when Judgment is given a - gainst the Plaintiff, he is said to be in tnifericordia profalfo clamorer suo: But when for the Defendant, then ’ tis said, Eat inde fine die.

SINE - CURES,, are Ecclesiastical Benefices with - out Cure o Souls. No Church where there is but one Incumbent, can properly be a Sine - cure. And tho ’ the Church being down, or the Parifli being become destitute of Pariftiioners, the Incum - bent may thereby be necessarily acquitted from the a & ual Performance of Publick Duty, yet he instill under an Obligation to do it, whenever a Church ( hall be built, and there are a competent num - ber of Inhabitants. And in the mean while, if the Church be Presentative, as most such Churches are, the Incumbent is Instituted in Curam Animarum; and such Benefices are rather Depopulations than Sine - cures, and ’ twill be proper for the new In - cumbent to read the Articles, and the Liturgy in the Church - yard, oc. and to do what other In - cumbents usually do. But a Reftory or a Portion of it may properly be a Sine - cure, if there be a Vicar Endowed, and then it doth not come within the Statute of Pluralities of H.. c.. Which declares that no Parsonage which hath a Vicar Endowed, ( hall be comprehended, H c,; So that here no Dispensation is necessary to hold this Sine - cure with a former Living. Nor need he read the Articles or Divine Service, as required by K I S K Elif. c. iz. which extends only to a Benefice with Cure. A Sine - cure Donative wants no Institution and Induction. But one Presentative must have both; especially if it consist in Glebe and Tithes, and not in aPortionof Money. But the Inftituti - on must; not run in Cur am Animarum, but in fieblo - riam jive Portionem fiefioria de A. B. cc. By the above mentioned Stat. H.. not only Pre - bends and Redories, with Vicarages Endowed, but Deanrics and Archdeaconries are declared to be Benefices without Cure.

singleorsimpleexcentricity.c: SINGLE, or Simple Excentricity. See Eccen - trinity.

singultus.c: SINGULTUS, or the Hickoup, is a Convul - five Motion of the Midriff, caused by tough and irregular Particles, forcing it to this disordinate Motion. Blanchard.

sinicalquadrant.c: SINICAL Quadrant; isTpade ofBrafs or Wood, with Sines drawn from each Side interfering one another, with an Index divided by Sines also, with ninety Degrees on the Limb, and two Sights to the Edge, to take the Altitude of the Sun. Sometimes instead of Sines, ’ tis divided all into el qual Parts: And is used by Seamen to solve by in - f p ed ion any Problem of Plain Sailing.

sinistersideorpart.c: SINISTER Side or Part of an Escutcheon, is the left Side Part. Vide Escutcheon.

sinner.c: SINNER, is a Line or String made of Rope - yarn, consisting generally of two, fix, or nine Strings which are divided into three Parts, and are planted over one another, and then it is beaten smooth and flat, with a Wooden Mallet, its use is to Serve the Ropes, that is to keep them from galling. SI non ones, is a Writ of Association, whereby, if all in Commission cannot meet at. the Day assign - ed, it is allowed, That two, or more of theist may. finish the Business.

sinus.c: SINUS, any Cavity in or between the VefTefs of an Animal Body, the Anatomists call a Sinus, and some Philosophical Writers call those FifTures or Cavities which are between the several Strata or Layers of the Earth, in Mines, &c. by this Term Sinus, for Sinus in Mathematicks. See Sine.
SINUS OJfium, are those Cavities of the Bones, which receive the Heads of other Bones.

SINUS, in the Dura Mater, is that strong and thick Membrane which covers all the Cavity of the Cranium. There are several eminent Sinus's or Chanels, which run between its External and In - ternal Membrane: Of these four principal ones are dually described; as. The Sinus Longitudinalis, and Sinus Later ales; and Sinus Vertebralis. /.. ) SI fie cogmfc ant, is a Writ that lies fora Credi - tor against his Debtor, for Money Numbred, and ovyned before the Sheriff in the County - court by the Debtor, to be due to the Creditor.

sinusmeningium.c: SINUS Meningium, are those Cavities which Galen calls the Ventricles of the Thick Membrane. The first and second, or the Lateral Sinus, are seated between the Brain and the Cer ebellum, and end in the vertebral Sinus ’ s. The third begins from the Os Cribriforme, and ends in the middle of the former Sinus ’ s. The fourth arises from the Pinealis Glandule, and ends in the middle of the lateral Sinus ’ s. The Insertion of these Sinus ’ s is called Trocular Herophili. The Sinus ’ s, after they have paired through the Scull, are partly continue - ed with the Jugular Veins, and partly descend through the whole length of the Spinal Marrow down to the Os Sacrum. The use of them is to supply the place of Veins, for they convey the Blood from the Brain and Cerebellum, partly into the Jugular Veins, and partly into the Vertebral Sinus ’ s. Blanchard. With us the Ventricles of the Brain are accounted only the three Partitions or Subdivisions of the Forinx and they serve as a Sink to drain away the excrementitious Matter of the Brain.

siphonaglass.c: SIPHON, a Glass or metalline crooked Pipe, Tube, or Cane. See Syphon. SI Becognofcant, is a Writ that lies for a Credi - tor against his Debtor, for Money numbered, that hath before the Sheriff in the County Court, ac - knowledged himself to owe his Creditor such a Sum, Received of him in pecuniis numeratis,

siriusthedog.c: SIRIUS, the Dog - star, a bright Star of the first Magnitude, in the Constellation Canis major, its Longitude is Degrees, Minutes, Latitude Degrees, a Minutes.

sirones.c: SIRONES, little Pufhes in the Palm of the Hand, and Sole of the Foot, containing certain small Infedts or Worms.

skarfedtheseaterm.c: SKARFED, the Sea Term, when one Piece of Timber is let and fatten'd into another. See Scarfed.

skeleton.c: SKELETON, of a Man or other Animal, is when the Bones are cleaned and dry, and put to - gether according to Art in their natural Order and Position.

skuppersandskupper.c: SKUPPERS, and Skupper - holes. See Scoper - holes.

slatch.c: SLATCH, when any Rope or Cable hangs slack, the Seamen call the middle Part which hangs hangs down, the Slatch of the Cable or Rope, so alio after long foul Weather, if there come a stall Interval of fair, they fay, this is a Slatch of fair Weather.

sleeperstimbers.c: SLEEPERS, Timbers lying before and aft in the bottom of a Ship as the Rung - heads do; the lowermost of them is bolted to the Rung - heads, and the uppermost to the Buttocks, in order to strengthen and fallen the Euttockj and f ( lungs.

slidingstiles.c: SLIDING Stiles, or Scales, are Instruments to be used without Compasses, in Gauging, Meafu - ring, &c. having their Lines fitted so as to answer Proportions by Infpedtion j they are very Ingeni - oily contrived and applied by Gunter, Partridge, Cogjhall, Everard, Hunt, and others, Who have Written particular Treatises about their Use and Application.

slingaword.c: SLING, a Word used variously at Sea, there are Slings to hoise up Casks or any other heavy things; which are made of Ropes, spliced into themselves at either end, with an Eye big enough to hold the thing to be Slung. There are other Slings which are made longer and with a small Eye at each end, one of which is put over the Breech of a Piece of Ordnance, and the other Eye comes over the end of an Iron Crow, which is put into the Mouth of the Piece, to Weigh and Hoise the Gun as they please. There are also Slings for the Yards, which is done by binding them fall to the Cross - tree aloft, and to the Head of the Mali with a strong Rope or Chain, that if the Tye should happen to break, or to be ( hot to pieces in a Fight, the Yard neverthe - less may not fall down upon the Hatches.

smelling.c: SMELLING, is probably occasioned by the Ef - fluvial of Odorous Bodies mingling themselves with the Air, and entring up the Noftriis, which are co - vered with a very Nervous and Sensible Coat, and there insinuating themselves into the Processes of the Olfadtory Nerve, do move it variously accord - ding to their various and different Nature, and so communicate to the Brain, such corresponding Mo - tions, as enables the Soul to judge differently of the Bodies emitting such Effluvia: And from hence when the Effluvia produces a grateful Sensation, we fay it hath a sweet Smell, but when a disagree - able one, we fay it ftinks.

smithing.c: SMITHING - Line, in a Ship, is a Small Rope fattened to the Missen - yard Arm, below at the Deck, and is alway furled up with the Miifen - fail, even to the upper end of the Yard, and from thence It comes down to the Poope. Its Use is to loose the Miifen - fail without striking down the Yard, which is easily done, because the Miifen - fail is furled up only with Rope - yarns; and therefore when this Rope is pulled hard, it breaks all the Rope - yarns, and so the Sail falls down of it self. The Word of Art is. Smite the Mijscn ( whence this Rope takes it Name; ) that is, hale by this Rope that the Sail may fall down.

snatchblocks.c: SNATCH Blocks, is a great Block in a Ship, with a Shiver in it, having a Notch cut thro ’ one of its Cheeks for the more ready receiving in of any Rope: For by this Notch, the middle part of a ’ Rope may be reeved into this Block, without paiTing it in end - ways This ready Block is com - monly fattened with a Strap about the Main - matt, close to the Upper Deck, and is chiefly used for the Fall of the Winding Tackle, which is reeved into this Block, and then brought to the Capstan.

snow.c: SNOW. The Learned Dr, Grew, in Philofc - f hi cal Trans actions, N.. gives the following Account of Snow, which seems very ead and just. , With Mr. Des Cartes, and Dr. Hook, he observes, That many parts hereof ate of a Regular Figure for the molt part being as it were so many little Rowels, or Stars of Points being perfect and transparent Ice, hs any one may fee upon a Pool, or Vessel of Water upon each of which Points, are fet other collateral Points, and those always at the fame Angles, - as are the main Points them - selves. ' a. Amongst these Regular Figures, tho ’ many of them are large and fair; yet from these taking our first Item, many others, alike Regular, but far less, may likewise be discovered. . Amongst these, not only Regular, but entire Parts of Snow, looking till more warily, we spial ! perceive, that there are divers others indeed ire - gular, which yet are chiefly the broken Points Parcels, and Fragments of the Regular ones, - That besides the broken parts, there are some others which seem to have loft their Regular - city, not so much in being broken, as by various Winds, first gently Thaw ’ d, and then - Froze into little irregular Clumpers again. From whence the true Notion, and external ! Nature of Snow, seemeth to appear, vi. That not only some few parts of Snow, but originally, the whole Body of it, or of a Snowy Cloud, is an infinite Mass of Icicles regularly figured not one Particle thereof, I fay, originally, not one ossa many Million ?, being indetermined, or irregular; That is to fay, a Cloud of Vapours being gather - ed into Drops, the said Drops forthwith de - ascend; upon which Descent, meeting with a soft freezing Wind, or at least putting thro ’ a Colder Region of the Air, each drop is immediately frozen into an Icicle, hooting it self forth into several Points or Stirice, on each Hand frontward its Cen - tre: But still continuing their descent, and meet ing with some sprinkling and intermixing Gales bf Warmer Air, or in their continual Motion and Wattage to and fro, touching upon each other j some are a little thaw ’ d, blunted, frosted, clump - er ’ d, others broken, but the most hanked and clung in several Parcels together, which we call Flanks of Snow. It being known what Snow is We understand, why, though it seem to be sort yet ’ tis truly hard. because true Ice, the inseparable property whereof is to be hard; seeming only to be loft, because upon the first touch of the Finger, upon any of its harp Edges or Points, they instantly thaw; or o - otherwise they would pierce our Fingers as so many Lancets, Why again, though Snow be true Ice and so hard and dense a Body, yet very light; because of the extream thinness of each Icicle in compariforf ' of its breadth - For so Gold, which though of all Bodies it be the most ponderous, yet being, beaten into Leaves, rides upon the least breath of Air and so in all other Bodies, where there is but little Mat - ter contained within large Dimensions, and post bly in no other Case, Aittv SOL S N O Also, how it is White, not because hard; for there are many soft Bodies. White; but because confiding of parts, all of them singly transparent, but being mixed together appear White as the Parts of Froth, Glass, Ice, and other transparent Bodies, whether soft or hard. Thus much for the External Nature of Snow let us next enquire into its Essential Nature. Now to make a Judgment of this, is by confi - during, what the general Figure of Snow is, and comparing the fame with such Regular Figures as we see in divers other Bodies, in that where we see the like Configurations, we may believe there is the like Subject wherein, or the like Efficient whereby but those and these are made. As for the Figure of Snow, ’ tis generally one, vi. that which is above described: Rarely of dis - ferent ones, which may be reduced chiefly to two general Circulars and Hexagonals, either Simple or Compounded together, more rarely, either to be seen of more than Points but if so, then not. of or o but. Or in single Shoots, as so ma - ny short, slender Cylinders, like those of Nitre. Or by one of those shoots, as the Axle - tree, and touching upon the Centre of a Pair of pointed Ici - cles, joyned together as the two Wheels. Or the fame Hexagonal Figure, and of the fame usual breadth; but continued in thickness and profundi - ty. All these are rare, the first described being the general Figure. As for the Configuration of other Bodies we Shall find, that there are divers which have some a less, others a more near resemblance thereto. Ni - tre is formed as is commonly known in long Cy - lindrical shoots, as also all Lixivial Salts for the most part resembling, tho ’ not perfectly, the fe - veral Points of each Starry Icicle of Snow. Salt of Harts - horn, Sal Armomac, and some other vol - tile Salts, besides their main and longer shoots have others shorter Branched out from them; re - fumbling as those the main, so these the Collateral Points of the Snow, but the Icicles of Urine are till more near: For in Salt of Harts - horn, altho ’ the Collateral shoots Hand at acute Angles with the Main, yet not by pairs at equal height: And in Sal Armoniack., altho ’ they stand Diametrically opposite, or at equal height yet withal at right, not acute Angles: Whereas in the Icicles of Urine, they stand at equal Heights, and at acute Angles both -; in both, like those of Snow. And it is ob - fervable that the Configuration of Feathers is like - wife the fame. The reason whereof is, because Fowls having no Organs for Evacuation of Urine, the Urinous Parts of their Blood are evacuated by the Habit or Skin, where they produce and nou - rish Feathers. From whence it should seem, That every Drop of Rain aforesaid, containing in it self some Spirit - tuous Particles, ( as from the height to which they are advanced, the prolific Vertue of Rain, and its easie tendency to Putrefa & ion, above other a -. ter, is argued they do ) and meeting with others in their Descent, of a Saline, and that partly Ni - trous, but chiefly Urinous, or of an acid - salinous Nature; the said Spirituous Parts are apprehended by them, and with those the Watry j and so the whole Drop is fix ’ d, yet not into any indifferent and irregular shape, depriving their Spirituous parts of their Motion in an instant; but according to the Energy of the Spirituous, as the Pencil, and the Specifick Nature, or determinate possibility of the Saline Parts, as the Ruler, ’ tis thus figured in - to a little Star. These things somewhat further considered and cleared, may add a little to that great deal of Light which the Honourable Mr. Boyle, hath given to the Nature of Cold, the Air, and the Bodies therein contained, in his Excellent Discourse thereof.

soc.c: SOC, is a Word signifying a Sewer, or Liberty of Jurifdi & ion; whence comes the Law Latins Word Soca, for a Seigniory enfranchised by the King, with liberty of holding a Court of his Sock -, : men or Socagers j that is, his Tenants, whose Te - j nure is hence called Socage.

soccage.c: SOCCAGE, is a Tenure of Lands by, or for certain inferior Services of Husbandry to be per - formed to the Lord of the Fee, or is a Tenure of Lands, when a Man is infeoffed freely without a - ny Service, W ard, Relief, or Marriage, and pays to his Lord such Duty as is called, Petit Sergeanty, &c. There is also Free, or Common Socage, and Bast Socage, or Villenage. Other Divisions thereof there are in Law Books: But by the Statute Car.. cap.. all Tenures still be adjudged, and taken to be turned into free and common Socage.

socmansorsokemans.c: SOCMANS, or Sokemans, are such Tenants as hold their Lands and Tenements by Socage Te - nure. SOLiEUS, is a Muscle that helps to extend the Foot.

solarcycle.c: SOLAR Cycle. See Cycle of the Sun.

solarspots.c: SOLAR Spots. See. Spots of the Sun.

solartear.c: SOLAR Tear, is either Tropical, or Siderial. Tropical Tear, is that Space of Time, wherein the Sun returns again to the fame Equinoctial, or Solstitial Point, which is always equal to Days, Hours, and about Minutes. The Siderial Tear is the Space wherein the Sun comes back to any particular Fixed Star, which is about Days, Hours, and Mi - nutes.

sole.c: SOLE - Tenant, is he or she that holds only in his or her own Right, without any other joined: As, if a Man and his Wife hold Land for their Lives, the Remainder to their Son here the Man dying, the Lord shall not have Heriot, because ' he dieth not Sole - Tenant.

solidingeometry.c: SOLID, in Geometry, is the Third Species ios Magnitude, having three Dimensions, Length, Breadth and Thickness; and is frequently used in the fame fence with Body. It may be conceived to be formed by the direst Motion, or the Revo - lation of any Superficies, of what Nature, or Fi - gure soever.

solidangle.c: SOLID Angle, is an Angle made by the meet - ing of three or more Planes, and those joining in a Point, like the Point of a Diamond well cut.

solidnumbers.c: SOLID Numbers, are those which arise from the Multiplication of a Plain Number, by any other whatsoever; as. is a solid Number made of, ( which is a Plane ) multiplied by j or of mul - tiplied by.

solidplace.c: SOLID Place. See Place solid. SOLID I sou

solidproblem.c: SOLID Problem, in Mathematicks, is one which can ’ t be Geometrically solved, but by the Interfe - cftion of a Circle, and a Conick Se & ion; or by the Intersection of two other Conick Sections be - sides the Circle. As, To describe an Isosceles Triangle on a given Right Line, vohofe Angle at the Safe, shall be trifle to that at the Vertex. This will help to Inscribe a Regular Heptagon, in a given Circle, and may be re solved by the In - terfedion of a Parabola and a. Circle. The following Problem also helps to Inscribe a Nonagon in a Circle; and may be solved by the Interledion of a Parabola, and an Hyperbola be - tween its Asymptotes: Vi To describe an Isosceles Triangle, vohofe Angle at the Base, Shall be Quadruple of that at the Vertex. And such a Problem as this, hath solutions, and no more; because Conick Sections can cut one another but in Points. How all such Problems are construed, Mr. Halley ( hews in Philofoph. Tranfacl. N..

solidity.c: SOLIDITY ( Tee Firmness ) is a Quality of a Natural Body contrary to Fluidity, and appears to consist in the Parts of Bodies being interwoven and intangled one with another, so that they cannot disuse themselves several ways, as Fluid Bodies can.

sollicitor.c: SOLLICITOR, is a Man employ ’ d to take care of, and follow Suits depending in Courts of Law, or Equity, formerly allowed only to Nobility, whose Menial Servants they were; but now too frequently used by others, to the damage of the People, and the increase of Champerty and Main - tenancy.

solstice.c: SOLSTICE, is the Time when the Sun entring the Tropical Points, is got furthest from the Equa - tor, and before he returns back towards it, seems to be for some time at a stand, being moved in the fame Parallel, andfcarce making any other Lines than versed Circles, so small is its Progress. These Solstices are two: Estival, or Summer Soljlice, when the Saw en - ters Cancer the ith of Sfune, making the longest Day, and the shortest Night. And the Hyemal. or Winter Soljlice, on the nth of December, when he enters Capricorn, the Nights being then at the longest, and Days at the shortest; that is, in Northern Regions, for under the Equa - tor there is no Variation, but a continual Equinox; and in the Southern Parts, the Sun ’ s Entrance into Capricorn, makes the longest Day; and into Cancer, the longest Night.
SOLSTICE, how to find the exadfc Times of Solstices. See under Tropick in Vol..

solubletartar.c: SOLUBLE Tartar, is made by boiling in Pints of Water, Ounces of Cream of Tartar, and Ounces of the Fix ’ d Salt of Tartar, for a - bout half an Hour in an Earthen Pan unglazed; and then when ’ tis cool, filtrating and evaporating it till ’ tis dry: t r Ounces and Drams of Salt will remain at the Bottom. This is th t Soluble Tartar. ’ Tis accounted a very good Aperitive Medicine. ’ T is called also a Vegetable Salt. Sometimes the Tinclure of Mars is added in this Preparation, and then ’ tis called Soluble Tartar Chalybeate, i An Emetic Tartar, is also made of this Sol able Tartar, and Liver of Antimony, which works as the common one

solvendosjfe.c: SOLVENDO Sjfe, a Term in Law, signifying that a Man hath wherewith to pay, or is a Perfoti folveiit.

solvent.c: SOLVENT, the fame with Diffolveht, being any Corroiive Liquor, or Menfiruun, that will diflblve Bodies.

solutiochymica.c: SOLUTIO Chymica is a resolving any Body into its Chymical Principles; which are, Spirit, Salt, Sulphur, Earth and Water.

solutio.c: SOLUTIO continui, is a Dissolution of the ti - any and Continuity of the Parts: As in Wounds, Ulcers, Fradhires, Sc.

solutioninmathematicks.c: SOLUTION, in Mathematicks, is the answer - ing of any Question, of the Resolution of any Problem.

solutions.c: SOLUTIONS feodi Militis Pariiamenti, and Solutione feodi Burgens Pariiamenti, are Writs whereby Knights of the Shire and Burgesses may recover their Allowance, if it be. denied.

somniferousorsleepingmedicines.c: SOMNIFEROUS, or Sleeping Medicines, are such which consisting of fetid Sulphureous Parts, dissipate ana extinguish the Animal Spirits, and hinder their Increase, whence follows Sleep. Blan - chard.

sophisticated.c: SOPHISTICATED, the fame with counterfeit - ted, debated, or adulterated; and is usually so - ken of Wines, Chymical Preparations, Sc. where they are not made good in their Kinds, thro ’ the Avarice of the Composer.

sorites.c: SORITES, is a fort of Argument composed of several Propositions, of which the second depends upon the first, the third upon the second, and so forward.

sorrow.c: SORROW, is uneasiness in the Mind, upon the thought of a Good loft, which might have been enjoy ’ d longer; or the sense of a present Evil.

sound.c: SOUND, seems to be produced by the subtile, and more Etherial Parts of the Air, being formed and modified into a great many small Masses or Contextures, exactly similar in Figure; whkh Contextures are made by the Collision and peculiar Motion of the Sonorous Body, and flying off from it, are diffused all around in the Medium, and there do affedt the Organ of our Ear in one and the fame manner, Sound, also appears not to be produced in the Air, so much by the swiftness, aS by the very fre - quent Repercuflions, and reciprocal Shakings of the Sonorous Body. Sir Isaac Newton demonstrates, fin Prop. J Lib.. of his Principles; ) That Sounds, because they arise from the Tremulous Motion of Bodies, are nothing else but the Propagation of the Pulse of the Air. And this he faith, is confirmed by those great Tremors that strong and grave Sound excite in Bodies round about, as the Ringing of Bells, noise of Cannon, Sc. And in another place he concludes, That Sounds do not consist in the Motion of any lether, of finer ' Air, but in the Agitation of the whole common Air; because he found by Experiments, That the Motion of Sound depended on the Density of the whole Air. He found by good Experiments, That a Sound moves Feet, Englifli, in a Second of Time, pag. ssp / S O s o Supposing the Air by the Pulse which causes i Sound, to be in a Motion, like that of the Water when its W aves roul; he calculates the Breadth of the Pulse, or the Distance between Wave and Wave, to be in the Sounds of all open Pipes, dou - ble the Length of those Pipes, which he grounds on an Experiment of Father Merfennus, in his Har - monicas, that an extended String made Vibra - tions in a Second, when it was an Unifone with the C, fa, at Pipe of an Organ, whose Length was Foot open, and Footftop ’ d, fag,. Why the Sound ceases always with the Motion of the Sonorous Body j and why they reach the Ear equally soon, when far off, or near: He hews in Prof.. Cor. where he proves, That the Num - ber of the Pulles propagated, is always the very fame with the Number of the Vibrations of ' the Tremulous Body, and that they are not by any means multiplied as they go from it. T he following, Properties have been observed of Sound; in many of which, there is a near Re - lation between it and Light. For. . As Light acquaints the Eye with the dise - rent Qualities, Magnitudes, and Figures of Bo - dies, so Sound in like manner informs the Ear of many of the fame Things, in the Sonorous Body. . As Light presently vanishes on the Removal, or Total Eclipse of the Radiating Body, so a Sound perifhes bassoon as the Undulation of the Air ceases, which Motion both produces and preferveth all Sounds. . The Diffusion of Sound from the Sonorous Foiy is Spherical, like the Radiation of Light from its Centre. . A greater Sound drowns a less, as a greater Light Ecclipfes a less. . Too Great, Loud, or Shrill a Sound is Qf - fenlive and Injurious to the Ear, as too great and bright a Light is to the Eye. . Sound also ( like Light ) moves sensibly from Place to Place, tho ’ nothing near so swift as Light. It is Reflected like Light from all hard Bodies; it is hindred and refracted, by palling thro ’ a Denser Medium. But it differs from Light in this, that whereas Light is always propagated in Right " Lines, the Motion of Sound is almost always Curvilinear. . Sound also differs much from Light in this, that it is very much weakened by Winds, and such like Motions of the Air, which yet have no Effect on Light. For Merfennus Computes -, that the Diameter of the Sphere of a Sound heard against the Wind is near a third Part less, than when com - ing with - the Wind. . A very small quantity of Body, serves to re - sect the Rays of right: as we perceive manifest - ly in small peices of Looking - glasses, &c. But there appears to be necessary a Body of much larger Dimensions to Return a Sound, or to make an Ec - cho. f. As to Refie & ion of Sounds: ’ Tis observed, that if one stand near the Reflecting Body, and the Sound be not very far off, tho ’ an Eccho be produced, yet it cannot be heard because the Di - red ! and Reflex Sound, enter the Ear almost at the fame time: But then the Sound appears to be ' stronger than ordinary, and lasts longer: Efpeciai - ly when the - Reflexion is made from divers Bodies at once; as from Arches and Vaulted Rooms, from whence the confused Bomb of Each like Places arises. And from hence probably may be deduced, the Reason why Concave Bodies are ( ceteris paribifs ) fitted to produce great and clear Sounds; such as Bells, ( fc. for in such Bodies the Sound is very swiftly and very often Reflected from Side to Side, and from one Part of the Cavity to another, and the Bell hanging at liberty, this produces great trem - brings and shakings of the whole Concave Body, which occafionsthe Sound to continue till they cease and are quiet. . There is one Phenomenon of Sounds that is indeed very wonderful, That all Sounds great or small, with the Wind or against it, from the fame Distance, come to the Ear at the fame Time. Dr. Holder ' in his Books of the Natural Grounds and Principles of Harmony; says. That if the tremulous Motion which caufeth Sound, be Uni - form, then it produces a Musical Note, or Sound: But if it be Difform, then it produces a Noise. The Florentine Academicks found a Sound to move one of their Miles ( vi. Biaccia, or Feet ) in Five Seconds of Time: There - fore according to them, it moves Foot in one Second. But Sir Isaac Newton found it to move but Foot, in a Second of Time. Sound, in Geography, is any great Indraught of the Sea, betwixt two Head - lands, where there is no Passage through. Sounding, when the Seamen try the Depth of the Water with a Line and Plummet, they call it Sounding. But their Sounding Line, as they call it, is a Line different from the Deep Sea Line, as being bigger than it, and hot much above Fa - them in length j and is marked at Fathom, with a piece of Black Leather betwixt the Strains; so also at Fathom, and at; but at ’ tis marked with a piece of White Leather, or Cloth, This Line can be used when the Ship is under Sail; but the Deep Sea Line cannot be used well, except the Ship be brought upon the Back - stays, ( See Deep Sea Lined ) To found the deepest Sea without a Line. Note, That care must be had of proportioning the Weight and Shape of the Lead, to the Bulk, Weight, and Figure of the Globe, after such a manner, as upon Experience shall be found most convenient. As for instance: If in the Depth of Fathom, measured by the Line, the Globe stays under Wa - ter, Seconds; then if the Ball stay Se - conds, the Depth of the Sea is Fathom and Foot, if the Ball be found to move equal Spaces in equal Times. And now Im mentioning the way of finding the Depth of the Sea, it may be of use to shew you how you may get Water from thence, which shall not communicate as it comes up with any of the Water above it.
