SOUND, Mr. Carre, of the R. Academy of Sci - ences at Paris, hath Published this Year a Book Sur la Theorie General du Son, cc. In which he Ihews that Sound, when considered with relation to Body, consists only in the Motion of the Air but in such a Motion as is very different from the Wind. The first Motion from whence Sound comes, is produced ( he thinks ) by little Vibrati - ons, Shakings repeated, which the Parts of the Sonorous Body occasions in the Air whereas Wind consists in a Local Motion of the Air, with - out V vibrations; and this he proves by fe veral Ex - periments. The Motion of the Air in Winds, will at strongly on Flame, but will not affedl the Ear with Sound, but on the Inter position of some Body which may occasion some Vibrations Whereas the Agitation of the Air in Sounds af feefts not Flame j for a lighted Candle put near a ' y ' r,. ' ' v. S O il Bell which hath been struck, will not have its Flame Agitated by the Sound. He concludes also, that Sound is not produced by a Total and Sensible Vibration of the Sonorous Body j but by insensible Vibrations of the little Parts, always helped, and sometimes occasioned by total Vibrations. Thus, when a Cord hangs loose, it will move forward and backward quick enough ( when struck ) without making any Sound; because thro ’ want of being straitly extended, each little part can ’ t make its Vibrationsby its self, and communicate them to the Air. In Sonorous Bodies, in the fame, or of different Matter, the difference of Sound, as to Grave or Acute, flows from the greater or lesser Spring of each Part, and from the more or less quickness with which these Parts do bend and unbend. Two Strings or Wires, one of Gold, and the other of Steel, of the fame Length, Thickness and Tenjion, yet will give a different Sound, vi. the Gold one more Grave, the Steel - wire, one more Acute be - cause the Parts of the Gold are more soft and Flex - ible, and have less Spring thanthofeof the Iron; and therefore will have less speedy, and weaker Vibrations. But yet Sound, be it Flat or Sharp, jis still Strong or Weak.; and ’ tis not the Strength or Weakjiefs of Sound, that renders it Flat or Sharp. Strong Sound arises from Great Vibrations in the Air, and from a great Quantity of it, moved in the fame time; and the weak Sound is occasioned by the just contrary: So that the Strength or Weakness of Sound, is in Proportion to the Quantity of Air Jiruck, and the Strength of the Vibrations: But Grave and Acute Sounds follow the Proportion of Greater or Lesser Number of the Vibrations of the Air in the fame Time, The Reverend Mr. William Derham, a very In - duftrious and Useful Member of the Royal Society, in Philosophical TranfaHions, No.. hath obli - ged the World with some very Curious and Care - ful Observations, and Experiments aboutthe Mo - tion of Sound: Being furnished with very good Instruments, and many Advantages to make them, which others have not been. - He observes, first, that there hath been a confi - durable difference in the Accounts given by good Authors, about the Velocity of the Motion of Sound. Sir If. Newton, in Princip. Lib.. Prop.. allows but S Feet for the Pregrek of Sound in a Second of Time. The Hon. Mr. Fr. Roberts, Phil. Trar / f. N ?.. Feet Mr. Boyl, in his EJfay on Languid and Unheeded Motion, lo o Feet. Dr. Walker, in Phil. Trans. N.. Feet. Mefcnnus in Baliflic. Prop.. Feet. Flamfteed and Halley, Feet. The Florentine Academy, Feet. The French Observ. Hiss. Acid. Regia, Feet. The Reason of this Diversity, he judges to arise, (. ) From these Gentlemens using not good Pendu - lum Clocks ordinarily, but a String and Plummet only, of such a length as to swing Seconds. But this latter way can ’ t be so exact, as. that by a Move - ment, because the Observer ’ s Eye mull first ob - serve the Slash ofthe Gun, &c. Fired; and then the Swing of the Pendulum, which takes up Time, and occasions much Confusion. (. ) From there not being distance enough be - tween the Sound and the Place of Observation. And (. ) From there being no regard had so the Winds, of which more below. Arid he judges that the little difference there is between the three last Numbers of,, arid, arises from there being good Pendulum Clocks made use of in these Observations, and the Distances be ing considerable. After this, he proposes to answer the following Qjieftions: . How far a Sound moves in a Second of Time, and consequently in any Time alien - ed ? . Whether the Report of a Gun, Discharged with its Mouth towards, comes sooner, then when its Mu le is from the Observer ? I. Whether Sounds move in the fame Time, the some Spaces, in all States of the Atmosphere, and heights of the Barometer ? . Whether they move faster by Day, or by Night ? . Whether they move swifter with, or flower a - gainst the Wind ? And how the Wind asses them ? . Whether Sounds move faster in Calm, or Still, than iri Windy and Turbulent Wea - ther ? . Whether a strong Transverse Wind, Accele - rates or Retards the Motion of Sound ? . Whether Sounds have the fame Degree of Velocity in Summer and in Winter ? . Whether they have the fame in Snowy, and clear Weather ? . Whether a great Sound and a small one have the fame Velocity ? . Whether the Sound of a Gun move equally swift at all the Elevations of the Gun ? . Whether different Strengths of Gun - powder change the Motion of the Sound of the Report ? . Whether the Velocity be the fame in all Heights of the Atmosphere above the Earth ? . Whether the Report be in the fame Time, if the Piece be Discharged in an Acclive or Dec live P position ? . Whether all kinds of Sounds, as of Guns, Bells, Beetles, c. have the fame Velocity ? . Whether Sounds be swiftest in the begin - ning of their Motion, and lowest in the end ? . Or whether they be not rather Equable, trioving equal Spaces in equal Time s ? . Whether Sound move equally swift in all Regions ? in North, South, cc. Climates ? . Whether Sound move in a right Line, the nearest way, or whether along the Earths Sur - face ? To Solve these Problems, Mr. Derham was at the trouble of getting, and had the Advantage of heating and seeing from the Tower of his Parilh - Church at Upminfter in EJfex, many Muskets Fired at the distance of r,,, and so far as to Miles; beyond which he could not hear in that Woody - place, the Report of a Musket. But tho ’ the Fi - rings these ffnall Arms did him much Service in his Design, he was much better served by the Ordnance, or great Guns on Black - heath for he could from his Church, aforesaid, always by Night, withhis naked Eye, and by Day, with a Telef - cope, see the Flafhes of the Sakers ( a fort of Gan - non ) there Fir ’ d, to Exercise her Majefties young Enginiers, and hear their Report very plainly. On these he made many repeated Observations and at last, by Favour of the Board of Ordnance, he got leave to have two Sakert ( fee that word in VoL sou sou Vol. i. ) to be placed one by another on the Heath, but with their Muzzles quite contrary ways; and on the th of Feb. ?, to bedifcharged continue - ally every half Hour, from in the Evening till at Night: There was a small Gale of Wind blowing JireCHy against the Sound. The Interval between the Fiafti and the Re - port ol each Gun, he always found to be about s o, or half Seconds of Time. He mentions both these Numbers, because the Sound of the Re - port always came double; the first within half Seconds, the second ( which he takes to be an Echo from the Wind - mill, or adjacent Hou - fes on Black - heath ) within. He observed no difference in the Time of the Sound ’ s Progress, when the Saber was Fired to - wards him, or from him, which answers his second Question. Nor did he find that any different Elevation of the several Muskets made any alteration in the Mo - tion of the Sound; which is an Answer to his nth Problem. And to Solve the z Query, he found, that different Quantities or Strengths of Powder, made no alteration in the Velocity of the Sounds Motion; tho ’ it manifestly did foin the Strength of the Noise. Nor did he find that there was any Variety in the Time of the Motion of the Sound, either by Night or Day; whether it were Clear or Cloudy; whether it Rained or Snowed, whether ' the Barometer were high or low, and whether it were Summer or Winter: Which Solves his,,,, Queries. He found also, ih Arifwer to his th Question; that all kinds of Sounds, as of Bells, Beetles, Muskets, &c. from the fame Distance came to his Ear in the fame Time. And the fame he found, as to Intense or Strong, and Languid or W eak Sounds which answers his oth Question. By Repeated and very accurate Observations, he also found the Motion and Time of the Progression of Sound, to be in all refpetfts equable. Which Solves the th Problem. That is, that Sound moves just, an English Mile in ', or,; half Seconds: two Miles in, three Miles in I, &c. and so on uniformly., As to his pastor th Question, he is confirmed, that Sound moves the nearest way, and that it doth not creep along the Earth ’ s Curved Surface: And he believes ( in Answer to the th Query ) that the Velocity of theSound is the fame in Accli - vites and Declivites; tho ’ he hath not had Oppor - unity of making Experiments enough to determine it exactly. From the Communications which his Friends in Italy have afforded him; he thinks the difference of Regions or Climates, makes no difference in the Motion of Sounds; which is an Answer to his th Question. He found that very thick Cloudy and Snowy Weather, did always lessen and dull th Noise made by the Discharge of Guns, &. c. Whereas in Fro - sty and clear Weather, they were much more au - edible, clear and ' distinct, than at any other times. By many repeated, and accurately made Expe - riments, he discovered, that contrary Winds do always retard the Motion of Sounds and that ia Proportion to their Strength; which is what the Florentine Virtuofi, and many others have formerly been entirely mistaken in; asserting, that Contra - piety of Winds occasion no Retardation of the Mo - tion of Sound, By Observations and Experiments, made with proper Instruments about the Velocity of the Mo - tion of Wind; he concludes, that in the greatest and most rapid Storms that ever blew, the Wind moves not above Miles an Hour, and perhaps not above; whereas Sounds may go above Miles in the fame time. And consequently, they cannot be the fame Particles of the Air or Atmo - sphere, which carry both; at least they can ’ t be moved after the fame manner. He concludes, as above - said, that the Velocity of Sound is, such that it ordinarily moves Feet, or an Englifit Mile in lr half Seconds: And that it moves in a half, and Feet, in a whole Second of Time. But that the Winds may so ate & it, by confpiririg with its Motion, as to carry it Feet in a half Second; or by being contrary to it, to retard it so, that it may not move more than Feet in a half Second of Time. He concludes, with Brewing the Uses that may be made of this Knowledge of the Velocity of the Motion of Sound. In measuring the Distances of Ships at Sea from one another, or of a Ship from Shoar; of Forts and Batteries one from another, or of any Places at Land Within the hearing of the Report of a Gun; of the Distances of Thunder, Clouds, &c. i In Philosophical TranfaElions, N -. you have an Account erf the Dodlrine of Sounds, by Narcissus, Bishop of Ferns and Leighlin, And in N., of the Swiftnels of Sounds, and their Reflections by Echoes. In the History of the Royal French Academy for A. D., They fay, it hath been experienced, ; that a Sound moves of their Toifes in a Se - cond, or middle French Leagues in an Hour. (. ) Thereforethey conclude, that the Air must be moved or ftruckat first with a very great Smart - ness or Swiftness.. All Conjectures and PKyfi - cal Reafohings, persuade us that this Motion or Stroke on the Air must be imprest by very brisk Vibrations of the small Parts of the Sonorous Bo - dy, in order that they may exert their Spring or Elastick Force., (. ) In philosophical Tranfattions, N.. you have an account of some Experiments of Mr. Haveksbee ’ s, whereby it appears plain - ly; that as Exhausting the common Air out of a Receiver, doth very much lessen the Noise made by the Bell there hung and struck; so crowding or conveying more Air into vessel, made o pur pole for such Condenfations of Air, did ve - ry sensibly augment the Sound of the included Bell.

space.c: SPACE, if considered, barely in Length, be - tween any two Beings, is the fame Idea that we have of Distance but if it be considered in Length, Breadth and Thickness, it is properly called Capa - city: And when confider ’ d between the Extremi - ? ies of Matter, which fills the Capacity of Space, S P E with something, Solid, Tangible, and Moveable, or with Body it is then called Extension, so that Ex - tension: is an Idea belonging to Body only; but Space Stis plain may be considered without it. So that Space, in the general signification, is the fame thing with Distance, confider ’ d every way, whe - ther there be any solid Matter in it or not. Space therefore, is either Absolute or Relative. Absolute Space, considered, in its own Nature, and without regard to any thing external, always remains the fame, and is immoveable; but field - i tive Space, is that moveable Dimension or Mea - lure of the former, which our Senses define by its Positions to Bodies within it and this the vulgar use for immoveable Space, Relative Space, in Magnitude and Figure, is al - ways the fame with Absolute, but ’ tis not necessary it should be so Numerically. Thus if you suppose a Ship to be indeed in absolute Reft, then the Places of all things within her, will be the fame Also - lutely and Relatively, and nothing will change its Place. But then suppose the Ship under Sail, or in Motion, and she will continually pass thro ’ new Parts of absolute Space: But all things on Board confider ’ d Relatively, in rested to the Ship, may be notwithstanding in the fame Places, or have the lame Situation andPofition, in regard to one another.

speciesinalgebra.c: SPECIES in Algebra, are those Letters, Notes, Marks, or Symbols, which represent the Quanti - ties in any Equation or Demonstration. This short and advantageous way of Notation, was first Introduced by Vieta, about the Year., and by it he made many discoveries in the Proceis of Algebra, not before taken notice of. The Pveafon why Vieta gave this Name of Spe - cies, to the Letters of the Alphabet subservient to Algebra, ar. d why he calls it ArithmeticaSpeci - rfa: S P E S P E bfa: Seems to have been in Imitation of the Ci - vilians, who call Cafes in Law, but abftra & edly be - tween John a - Nokes and John a - Stiles, or between A, B, and C, supposing those Letters to stand for any Persons indefinitely such Cafes, I fay, they call Species. Wherefore since the Letters of the Alphabet will also as well represent Quantities, as Persons, and that too Indefinitely one Quantity as well as another, they may properly enough be cal - led Species that is Symbols, Marks or Chara - ters. From whence the Litteral Algebra is fre - quently now a - days called Specious Arithmetic, or Algebra in Species.

specifickgravity.c: SPECIFICK Gravity, is the Appropriate and peculiar Gravity or Weight, which any Species of Natural Bodies have, and by which they are Plainly Distinguishable from all other Bodies of Different kinds. By some bis not improperly called Relative Gravity, to distinguish it from Absolute Gravity, which encreases in Proportion to the Big - ness of the Body weighed. Thus if any Body weigh a Pound, one as big age will weigh two Pounds: And let the Bodies be of what Nature or Degree of Specifick Gravity soever, a Pound of one will be as much as a Pound of the other Absolutely considered: hus, as is commonly said, a Pound of Feathers, is as heavy as a Pound of Lead. But if you con'lder Lead and Feathers Relatively, the Specifick Gravity of the Former, will be much greater than that of the Latter. Or Lead, or Bulk, for Bulk will be much heavier than Sea - thers: And Gold heavier than Lead, c. ’ Tis of so great Advantage in many respects s will appear below to find truly the Specifick Gravi - ties of Bodies, that many Curious Ways have been thought of, and experimented for this Purpose. As by forming exaCt Cubes of different fubftan - ces, and taking their Weight accurately in Nice Scales; and by melting Metals of different Gravities, and then calling them in Moulds of the fame Dimensions. But for Practice and Univer - sal Use, nothing is better than the following Me - tho, which is to weigh any Body first in Air, and then in Water which latter being consider - bly a Denier Fluid than Air, will buoy up the Bo - dy immersed in it in part and will consequently make it weigh less there than in the Air. And if after this you substract the W eight found in the Water, from the former in the Air a Remainder or Difference will be found, which is the Weight of as much Water as is equal to the Bulk of the Body. As Archimedes hath demon - rated Mathematically add Mr. Boyle Physically and Experimentally, in his Hy draft at i cal Paradoxes. So that by tins means having two Bodies, one Firm, and the other. Li - quid, with the Weight of each part, tis very easie to find the Proportion that one hath to the ae - ther, Bulk for Bulk by only dividing the greater by the lesser; for the Quotient will hew the Specifick Gravity of the heavier Body compared with as much Water as is equal to it in Bulk. As if the Quotient be,,, or the Body will accordingly be twice, thrice,, or times as hea - vy as Common Water. The Application of which Rule, and the great; Advantages which may be made of the Ule of it. - You will find in the following Problems or Expe - riments. I. To find the Specifick Gravity of such Bodies as will JinJ in Water, and not be dissolved by it. Having ready a Pair of good small Scales which will turn with the of a Grain, ( or Part may do well enough ) drill a small Hole in the Middle of one Scale, thro ’ which put a Horse - hair about a Foot in length with a Knot at the upper end of it, and a Loop at the other, put as much Horse - hair in the opposite Scale, as will serve to Equiponderate the other, and having well adjusted your Scales: Weigh first the Body in the Air carefully turn the Weight into Grains, ( ’ twill be best to use Troy Weight and Writedown the Number on a Piece of Paper. Then fatten the Body to the Horse - hair, and leisurely immerse it into a Vessel of Rain; or Spring Water, and putting Weights into the oppo - site Scale, find its Weight exactly in the Water, ( where it must swim about freely, and not touch the Bottom or Sides of the Vessel. ) Turn also this Weight into Grains, and fubitradt it from the for - mer Weight in Air, and. note the Remainder by which Remainder divide the first found Weight in Air and the Quotient will be the Proportion that the Body bears to Water that is, will drew the Specifick Gravity in respect of Water, which is pitched on as a Standard to compare it by. Example. A Piece of white Marble weighed in Air Grains, and in Water Grains which fubftra - died from the former Weight left Grains by which Remainder dividing the Weight in Air , the Quotient was - r, which is the Speci - sick Gravity of Marble, in reipedt of as much Wa - ter as is equal to it in Bulk. N. B. If you practice this much, ’ twill be best to hang your Scales upon a Gibbet, or some other Reft, where they may hang freely and so you will have both your Hands at liberty for more nice - ly adjusting the Balance, and your Arm will not be weary with holding the Scale and be sure that the Scales play freely, and are no way tangled, and that you do not wet your Weights, nor Scales fora little carle ( ness may produce great Errors in such Cafes; Let also the Body hang a while in the; Water before you weigh it, and move it up and down, arid gently knock it against the Sides of the Vessel, to extricate it from all Bubbles of Air, that " else sticking. to it, may buoy it up a little, and con - ' sequently S p E S P E fequendy induce you to mistake its Weight. You Ihould also have a small pair of Plyers, or Tongs, to take up your Grains withal, left you let them fall which with your Fingers you may be apt to do, and so occasion your self a needless trouble. ' Twill be convenient also to make a little Net of Horse - hair ( of small Malh. es ) to hold round, or small Bodies, that cannot conveniently be fastened with one Hair only; be sure always to Equipoise your Scales, before you begin to weigh. The Vfes of this Experiment. . Since common Stone, Marble, and Rock - Chrystal, &c. ( See the Table of Specifick. Gravity ) are to W ater, but as f ( or to; ) if you find a piece of strong Matter, whose Specifick. Gravity, exceeds that Proportion, you may conclude, That it hath in it something of a Mineral, or Metalline Nature, in proportion to its excess above the Weight of common Stone. . By this Method also, a Body may be exami - ned, whether it be of a stony Nature, or not ? So Coral and Pearls, will be discovered to approach rather to a Stony, than to a common Vegetable, or Animal Nature; and Begoar, and the Stones found in the Bladders of Men, or other Animals, will by their great lightness Ihew themselves of a very different Constitution from ordinary Stones. . By this Method, you may make an Estimate of the Goodness of several Stones, or Bodies of the fame Kind, or Denomination: For having found the Gravity of such as are Excellent, all o thers of lesser Goodness, may easily be diftingui - shed, as they are any way diverse from that Stan - dard. . And thus also Genuine Stones, or Minerals, may be easily distinguished from falfeones; and counterfeit Money readily known from Sterling, tho ’ never so well wash ’ d over, or gilded for ha - ving by your own Trials, or by the help of such a Table as is here annexed, gotten the Specifick Gra - city of such Stones, Gems, or Corns, as are True and Genuine, let that be the Standard whereby to estimate others by which Iaft use, is of universal Advantage, and may assist the Physician, Apothe - cary, or Druggist in the Drugs, the Jeweller in Gems, and Precious Stones, and the African Mer - chant, in the Choice of theSandorDuft Gold, which is often Counterfeit. Had the Curious Dampicr known this Method, he might perhaps have trucked and gotten some of the Indian yellow Rings at the Bafhee Ifiand vid. Dampicr s Travels, Edit,. Chap.. p.. ) which it appears he had no great Encouragement to do, not being able exactly to diftinguifli whether they were Gold or not. II. To weigh Mercury, or such heavy Fluids that will sink L into, and not mingle with Water as also the Fragments nf or small Precious Stones, Pearls, See. and all Powders that are heavier than Water, small Sands, Filings of Metals, Gold Grains, or Dv. fi, and such like small things about which a Horse - hair cannot be fafined. To provide a small Glass Jar, or a little Silver or Brass Cup but Glass is best when it can be had ) with two Handles or Egrs to it, and that shall hold about an Ounce and a fdalf, or two Ounces of Water and weighing it carefully in the Air first, note exa & dy its Weight, which lay by in some ready Place ) then also find the Glass s Weight in Water, and lay the Weights carefully by, by themselves; and if you intend to make frequent use of this Practice, ’ twill be better to get two pieces of Lead, one of the weight of the Gl fs in the Air, the other ' of its weight in Water, which ’ will be always in readiness. This done, put the Mercury, Liquor, or Powder ' you intend to weigh into your Glass, ( which may be called the Hydrcfia - tical Bucket ) and putting into the opposite Scale the before - found weight of the Bucket, find the weight of the Matter in. Air, and write it down ( as in Ex - pediment. ) then take the Bucket out of the Scale, and pour into it by degrees ( that it may mingle well with it, and exclude all Air ) Water enough to cover the Matter, or wet it throughly and then putting into the opposite Scale the weight that an - Iwers to the Bucket in Water, fasten your Bucket by a Horse - hair to your Scale, and let it down gently into a Vessel of Water, and so find its weight carefully in the Water then ( as in Experiment. ) Subftradt that from the weight in Air, and by the Remainder divide he weight in Air, and the Quo - tient will be the specifick Gravity of the Liquor, Powder, &c. to as ) nuch Water as is equal to it in Bulk. III. To weigh such solid Bodies as will dissolve in, or be injured in Water. Weigh them ( as before ) first in Air, and then in - stead of Water, use the clear Oil or Spirit of Tur pontine, which is cheap enough, and may be had at any Bruggifts, in which no Salts, nor Vitriols, nor Acid Sublimates will dissolve and proceed in all things, as if you weighed the Body in Water and so you will obtain the specifick Gravity of the Body in respect of Oil of Turpentine which may be the Rule for these forts of Bodies, as common Water was for the others. And this way will have the fame Use as the other: For having at any time weighed a piece of any Body ( as suppose Mercurius dulcis ) in the Oil, that you know is good that may be your Standard to try more of the fame Sublimate for the future for if you find it hath not the lame specifick Gravity that the for - mer ( which you weighed ) had, but is lighter, you may conclude it hath notits due proportion of Mer - cury; and consequently, is adulterated, as indeed that which is Sold in the Druggists Shops often is and therefore those that deal much in such things, may make a Table ( from their own Experience ) of the weights of Bodies in rested of Oil of Tur - pontine, which will be of ready Use to them: And then their specifick Gravity in refpeeft of Water, ( by a little Calculation ) may be easily enough found by the following Experiment. IV. To find the Specifick. Gravity of Liquids and Fluids. . These are of two forts, and consequently ’ twill be expedient to be furnished with a double Standard to examine them by. In order therefore to find the weight of Common Water, Beer, Ale, Burning Spirits, or any Vegetable or Animal Li - quors get either a piece of Amber or Bed hard Seal - ing S PE S P E iti Wax, or a Roll of common Brim ft one, and weigh it first in the Air, and then in the Liquor you in - tend to examine; and ( proceeding as in Exper. r. ) you will thence find the specifick Gravity of that Body in respect of the Flu id, and consequently of the Fluid in respect of that Body: And therefore pitch - ing on that Body as your common Standard, ’ tis easie to compare the Weight of all Liquids of the first kind in reference to it; for those in which the Body weighs lefts, will be the Heavier Liquors: and those in which it weighs more, lighter, in proportion to the decrease or increase of the weights of your Standard in the Fluid, .. - / . But to find the Weights of strong briny Sea - water, saline Aienftrua, and all acid Spirits and Stygian - waters, as the Oil of Vitriol, Aqua - fort is, &c. ’ twill be necessary to employ a heavier Body for your Standard, and therefore in such, weigh either a piece of RocftChryftal, or which will do as well, white Marble, ora piece offolid Glass such as the Tobacco stoppers of that Metal, &c. which being more ponderous, will sink in these Liquors, in which Amber or Wax will not; and proceed as above in the former part of this Expe - riments. V E S. . By these Experiments, the goodness of all kinds of Liquors may be examined For, as to the first kind of Liquors before - mentioned, ’ tis probable, the more fine and spirituous they are, the lighter they will be, and the more your piece I of Amber or Sealing - wax will weigh in them j which having once weighed in some Liquor of the kind, that you were allured was good, the weight of your Piece in that, may be the Standard to com - pare others by. But the latter fort of Liquors will require a contrary way of estimation; for the more ponderous they are, the better they may be judged to repand consequently, the lels your piece of Marble or Glass weighs in them, the greater de - gree of goodness you may conclude them to con - tain. By weighing also the Solid in a parcel of any kind of these that you have proved as good, its weight may be the Standard, to compute the goodness of those of the lame fort of Liquors. - - Hence also you may tost accurately discover, whether you are imposed upon by the Merchant, Vintner, or Distiller, &c. in Quantities of PVine or Spirits, which you have bought on the Credit of the Sample that was shewed you to examine for if you find that the specifick Gravity of the whole Vessel stent y ou home, is different from that parcel which you tried, you may be assured, that ’ tis some way mix ’ d and adulterated, . The Chymist also may by this means adjust his Menfttrua for the dissolving of Mineral or Me - tallick Bodies to the belt advantage by so tem - pering them, ( either by weakening their Strength, or increasing it ) that they shall prove the most ex - perite Diffolvents: For many know very well, that a Menftmum may as well be too strong, as too weak: and therefore the specifick Gravity of an apt Menstruum may perhaps be the best guide to pro - portion another for the fame purpose. V. Vo find the stolid Content of ' any small Body, tho never so irregular, ( if it be heavier than Water ) by weighing it in Water, Mr. Boyle, by many curious Trials, found that a Cubic Inch of Water is equal in weight to about a Grains, or half an Ounce, and Grains Troys Which Number of Grains is very happy for such Trials, because of its many aliquot Parts and al - so, because every Grains answers to just ft of an Inch. Suppose therefore you weigh a Body first in Air, and then in Water, and shail find it in the latter Medium to lose of its we ghtfinAir just Grains or ft Ounce Grains, you may conclude that the solid Content of that Body is just one Cubic Inch and if it lose but f or ft, or ft of that number of Grains, the Content is ft, ft, ft of a Cubic Inch So on the other side, if it lose more than gr as,, or times that weight its solid Content will be accordingly,, or Cubic Inches. The like is true of all other proportional Decrements of the Bodies weight, in comparison of, the Stan - dard for one Cubick Inch. The reason of this Process is clear enough, if we confider that every Body weighed in Water Jofes there so much of its weight as the Water a - mounts to, which is equal to that Body in Bulk or in other words, That it weighs lels in Water, than in Air, by the weight of as much Water as is equal to the Body in bulk, which is the Fun - damental Theorem of all Hydrostaticks, and is Mathematically demonstrated by Archimedes, and Physically by Mr. Boyle, in his Hydrostatical Para - does. And since also, as is before declared, a Cubick Inch of Water weighs exactly Grains, what ever Body loses in Water just that Sum ( of its for - mer weight in Air ) must needs be in Solid Content equal to a Cubick Inch for the Decrement of its weight is equal to the weight of as much Wa - ter as its bulk takes up, ( by the universal Theorem, ) and that is found to be in weight Gr. which is exadlly equal to one Cubick Inch therefore the Content of that Body is just so much. This is more - exact than any Mensuration can be for small Bodies ’ tis very expeditious, and may be of good use ( besides its Curiosity, ) in a great many Cafes, as is obvious to any thinking Person. VI. To find the solid Content of a Body lighter than Water, by its weight in that Medium. This Experiment will have two Cafes. . When the Body to be measured will not be ' injured by the Contact of the Water, Weigh the ' Body in Air and then take a piece of Lead, or some such heavy Metal, and of a known and even weight, ( as suppose a Penny - weight or Half a Penny - weight, &c. to avoid Fractions ) and capa - ble of sinking your Body in Water. specisickmedicines.c: SPECISICK Medicines, are such as have a Pe - CuliarVertue against feme Disease; as the Quinqui - na, or Cortex Peruviana, hath to cure Intermitting Fevers: And Physicians mention in their Books three kinds of Specifick Medicines. S P E . Such as are Eminently, and Peculiarly Friend - ly to this or that Part of the Body, as to the Heart, the Brain, the Stomach, S c. . Such as do seem to Attract, Expel, or Evacu - ate some determinate Humour by a kind of Spe - cifick Power, that they ate endowed with. Thus Jalap Purges Watry Humors, Rhubarb Bile, &c. And, . Such as have a Virtue to cure by some hidden Property, this or that Particular Disease. That there are such Medicines as these, in the latter and most proper Sense of the Word, Mr. Bcyie makes very probable, by these Reasons. . The Concurrent Testimony of Experience both Ancient and Modern. Galen promised a Book on this Subject, but it is loft if he ever Wrote it. . ’ Tis manifest that Inconsiderable Quantities of Poyfons can do very great mifehief, and pro - due great and dismal Effects without any mani - sest Quality appearing to be in them: And there - fore by Parity of Reason, one would conclude, Me - dicines may be found which shall heal and do good the fame way. . The Testimony of Physicians themselves who in their Writings, do always mention some one Specifick or other, which they believed was really such And certainly it would be well worth while to keep an account of the Operations of as many pretended Specificks, as can come to any Phyfici - ans knowledge, and by no means to rejeeft all things of that Nature, because a Reason cannot presently be given for the Cure; for if we should always do so, we must rejeeft almost every thing.

spellaseaword.c: SPELL, a Sea Word signifying to let go the Shears and Bowlings of a Sail, ( chiefly the Missen ) and Bracing the Weather Brace in the Wind, that the Sail may lie loose in the Wind: This is done, when a Sail hath too much Wind in it, and there is Danger of Wronging the Mast. This Word is rnoftly used about the Mijfen - fail. For there in - stead of saying take in the Missen and Peek it up; they fay in one Word Spell the Missen. To do a Spell also with them, signifies doing any Work for a short time, and then leaving it: There - fore a Fresh Spell is when Frefli Men come ro Work; and to give a Spell, is all one as ro fay Work in such an ones Room.

spenttheseamen.c: SPENT, The Seamen fay a Ship hath Spent any Mast, or Yard, when it is broken down by foul Weather, or any such accident: But if it be done by an Enemies Shot in Fight, they fay such a Yard or Mass was Jhot by the Beard.

spermatickvessels.c: SPERMATICK Vessels, and Parts, are those Arteries and Veins, which bring the Blood to, and convey it from the Testicles: Likevnfe those Vessels through which the Seed passes: Likewise all I all Whitish Parts of the Body, which because of their Colour, were Anciently thought to be made of the heed: Of this fort are the Nerves, Bones, Membranes, Griftles, &c.

sphacelus.c: SPHACELUS, is a sudden Extinction of Life and sense in every Part. SPHiENOIDALIS is a Suture that fur - rounds the Os Sphmoides, separates it from the Os Occipitis, from the Os Petr of uni, and from the Os Frontis.

spheenqides.c: SPHEENQIDES, is a Bone of the Cranium, common both to the Skull and - upper Jaw; it is of a very irregular Figure; and is situated in the middle of the Balls of the Skull, and is joyned to all the Bones of the Cranium, by the Sutura Space - noidalis, except in the middle of its Sides, where it is continued to the OJfa Petrofa as if they were one Bone. This Bone has a small Protuberance in the Middle thereof, from which the Muscles of the Uvula arise: On its Inside it has Processes call - ed Clinoides. Betwixt the two Tables of this Bone, Under the Celia Tunica, there is a Sinus divided in two in the Middle, which opens by two Holes into the Cavity of the Nostrils. In this Bone some fay, there are also iz Holes; by the first and second oafs the Optick Nerves; by the reft pass other Nerves for the Motion of other Parts, as also of Veins and Arteries.

sphjenopalatinus.c: SPHJENOPALATINUS, is a Muscle of the Gargareon, which descends from a round fiefhy Origination at a Process of the Os Sphanoidcs, which is in a direCt Line between the Ala Uefper - tilionis, and ProceJJ'us Sty hides, thence it becomes a round fiefhy Belly in half its Progress, grows less again near its lateral Inferdon to the Posterior Part of the Gargareon. This with its Partner aCting, draw the Garga - reon with the Uvula upwards and backwards; which hinders the masticated Aliment from Regur - agitating through the Foramina Narium in Degluti - tion. SPHiENOPHARlNGALUS, is a pair of Muf - cles arising from the Sinus of the inner Wing of the Os Cuneiforme, and going Obliquely downward, is extended into the Sides of the Gullet; it dilates the Gullet. SPHiENOlS. See Os Cuneforme. SPH NOPTERIGOPALATINUS. SeePte - rigopal annus.

spheroid.c: SPHEROID, is a solid Figure made by the Ro -; tation of a Semi - Elliffs about its Axis and is al - ways equal to j of its circumscribing Cylinder. Archim. de Conoid, & Spheroid.. &..

sphincter.c: SPHINCTER, is a Muscle that contracts the Gullet, Anus, Bladder, & ? ?.

sphincteram.c: SPHINCTER Am, is a large; t - hick, fleshy I Muscle encompassing the Anus Its Figure and Se j ries of Fibres Externally, immediately under the Skip, incline to an Oblong Oval: It is conneCteii forward, to the Accelerator ZJrina backwards, to die Os Coccygis its Fibres are Circular for near ! two Inches in breadth it is much larger in Men than in other Animals, in whom by reason of the ereCt Position of the Body, there is greater Force required to retain the Faces, which is the Office of this Muscle.

sphinctervagina.c: SPHINCTER Vagina, is a Muscle lying ime - diately under the Clitoris, encompassing the Vagi - na with circular Fibres Fingers in breadth: In Lome Subjedrs ( faith Mr. Cowper ) it scarce appear - eth fleshy. When this Muscle aCts, it - not only straitens the Vagina, but thereby also it hinders the Blood in its return from the Plexus retiformisei the Pudendum, by compressing some of its Veins that pass underneath, by which means the Labia be - come distended, and the Vagina contracted.

sphinctervejica.c: SPHINCTER Vejica, is a Muscle seated in the upper part of the Neck of the Bladder, immedi -, ately S P I s p l ately above the Glandula Prcjlata; whose Con - traction hinders the Involuntary Egress of the Urine.

sphygmica.c: SPHYGMICA, is that part of Physick which treats of Pulses. Blanchard.

spikes.c: SPIKES, or as the Seamen call them Specks, are large long Iron Nails with flat Heads; they are of divers lengths, feme a Foot or two long, and some are jagged, lo that they cannot be drawn out again. They are used to fallen the Planks and Timbers. They call also a kind of small Fidd, which serves them to open and Iplice small Ropes, a Marling Spike.

spiking.c: SPIKING up the Ordnance, is faftning a Coin, or Quoin with Spikes to the Deck, close to the Breech of the Carriages of the Great Guns, that they may keep close and firm to the Ship - sides and not break loose when the Ship Bolls, and by that means endanger the breaking out of the Butt - head of a Plank.

spinadorsi.c: SPINA Dorsi, are the hinder. Prominences of the Vertebra.

spinaventofa.c: SPINA Ventofa, is an Ulceration, in which the Bones are eaten by a malignant Humour without any pain of the Periosteum, or Membrane that covers the Bone: After that, a Swelling being risen without any Pain, the Part aftedled is quite eaten out with the Ulcer, from whence frequently sol - lows a ncccffity of Amputation.

spinaliscolli.c: SPINALIS Colli, is a Muscle lo called, because it accompanies the Spines of the Neck; it arises from the five Superior Transverse Processes of the Vertebra of the Thorax, and Inferior of the Neck, and in its Ascent becomes more fleshy, and is lo in - terred largely into the Inferior Part of the Vertebra of the Neck laterally, ( c. These draw the Ver - terra of the Neck directly backwards.

spindle.c: SPINDLE, is the finalleft part of a Ship ’ s Cap - flan which is betwixt the two Decks. The Spin - dle of the Jeer Capjlan hath Whelps to heave the Viol. Also the Axis of the Wheel of a Watch or Clock is called the Spindle, and its Ends the Pevets.

spinetheback.c: SPINE, the Back - Bone, or long jointed Chine - Bone that goes down the Back.

spinsteraterminlaw.c: SPINSTER, a Term in Law, being an addition usually given to all unmarried Women, from the Viicount ’ s Daughter downward.

If a right Line as A B, having one end fix ’ d at B, he equally moved round, so as with the other end B, to describe the Perphery of a Circle; and at the fame time a Point be conceived to move forward equally from B towards A in the right Line B A, so as that the Point describes that Line, while the Line generates the Circle. If also you conceive the Point B to move twice as flow as the Line A B, lo as that it flail get but half way along B A when that Line flail have for - med the Circle; and if then you imagine a new Revolution to be made of the Line carrying the Point, so that they flail end their Motion at Iaft together; there will be formed a Double Spiral Line, and two Spiral Spaces as you see in the Fi - gure. Because whatever parts of the Circumference the Point A describes, as suppose, the Point B will also have run over Parts of the Line A B, . Any Lines drawn from B to the second Spiral, as B, B, ( c. are to each other, as the a - foresaid Arks, together with the whole Periphe - ry added on both sides: For at the fame time that the Point A runs over, or the whole Peri - sphery, and perhaps parts mote, flail that Point B have run over and parts of the Line ft B, which is now supposed to be divided into equal parts. Proportional Spirals, are such Spiral Lines as the Rhumb Lines on the Terrestrial Globe, which be - cause they make equal Angles with every Meri - dian, must also ( as we shew in Prop.. of She - rick Geometry, which fee ) make equal Angles with the Meridians in the Stereographick Prove & i - on the Plane of the Equator; and therefore will be, as the Learned Capt. spirit.c: SPIRIT, which the Chymifts call Mercury, is one of the Principles separable from a Mixt, by Fire; ’ tis subtil, light, penetrating, and aiftive, and hath its Particles in a very quick Motion,, This is probably that which causes the Growth and Encrease of all Bodies; but where it abounds most, those Bodies do foOneft corrupt, because of its rapid motion. This appears in Vegetable and Animal Bodies, which yield the greatest Quantity of Spirit; whereas most Minerals, as having but a small proportion of Spirit in them, are al - most incorruptible. This Principle is never drawn pure, ’ any more ’ than the others; and when it comes over involved in a little Oil, ’ tis called an Ardent Spirit, such as Spirit of Wine; which therefore stipule rather be - called ah Exalted Oil; and when it hath in it a little Volatile Salt dissolved, ’ tis called a Volatile Spirit, as the Spirit of Hartfhom, Urine, ( c. If it be impregnated with Acid Salts, its volatility is then check ’ d, and ’ tis called an Acid or Fixt Spirit, as Spirit of Salj, Vitriol, Alluiii, &. which truly are only an Acid Salt dissolved and put into Fusion by a strong Fife.

spiritofniter.c: SPIRIT of Niter is thus drawn: Mix one part of Salt - peter with three times as much Potters - earth dried; put this Mixture into a large Earthen Retort, and let it in a close Reverberatory Fire; distill off the Phlegm with a small Fire in about or Hours, and when no more Drops will come. Lute on a very large Receiver, and encrease the Fire gradually to the d degree, some more vol - tile Spirits will come out in white Clouds: Keep the Fire thus about two Hours, and then encrease it to the greatest violence you can give ir, the Va - pours will come Red; continue the Fire till no more red Fumes come; in Hours the Opera - tion will be Over. If you used Pounds of Nitre, you will draw Pound Ounces of Phlegm and Spirit together. The Vessels had need be large, and f of the Retort left empty, else there will be danger of breaking all to pieces, the Spirits come forth with that violence. This Spirit is the belt Aqua - fort is, and is chiefly used for Solution of Metals. But when dulcified, is a good Medicine inwardly in many cafes.

spiritofsalt.c: SPIRIT of Salt is made by drying and pow - during the Salt, andahen mixing of it with thrice its weight of Potters - Earth powdred: A Paste is made of these two with a little Rain - water, and then the Paste is made into little Balls or Pellets about as big as Nuts. A large Earthen Retort or Glass one coated, hath one third of it filled with these, S P L S P O these, and being placed in a Reverberatory Fire, hath a large Receiver fitted to it. The Jun & ures must not be Luted at first, but a very moderate Fire used for a time, to distil out all the Water: But as soon as you fee some little white Clouds appear, throw out the insipid Liquor in the Receiver, and Lute it well to the Retort: Then en - crease the Fire by degrees to the highest, and so let it continue or Hours, or till no more Clouds appear i when the Operation is ended, you will find the Spirit of Salt in the Receiver. Some, rectifie this Spirit afterwards in a Cucurbite, by drawing off some of the weaker Spirit in a gentle Sand - heat, and then what remains is very strong of a yellow colour, and very weighty. If equal parts. of this acid Spirit and Spirit of Wine are mixed together, and digested for about or Days, his called Spirit of Salt dulcified. Spirit of Salt will dissolve Leaf Gold, and will precipitate what Aqua Fortis hath dillolved. Which shews how very differently formed and figured the Points ancf Pores of Acid Menstruums may be, and frequently are.

spiritofsulphur.c: SPIRIT of Sulphur, commonly call ’ d Oil of Sulphur, per Campanam, ( from the Vessels form be - ing like a Glass Bell, in which it is usually Drawn ) is only the acid Part of Sulphur turned into a Li - quor by the means of Fire. Lemery uses a great Glass Tunnel for this Operation; which seems to be the belt way of drawing this Spirit, vid. p.. last Edition. Some make use of Salt - petre in the drawing of Spirit of Sulphur, but that is not a good Practice, because the Nitre alters something of the mixture of the Spirit.

spirits.c: SPIRITS in an Animal Body, were reckon ’ d of three forts the Animal Spirits in the Brain, the Vital in the Heart, the Natural in the Liver: But late Authors distinguish ’ em only into two kinds the Animal in the Brain, the Vital and Natural ( which are accounted the fame ) in the mass of Blood. The Animal Spirits are a very thin Li - quor, which distilling from the Blood in the out - ward or Cortical Substance of the Brain, are by the proper Ferment of the Brain exalted into Spirit, and thence through the Medullar Substance of the Brain, the Corpus Callofum, and Medulla Oblongata, are derived into the Nerves and Spinal Marrow, and in them perform all the Actions of Sense and Motion. The Vital or Natural Spirits are the fubtileft parts of the Blood which actuate and ferment it, and make it fit for Nourishment.

splanchnica.c: SPLANCHNICA, are Medicines proper against Diseases of the Intestines.

splen.c: SPLEN, five Lien, the Spleen, is a Receptacle for the fait and earthy Excrements of the Blood, that there, by the Assistance of the Animal Spirits, it may be volatilize ’ d, and returning again into the Blood, may concur to its farther Fermentation. The Spleen consists of a great number of little Blad - ders, between which the Glandules are scattered up and down, and supply the place of Veins. The Spleen has like wife an Artery, Nerves, and Ly - phatick Vessels, first discover ’ d by Fr. Buifch, says Blanchard. But you will find a much better Account of it in Gibfori s Anatomy, p.. See Vol..

splenia.c: SPLENIA, are Bolfters made of Linen, three, four, or five times doubled, even to the thickness of the Spleen:, They are used upon Wounds, Ulcers, and Fratftures. The Figure is threefold, according to the manner of Application. vi. at length, obliquely, or transversely: They are called also Flumaceoli, and Flagula. Blanchard, -

spleneticartery.c: SPLENETIC Artery, is said by some to be the greatest branch of the Ceeliaca, whence ic goes to the Spleen, ' and therein ends.

splfniimufculi.c: SPLFNII Mufculi, arise partly from the five lower Vertebra of the Neck; and partly from the points of five of the upper Vertebra of the Tho - rax: The Fibres of these Muscles tend obliquely, and are fastened to the hinder part of the Head. The use of ’ errris to draw the Head backward. It hath its Name from its Figure, being something like to an Ox ’ s Spleen.

splice.c: SPLICE: at Sea they lay a Cable or Rope is spliced, when the ends of two pieces being untwf sted, the leveral Strands are wrought into one an - other by a Fidd. Alio when an Eye is to be made at the end of a Rope, the ends of the Strands are by a Fidd drawn into the ends of the other Ropes Strands and this is called a Splice.

splittheseamen.c: SPLIT the Seamen fay when a Sail is blown to pieces, it ’ s Split.

spoliation.c: SPOLIATION, is a Writ that lies for one In - cumbent against another, in any case where the Right of the Patronage cometh not in Debate: As if a Parfori be made a Bishop, and hath Difpenfa - tion to keep his Re tory, and afterwards the Patron present another to the Church, which is Instituted and Indudted; the Bishop shall have against this Incumbent, a Writ of Spoliation in Court Cbri - Jlian. SPONDiEUS, is the Foot of a Latin Verse, consisting of two Syllables, and both of ’ em long, as Ingens.

spooning.c: SPOONING, when a Ship being under Sail in a Storm at Sea, cannot bear it, but is forced to put right before the Wind; then the Seamen lay, she spoon; and when in such a case there is danger left Ihe Ihould bring her Mails by the Board with her rowling about, or Seel under Water, and so Founder, they usually fet up the Fore - fail to make her go the Heavier, especially if there be Sea - room enough and this they call Spooning with the Fore - fail.

sporadicmorbi.c: SPORADIC Morbi, are those Diseases which ( tho ’ different in nature ) seize several people at the fame time, and in the fame Country.

spots.c: SPOTS in the Sun. ’ Tis certain those epdke Masses which sometimes appear at the Sun, are not Planets revolving at any, even the least distance from him, but Spots or Macula adhering to him; for whereas they revolve but once in about Days; on calculation it will appear, that a Planet near the Sun ’ s Surface, as these must be, cannot have above Hours allowed for its periodical Re - volution, which being so different from the fore - mention ’ d space of Days, quite decides that Controversie, and demonstrates those Masses to be real Macula adhering to the Body of the Sun, as is here asserted. Anno, April th, H. A. M, the Ho - nourable Mr. Boyle observed a Spot in the lower Limb of the Sun, a little towards the South of its Equator, which was entred about jf - of the Sun ’ s Diameter, it self being about r s in its Ihorteft Diameter of that of the Sun, its longest about f of the fame. May the th, about in the Morning, it ap - peared near about the fame distance from the Weft - ward Limb, a little South of its Equator; tho ’ at first it appear ’ d to be from the Eastward Limb, a little South also of its Equator, May the th, it difap S P o S P R difappeared. This Spot was very dark, and almost of a Quadrangular form, and was enclosed round with a kind of duskish Cloud. May the th, the fame Spot appear ’ d again, and seemed to be in a part of the fame Line it had formerly traced, and was entered about of its Diameter, about h. P. M. At which time, there appear ’ d another Spot, which upon its entrance was not above h Parc t ie Sun ’ s Diameter: It ap - pear ’ d to be longest towards the North and South, and shortest towards the East and Weft; and there seemed to be dispersed about it divers small Clouds here and there. Anno, August the nth, h. P. M. SPOTS in the Sun, besides what may be con - clouded about these Solar Spots, being no Planets revolving round the Sun ’ s Body, as some have thought. Dr. Hook, in his Opera Post. draws these further Conclusions: i. That these Bodies are ei - ther Opake, and so hinder the Sun ’ s Light from parting thro ’ them, orelfe are Incombustible and dark Bodies, which will afford no Light at all for a certainTime, and do as it were quench and dea - den that part of the Sun where they rife, ( a. ) There appear in some parts of the Sun ’ s Face, also Nebula or Clouds; in some others Facula or Blazes, which give a clearer Light than the other Parts of his Bo - dy. The Spots are fubjedfc to Increase and Dea - crease, having sometimes covered a part of the Sun bigger than all Europe, and sometimes bigger than the whole Surface of the Earth. (. ) The Motion of these Spots is always from Bast to Weft, according to the Order of a Line of Sines, begin - ning from the Centre, of which the Semi - Diame - cer of the Sun is Radius. And this Motion ap - pears to be in a straight Line in the beginning of June and December; when the Earth is in that part of the Plain of the Ecliptick, which cuts the Plainof the Equinoctial of the Sun ’ s Turbinated Motion. At other times the Line of their Motion is incurvated and bent into an Ellipsis; which is greatest when the Earth happens to be in those parts of the Ecliptick, which are the extream Li - mits of it, compared to the Plain of the Sun ’ s E - quint & ial: And this also is twice a Year, vi. in the middle between the Nodes, both Plains pas - sing thro ’ the Centre of the Sun, that is, about the beginning of March and September, Whence he deduces by undeniable Demonstration, that the Sun is of a Globular Figure, and that it moves on its own Axis from East to Weft ' As also that the Axis of his turbinated Motion remains fix ’ d, and is always directed towards the fame Point in the Heayens, as the Earth ’ s Axis ’ is found to do; as al - so the Axis is of Jupiter and Saturn, as far as can yet be discovered by the Spots, Satellites and Ring, of these Planets. (. ) He observes also, that there is a kind of Torrid Zone, or certain Space or Breadth on each side the Sun ’ s Equator towards the Poles, in which these Macula, Nebula - and FacuU do appear most. Whereas without these Limits, or in the temperate Zones ( as with regard to our Earth they may be called ) they appear but seldom, and never towards the Polar Parts.

spring.c: SPRING of the Air, or its E ! aft i cal Force, fee more in Air. That there is such a Spring or Elasticity in the Air, is clear from the following Experiments. . That Bladders but half blown up, and ha - ving their Necks well tied, did swell in the ex - haunted Receiver as if Blown to their full Dimen - lions; and that full blown Bladders, and even thin square Glass Viols wellftop ’ d, will break to pieces when once the Air is well pump ’ d out of the Receiver. . A glass Syphon, whose recurved Leg was turn ’ d up parallel to the upper and longer, and was sealed Hermetically at the end of the lesser or lliorter Leg, had a Quantity of Quicksilver poured into it, and by its being moved often up and down, the Air in the sealed and shorter Leg, was brought to the fame Temperament of the Ex - ternal. After this, more Mercury was poured in, till the Air in the sealed Leg was compressed into about half its usual Dimensions, and then the Mercury in the longer Leg was Inches higher than that in the shorter: By which it appears plain - ly, That the Spring of the Air in the Sealed Leg was so great, as to equiponderate a Column of Mercury of Inches in Length. Boyle against Linus. . A Viol filled to but a th part with Quick - silver, had a long and slender glass Pipe fattened into its Neck, with Sealing - Wax or Cement, whose lower Orifice was a good way under the Quicksilver in the Viol; then having blown in a little Air, to try whether the Viol were Well slope ’ d, it was conveyed into a long and slender Receiver; and after the Air was drawn off by the Pump, the Spring of the included Air within the Bottle, impelled the Mercury up to the Height of Inches in the Pipe, and there kept it fu - spender; till upon the re - admission of the Air s the Quicksilver fell down to its first station in the Pipe. This Experiment Mr. Boyle often tried, an with desired Success. And ' And. when it was tried with a Bottle that held a Quart, the Spring of such a Quantity of Air was able to raise the Mercury up to Inches But nothing could make it raise above the common Height of the Quicksilver in the Ba - rofcope. . Into a Copper Vessel of a Cylindrical shape, was put almost Water enough to fill it, and then was immersed into it and kept under Water by a Weight, a square glass Viol that would hold or o Ounces of Water, and was well slope ’ d: After this, Mr. Boyle placed the Copper Vessel in his Penumatical Engine, and pumping up the Air, he found, That the Spring of the Air incur ded in the Viol broke it all to pieces, tho ’ under Water, with a great Noise, and made a kind of Smoak or Mist appear above the Surface of the Water. Which Experiment proves both the great Force of the Natural Spring of the Air, when the weight of the Atmosphere is removed; and also that the weight of the Atmosphere adts upon Bodies under Water for that could by its universal pores - sure keep the Spring of the Air in the Bottle bent while it was - under the Surface of the Water; but when once that, by plying the Pump, was taken off, the Elastick Particles unbent themselves vio - lently, and broke the Viol. See the Experimentt about the Pressure of the Airs Spring cn Bodies under Water. The Spring of the Air, is equal every where in a Natural date to the weight of the Incumbent At - mosphere j just as if a Person should squeeze or compress together either by the force of his Hand, or by a Weight, any parcel of Wool, or such Elastick Bodies, the Wool would by its Spring equally prels against the Hand or Weight. Ac - cording to the d Axiom of Sir Isaac Newtons ' Principia, Aclioni cmtrariam temper & cequalem else ReaBionem. The Accurate Dr. Hool on Experiments well made, thinks we may conclude the Spring of the Air to be Reciprocal to its Extension. Micrograph. p.. And the Resistance of the Spring of the Air, is found to be nearly equal to the Weight or Force that compresses it; and the Spaces that the fame Air occupies under differing Pressures, are Reci - procally as those Pressures. The Quantity of the dilatation and expansion of Air only by the Operation of its Spring, without any additional Heat, Mr. Boyle found to be so great, that a Bubble of Air included in a proper Glass Pipe almost filled with Water, was exten - ded to above o times its former Dimensions; and he believes would Ifeve taken up times its former room, had the Tube been Jong enough to have tried the Experiment. New. Exper. Phyf. Mech. Edit... p.,. He found also, that a Cylinder fair of an Inch in Diameter, and less than two Inches in Length, would, when included in a Bladder, and the weight of the Atmosphere taken off by Pumping, by its bare Spring only, raise a weight of above x o Pounds Averdupois. He found also, that the Spring of a Cylinder of Air of Inches Diameter, and of the former length, was in the fame Engine able to raise up Pound weight. Whence it appears, that the Force of the Spring of different Cylinders fair is in a duplicate Ra - tio, to the Diameters of those Cylinders. ' " ' Il ‘ l l u wia The Spring of the Air, may be explicated either by supposing the Air near the Earth to consist of an Heap of such little Springy or Elastick Bodies ly - ing one upon another resembling those of a Fleece of Wool: Or else according to D. Cartes his way by sup - posing That the Air is nothing but a Congeries of flexible Particles of several kinds of Figures and Sizes, which are raised by Heat into the fluid and subtil Ethereal Matter that surrounds the Earth, and by the continual agitation of that Matter wherein those Particles swim, are so whirled about, that each Corpuscle endeavours to beat off all others from coming within the little Sphere requi - site to its Motion about its own Center, and ( in case any, by intruding into that Sphere ( hall op - pose its free Rotation, ) to drive it away.

springsandfountains.c: SPRINGS and Fountains '. Concerning the Origin of these, there is much Dispute, especially of such as are found on the tops of high Moon - tains. Some, as Dr. Hool, Dr. Plott, and many others, think that they arise from the Sea - water percolated through the Bowels of the Earth, which by that means, being deprived of its Salt, is rendred much Lighter than before, and so is capable of Rising up to the height we commonly find Springs at, as Water Rises in a Filtre, or in very small Tubes '; ( c. And Dr. Hook, hath a pretty Experiment about this, in his Microgr. p.. But I cannot fee how by this Hypothesis, sup - posing the Gravity of the whole Atmosphere could be taken oft ) Water can rife above or Foot above the level of the Ocean. The Learned Capt Halley supposes them to be caused from the Vapours exhaled by the Sun out of the Sea, ( c. Of which, fee an Account under the Word Vapour. The Ingenious Dr. Woodward, in his Natural History of the Earth supposes, That the great A - abyss of Waters, placed in the Bowels of the Earth, is the Standing Fund and Promptuary which flip - plies Water to the Surface of the Earth, and fur - nifties as well Springs and Rivers, as Vapours and Rain. For he asserts, That there is a nearly uniform, and constant Fire or Heat, disseminated, thro ’ out the Body of the Earth, and especially in the In - senior parts of it: The Bottoms of the deeper Mines being very sultry, and the Stone and Ores there be - ing very sensibly hot even in Winter, That ns M this S P R S P R this Subterraneous Heat which evaporates and ele - vates the Waters of the Abyss, buying it up india - ferently on all Sides, and towards all parts of the Surface of the Globe. That this riling Vapour, or Water, pervades not only the Fissures and Intervals of the Strata, but the very Bodies of the Strata themselves, permeating the Interstices of the Sand, Earth, or other Matter, whereof they consist; yea, even the most firm and dense Marble and Sand - Stone; for these give ad - mission to it, tho ’ in lesser Quantity, and are al - ways found saturated with it which is the rea - fon that they are softer, and can be cut much more easily when they are first taken out of the Earth, than they can afterwards, when they have lain some time exposed to the Air, and when that Hu - midity is evaporated. This Vapour he asserts to proceed dire & ly up to - wards the Surface of the Globe, on all sides, unless when impeded and diverted by the Interpolation of Strata of Marble, the denser forts of Stone, or o - ther like Matter, which is so close and compatft, that it can admit it only in a smaller Quantity, and this very slowly too. And when it is thus intercepted in its Passage, the Vapour which cannot penetrate the Stratum dire & ly, will some of it glide along the lower Surface of the Stratum, permeating the Horizon - tal Interval, which is betwixt that and the next. Stratum lying underneath it; the reft will pass the Interstices of the Mass of the subjacent Strata, Whether they be of later Stone, of Sand, Marie, or the like, with a Direction parallel to the lire of those Strata, till it arrives at their perpendicular Intervals, And when the Water is once come to these Inter - vals, in case the Strata, whereby the ascending Va - pour was collected and condensed into Water, ( as we usually speak ) in like manner as by an Alem - back, happen to be raised above the Level of the Earth ’ s Surface; as those Strata always are, where - of Monntains do consist j then the Water being like wife got above the said Level, flows forth of those Intervals or Apertures; and if there be no Obstacle without, forms Brooks and Rivers. But, where the Strata, which so condense it, are not higher than the mean Surface of the Earth, it stag - nates at the Apertures, and only forms standing Springs. He adds, That tho ’ this Supply of Water from the Abyss, be continual, and nearly the fame at all Seasons, and alike to all parts of the Globe, yet when it arrives at or near the Surface of the Earth, where the Heat ( the Agent which evaporates and bears it up ) is not so conjlant and uniform, as is that resident within the Globe, bur is lubjecft to Vi - cilfitudes and Alterations, being at certain Seasons greater than at others; being alio greater in some Climates and Parts of the Earth than in others: It thence happens that the Quantity of Water at the Surface of the Earth, tho ’ sent up from the Abyss with an almost constant equality, is various and un - certain, as is the Heat there at some Seasons, and in some Countries, the Surface abounding, and being even drown ’ d with the Plenty of it, the Springs full, and the Rivers high: At other Seasons, and in ether Countries, both Springs and Rivers may be exceeding low, and sometimes totally fail. When the Heat in the exterior parts of the Earth, and in the Ambient Air, is as intense as that in the interior parts of ir, than all that Water which passes the Strata directly, mounting tip in separate Parcels, or in Form of Vapour, does notftop at the Surface, because the Heat there, is equal both in Quantity and Power to That underneath, which brought it out of the Abyss. This Heat therefore takes it here, and hears it up, part of in immediately out of the Surface of the Earth; the reft thro ’ the Tubes and Vessels of the Vegetables which grow thereon, Herbs Shrubs, and Trees, and along with it a fort of Vegetative Terrestrial Matter, which it detaches from out the uppermost Stratum wherein these are placed; this it deposer in them for their Nutriment, as it passes thro ’ them, and issuing out at their Tops and Extre - mities, it marches still on, and is elevated up into the Atmosphere, to such an height, that the Heat there being Less, it becomes condensed, unites and combines into small Mafies, or Drops, and at length falls down again in Rain, Dew, Hail, or Snow. And for the other part of the Water which was condensed at the Surface of the Earth, and sent forth collectively into standing Springs and Rivers; this also sustains a Diminunition from the Heat above, being evaporated more or less in proportion to the greater or lesser Intenlenefs of the Heat, and the greater or lesser Extent of the Surface of the Water so sent forth. And as these Evaporations are at Jome times great - ter, according to the greater Heat of the Sun, so where ever they alight again in Rain, ’ tis so much superior in Quantity, to the Rain of colder Seasons, as the Sun ’ s Power is then superior to its Power in Those Seasons: This is apparent in our Northern Clime, where the Sun ’ s Power is never very great, but yet our Rains in June, July, and Augufl, are much greater than those of the colder Months, the Drops larger, and consequently heavier, and falling much thicker and falter than at other times. But much more apparent is this in the Regions of the Earth, nearer to, or under the Equator, where the Sun having a much greater force, their Rains ( which are Periodical, happening usually a - bout the fame time, and lasting several Months ) fall in such Quantities as to be more like descend - ing Rivers than Showers j and by these are caused the mighty Inundations of the Nile, and other Ri - vers in those Regions. But when the Heat in the exterior parts of the Earth, and in the Ambient Air, is less than that in the interior the Evaporations are iikewile less; and the Springs and Rivers do not only cease to be diminished, proportionably to the Relaxation of the Heat, but are much augmented, a great part of the Water which ascends to the Surface of the Earth, stopping there for want of Heat to amount it thence up into the Atmosphere, and saturating the fuperfi - cial, or uppermost Strata with Water; which by degrees drains down into Wells, Springs, and Ri - vers, and so makes an Addition ro them; and is the Reason that these abound with Water in the Col - der Seafcms, so much more than they do in the Hotter. And the Water which is thus dispensed to the Earth and. Atmosphere from the great Abyss, being carried down by Rains and by Rivers, into the O - can, which communicates with the Abyss, is by that means restored back again to it; and from thence it returns again in a continual Circulation, s Q U to the Surface of the Earth, in Vapours and Springs.

springyorel.c: SPRINGY, or El aft id Bodies, are such as ha - ving had their Figure changed by the Stroak or Percussion of another Body, can recover again their former Figure; which Bodies which are not Elastical will not do. Thus, If a piece of Steel be bent any way, it will recover again its former straitness, but a piece of Lead will stand bent in any form.

spunging.c: SPUNGING of a great Gun, is clearing of her Inside, after she hath been discharged, with a Wad of Sheep - skins, or the like, rolled about one end of the Rammer: Its design is to prevent any parts of Fire from remaining in her; which would endanger the Life of him who should load, or charge her again.

spun.c: SPUN - YARN, or Rope - yarn, whole Ends are beaten or scraped thin, in order to fallen one piece to another, that so it may be as long as is necessary: It is of use to make Caburns, and for many other Purposes aboard a Ship. SPURIiE. See Noth cost.

spurkets.c: SPURKETS, are the Spaces in a Ships Side, betwixt the upper and lower Futtocks, or betwixt the Rungs fore and aft.

squammosasutura.c: SQUAMMOSA Sutura, is one of the Sutures of the Bones of the Skull; so called, because the Parts of the Bones united by the Suture, do lie ve - ry Hope, and like Scales.

SQUARE hollow, or hollow Square, in the Aft Military, is a Body of Foot drawn up with an empty Space in the middle, for the Colours, Drums and Baggage, facing and cover ’ d by the Pikes every way to keep off Horse.

squarefigure.c: SQUARE Figure, in Geometry, is one whose Right - lined Sides are all equal, and its Angles all right. See Quadrilateral: For its Area, lee Area.
