squaring.c: SQUARING. By the Word Squaring, Mathe - maticians understand the making of a Square equal to any Figure given. Thus the Quadrature or Squaring of the Circle, is the finding a Square equal to the Area of a Circle, which hath not yet been done Geometrically -

squinancyorquinfey.c: SQUINANCY, or Quinfey, a Swelling and In - flammation in the Throat. See Angina.

stigma.c: STIGMA, are Juices of Plants mix ’ d together in order to Distillation.

stalactites.c: STALACTITES, are a fort of stony, sparry Icefiles which hang down from the Top or Ar - ches of Grotto ’ s, Caves, or Subterranean Caverns, and from the Roofs of the Buildings and Capitals of the Pillars of such Places as are built over the Therm or Hot Springs Of this kind are the Sal Alumen and Vitriolum StalaBicum, the Afinera Ferri - JlalaElicd, the Vitriolum Capillare, and the Alumen Capillare, &c. These Staladficte Dr. Wood - ward faith, should rather be called Stagonita,

staminainbotany.c: STAMINA, in Botany, are those little fine Threds or Capillaments which grow up within the Flowers of Plants encompassing round the Style, and on which the Apices grow, at their extremities. Whence the Botanists call that a ST AMINEOUS Flower, which is so far simper - sect, as to want those coloured Leaves which are called Pet alee, and consists only of the Stylus and the Stamina. And such Plants as do bear these Stamineous Flowers Mr. Ray, makes to constitute a large Genus of Plants., which he calls Plerbce flere Imperfeclo five apetalo Stamineove. And these he divides into such as, . Have their Fruit or Seed totally divided from the Flower; and these are such Plants as are said to be of different Sexes: The reason of which is, that from the fame Seed some Plant shall arise with Flowers and no Fruit, and others with Fruit and no Flowers: As Hops, Hemp, Jlinging Nettles, Spinach, Cynocrumbe, Mercarialis, and Phyllon. z. Such as have their Fruit only a little disjoin ’ d from their Flowers; as the Ambrosia, Bardana minor, picinus, and the Heliotropium Tricoccon. '. Such as have their Fruit immediately conti - guous, or adhering to their Flower: And the Seed of these is either, . Triangular: Und of this fort, some are lucid and shining, as the Lapathum, phabarbarum, and Bi Jlorta; to which also may be reckoned the Perjicaria. Others are rough and not shining; as the HeU leberus Albus, Fegopyrum, Convolvulus nicer, and the Polygonum. . Such as have a roundish Seed a little flat - ted or compressed, or of any other Figure but the former Triquetrous or Triangular one. And these have their Flower, or the Calyx of the Flower adhering to the Bottom or Basis of the Seed or Fruit; as the Potatnogiton, Blitum SU - vejlre, Porietaria, Atriplex, Blitum Sativum, Amuranthes Hoclocerieus, and the Saxifraga Au - rea. . Such whose Flowers adhere to the top or uppermost of the Seed; as the Beta, Afarum, Archimilla. m And to these kind of Plants, Mr. pay reduces also the Kaligeniculatum, Sedum fruticofum, the Scoparia, or Belvidere of the Italians,

stanchions.c: STANCHIONS in a Ship, are those Timbers which being fet up Pillarwife, do support and strengthen the waft Trees.

standingpart.c: STANDING Part of the Sheat, is that pare which is made fast to a Ring at the Ship ’ s Quar - ter. When they lay, Over - hale the Sheat, they mean, Hale upon the standing Part But when they fay, Hale the Sheat barely, they intend it only of the Running Part.
STANDING Part of a Tackle aboard a Ship, is the end of the Rope where the Block is seized or fastned; as the other which is haled, is called Fall.

standingpopes.c: STANDING Popes, are those Ropes which do not run in any Blocks, but are fet taught, or let slack, as occasion serves, as the Sheat - stays, Back - stays, and the like.

stapes.c: STAPES, or the Stirrop, because of its refem - balance to a Stirrop, is a little Bone in the Ear, of a Triangular Figure and is made of two Branches fet upon a flat Basis, which Hands upon the Fora - men Oval the Union of the two Branches is called the Head of the Stapes, in which there is a final Cavity, wherein lies another little Bone.

staphyloma.c: STAPHYLOMA, is a Diseases the Eye, in which the two Tunicks of the Eye, Cornea and ‘ Uvea, being broken, fall outward in the shape of a Grape.

starinfortification.c: STAR, in Fortification, is a Work with several Faces, generally composed of from to Points with Saliant, and Re - entring Angles Flanking one another; every one of its Sides containing from to Fathoms.

starboardtheright.c: STARBOARD, the Right - hand side of a Ship, as Larboard is the left: Thus they fay, Starboard the Helm, or Helm a Starboard; when he that Conds would have the Man at the Helm put the Helm to the Right - side of the Ship. STAR - So ? ' / -. See Fort.

staticalbar.c: STATICAL Bar of cope, an Instrument Invented by the Honourable Mr. R Boyle, whose Deicrip - tion - see in Baroscope.

staticks.c: STATICKS, is a Science purely Speculative, being a Species of Mecbanickj, conversant about Weights, and Ihewing the Properties of the Hea - viness and Lightness, or Nquilibria of Bodies. When it is restrained to the Specifick Weights and AEqui - , S T A , rf ii. ' ' in ' ' ' ‘ ll - ' " " " ' ' ' ' Ha ii . / Equilibria of Liquors, it is called HydroJiatickj which fee. ST ATION, in Astronomy, ' signifies certain Places of the fydiack, where a Planet being ar - rived, seems to hand still forfome time in, the fame Degree, either in ascending to its Apogee, or descending to its Perigee.

station.c: STATION, is a Place where a Man fixes him - self and his Instrument, to take ( as in Surveying ) any Angles or Distances. ST ATION - L ine. See Line: of Station,

STATION - ?, is an Instrument confiding of two Rulers that Hide to ten Foot, divided into Feet and Inches, with a moving Vane or Sight; two of which are used with a Level; and on the Edges, there are the Links of the Gunters Chain divided. It is used in Surveying for the mote easie xaking - Off - sets.

stationary.c: STATIONARY; a Planet isfaid to be Station - nary, when to any Eye placed on the Earth, it ap - pears for some time to stand still, and to have no progressive Motion forward in its Orbit round the Sun.
STATIONARY, how to an Eye placed at the Larth, a Planet appears to land still or be Station - nary; fee under the word Direti in this Vol.,

statute.c: STATUTE, is a Word that hath divers fignifi - cations: as first, it lignifies an Ad of Parliament made by the King and the Three Estates of the Realm; in which sense it is either General or Spe - cial. In another signification, Statute is a Short Writing, called a Statute - Merchant, or a Statute Staple; which fee. Statutes are also vulgarly ta - ken for the Petit - Seffwns, by Eli. cap..

STATUTE - Mm wr, is a Bond acknowledged before one of the Clerks of the Stafztfcfj - Merehant and Mayor, or Chief Warden of the City of Lon - don, or two Merchants of the laid City for that purpose assigned, or before the Mayor, Chief Warden, or Matter of other Cities or good Towns, or other sufficient Men for that purpose appointed. Sealed with the Seal of the Debtor and of the King, which is of two pieces; the greater is kept by the Mayor, Chief - Warden, &c, and the letter by the laid Clerks.

STATUTE - Staple, is lb called either Properly or Improperly. A Statute - Staple, properly so Cal - led, is a Bond of Record, acknowledged before the Mayor of the Staple, in the Presence of one of the two Constables of the fame Staple; for Which Seal, the Fee is of every Pound, if the Sum ex - ceed not l. an Half - penny; and if it exceed /. a Farthing; and by virtue of such Statute - Staple,, the Creditor may forthwith have Execu - tion of the Body, Lands, and Goods of the Deb - tor. Statute - Staple improper, is a Bond of Record, founded upon the Stat. H.. cap.. Of the na - ture of a proper Statute - Staple, as to the Force and Execution of it; and acknowledged before one of the Chief Justices; and in their Absence, before the Mayor of the Staple, and Recorder of Lon - don. )

statutumdelaborariis.c: STATUTUM de Laborariis, is a Writ Judicial, for the Apprehending of such Labourers as refuse to Work according to the Statute, Peg. Judic. Sol..

statutomercatorio.c: STATUTO Mercatorio, is a Writ for the Im - prisoning of him that has forfeited a Bond Called Statute - Merchant, until the Debt be satisfied. Of thcfe, there is one against Lay - persons, and another against Ecclesiastical.

statuto.c: STATUTO - Sf y /, is a Writ that lies to take his Body to Prison, and seize upon his Lands and S T E Goods, that hath forfeited a Bond called Statute - Staple,

stays.c: STAYS in a Ship; are Ropes whole so is to keep the Matt from failing aft: All Matts, Top - Matts, and Flag - Staves have Stays, except the Sprit - fail Top - matt; the Stay of the Main - matt which is called the Main - Lay, is by a Lannier fastned to a Collar, Which comes about a Knee belonging to the Head; the Main - top - mdfl Stay is fastned to the Head of the Fore - matt, by a Strap and a dead Man ’ s Eye, and so is the Main - top - gallant - mass stayed to the Head of the Fore - top - matt; the Fore - matt and Matts belonging to it, are in the fame manner stayed to the Boit - sprit and Sprit fail Top - fail Matt; which stays do like - wife stay the Bolt - sprit it self. The ALijfcn - say comes to the Main - matt by the Half - Deck, and the Topmast - stays come to the Shrouds With Crows - feet. The length of the Stay is the fame with that of the Matt it belongs to. The Main - matt, Fore - matt; with the Matts be - longing to them, have also Back - flays, which help to keep the Matt from pitching forward, or over - board, because they go on either side of the Ship To bring a Ship upon the ST A YES ' or to flay her, is in order to her Tack - ing, which is thus done: At the fame time bear up the Helm, lei fly the Fore - fail Sheat, let go the Fore - bowling, Brace the Weather - brace of the Fore - fail; the fame is also done to the Top - fail and Top - gallant - fail, only their Shears must be kept fast. If the Sprit - fail be out, then at the fame time let go the Sprit - fail Sheat also, with the Fore - sheet, and Brace the Weather - Brace: But the Tacks, S heats, Bracings, and Bowlings, of the Main fail. Main - top fail, and MijJen are not altered. And When the Wind comes in at the Bow, which before was the Lee - Bow, it drives all the Sails backward against the Shrouds and Matts, so that the Ship makes no way for - ward, but drives with her Broad - side. Those are reckoned the best Ships, which will stay with the feweft Sails.

steadyawordofcommandatsea.h: STEADY a Word of Command at Sea
steadyawordofcommandatsea.c: STEADY, a Word of Command at Sea, from him that Conns to the Man at Helm, to keep the Ship steady in her Course, and not to make Angles ' or Yaws ( as they call them, ) in or out.

steatocele.c: STEATOCELE, is a Rupture or Tumor in the Scrotum of a Fatty or Suet - like Confidence. Blan - chard.

steatoma.c: STEATOMA, is a preternatural Swelling which consists of a Matter almost like Suet of the fame ' Colour throughout, soft; and tho ’ not easily yield - ing to the Touch, yet suddenly returns, the Sing - ers being removed, to its proper Shape and Big - ness.

steel.c: STEEL, is made, according to Mr. Lcmery, p., by Stratifying of Plates of Iron in a large Furnace, with the Horns or Nails of Animals, un - der which is made a very great Fire Thus is the Iron calcined; but when red Hot, and near Melt - ing, they take the Plates out and dip them suddenly in cold Water, and so they become Steel. Steel is not so good as Iron for Medicipal Opera - tion, because the volatile Parts are mostly purged - away in the Calcination, and what remains is hard - ly dissolvable by the Juice in the Body,

steer.c: STEER: To Steer a Ship, is to guide or go - very her by the Helm. He is the best Steersman that uses the leaf ): Motion in putting the Helm over to and again, and that keeps the Ship best from making S T E S T E making Yaws; that is, from running in and out. There are three ways to Steer by, . By any Mark on the Land, fbas to keep the Ship Even by it. . By the Compass, which is to keep the Ship's Head upon such a Rhumb or Points the Compass, as belt leads to her desired Port. . To Steer as one is hidden or Conned, which is the Duty ( in a great Ship ) of him that is taking his Turn at Helm.

steerageapart.c: STEERAGE, a Part of a Ship where he stand - eth that Steereth; that is, Guides the Helm or rudder of the Ship; and this in a Man of War is always before the Bulk - head of the great Cabbin; and where - ever the Steersman be placed, he must stand so, as that he can see the Letch of the Sails, whether they be in the Wind or not.

steeve.c: STEEVE i the Seamen fay that the Box - sprit or the Beak - head of the Ship doth Steeve, when either Hands too upright, and not straight enough for - wards.

steganography.c: STEGANOGRAPHY, is the Art of secret Writing, which is known only to the Persons cor - desponding with one another; and which if the Letters Ihould be Opened, no one is supposed to be able to discover, or Decypher, as ' tis called. Tho ’ now - a - days hardly any thing can be Written by this Art, but what may be Decyphered, and the Sense and Meaning of it discovered. And in this Art of Decyphering, that Excellent Mathematician Dr. Wallis, is admirably ready.

stegnosis.c: STEGNOSIS, is a conftridlion or flopping up of the Pores. STEGNOTIC. See Ajlringentia.

stellateplants.c: STELLATE Plants, are by the Botanists called such Plants as have their Leaves growing on the Stalks at certain Intervals or Distances, in the form of a Radiant Star; and according to Mr. Ray. this is the Tenth Genus of English Plants: Of this kind is Cruciata or Cross - wort, MoUugo, Wild - madder, Afperula or Woodruff, Gallium or Ladies Bed - jh avo, Aparine or Cleavers, Rubin TinElorum or Dyers Madder. To which he adds, as a - kin to to this Genus, the Najlurtium Indicum, Indian Crelfe, or Yellow Larl spur,

stem.c: STEM of a Ship, is that main piece of Timber which comes bowing or bending from the Keel below where it is fear fed, ( as they call itTthat is, pieced in, right before the Fore - castle; this Stem it is which guides the Rake of the Ship; and all the B. ut - ends of the Planks ( forwards ) are fix ’ d into it. This in the Section of a First - Rate Ship, is called the Main flem.

stentorophonic.c: STENTOROPHONIC - T ?, or Instrument, is the Speaking - Trumpet, Invented by Sir Samuel JLforeland.

step.c: STEP, that piece of Timber in a Ship whereon the Mails or Capstan. do stand at Bottom, is cal - led the Step of the Mall or Capstan. STERCOROSyS Fluxus, is that in which much Liquid Excrement is often voided, pro - ceeding from Excfementitious Meats corrupted in the Stomach, or a great quantity of Excrements heaped up in the Intestines Blanchard.

stereobata.c: STEREOBATA A, in Architecture, is the Greeks Word for the first beginning of the Wall of any Building, and immediately standing on the Sun - dation: This is wrongly confounded with Sty Ida - ta, which is the beginning of a Column, or its Pedestal.

stereography.c: STEREOGRAPHY, is the Art of drawing the forms of Solids upon a Plane.

stereographickprojeclim.c: STEREOGRAPHICK Projeclim. See Prove - Elion of the Sphere in Plano.

stereometry.c: STEREOMETRY, is the Art of Measuring all forts of Solid Bodies j which how to do, you will find under the proper Names of each Body.

stern.c: STERN of a Ship, is all the hindermost or af - termoft Part of her, generally speaking: But pro - perly, ’ tis only the outmost Part of her, Abaft.

sternfast.c: STERNFAST, is some faftnings of Ropes, &c. behind the Stern of a Ship, to which a Cable or Hawser may be brought or fixed, in order to hold her Stern to a wharf, &c.

sternpost.c: STERNPOST, is a great Timber let into the Keel at the. Stern of a Ship, somewhat sloping, into which are fastned the after Planks; and on this Poll, by its Pintle and Gudgeons hangs the Rudder.

sternohyoides.c: STERNOHYOIDES, is that Pair of Muscles which is commonly by Anatomiftsfaid to arifefrom the uppermost part of the Breast - Bone: But this is since proved a Mistake, for they arise from the Internal part of the Clavicula, next where its Ori - gination is broad ana fleshy, and ascends direilly over the Sternothyreoidaus and Larynx, of an equal Breadth and Thickness, to its Insertion at the Ba - lls of the Fore - Bone of the Os Hy aides. This with its Partner ailing, pulls the Os Plyoidet, together with the Tongue and Larynx, dire illy down - wards.

sternothyroeides.c: STERNOTHYROEIDES, is a pair of Muf - cles which do arise broad and fleshy from the up - per and Internal Part of the Sternum, whence af - cending on the sides of the Wind - pipe, over the Glandulx. Thyroide a, it ’ s inferred to the inferiour Part of the Thyroidal or Scutiformal Cartilage. This, with its Partner, pulls the Larynx down - ward, and lengthens the Canalis or distance be tween the Rimula and Tip of the Tongue, ( which latter seems to be the true Pleclrum Vocis ) whereby the Tone of the Voice is rendered grave.

sternumos.c: STERNUM Os, the Breast - Bone, is joined to the Ribs in the foremost part of the Breast, con - siding of or Bones, and frequently in those that are come to ripeness of Age, grows into one Bone; to this is joined in the lower part of it, the Cartilage Ensiformis.

sternutationsneezing.c: STERNUTATION, Sneezing, is a forcible driving out of the Head some Sharp Matter which vellicates and disturb the Nerves and Fibres: Or, as some fay, ’ tis an involuntary Motion of the Brain, which contrails the Muscles of the Thorax and Abdomen, to the intent that the Mar - ter which vellicates the Nostrils and Brain may be driven our.

sternutatorium.c: STERNUTATORIUM, see Sternut amentum, a Sneezing Medicine, or Snuff.

steward.c: STEWARD of a Ship, is he that receives all the Viituals from the Purser; and he is to fee it well Stowed in the Hold; in his Custody are all things of that nature belonging to the Ship ’ s use. He is to look after the Bread, and to diilribute out the several Meffes of Victuals in the Ship. He hath an Apartment for himself in the Hold, which is called the Steward ’ s Room, where he Sleeps and Eats, STILE, S T o

stileindyalling.c: STILE, in Dyalling, is the Gnomon or Cock of a Dyal, that casts the Shadow upon the Hour - Lines and is always parallel to the Axis of the Earth, in all kinds of Dyals.

stillatitiousoils.c: STILL ATITIOUS Oils, in Chymistry, are such as are Extracted out of Mixts, by the Force of Fire; and hereby are distinguished from such as are made by Expression, or by Pressing. STILLICIDIUM Vrinae.. See Stranguria.

stirrup.c: STIRRUP of a Ship, is a piece of Timber put upon a Ship ’ s Keel, when some of her See / happens to be beaten off, and they can ’ t come con - veniently to put or fit in a new piece; then they patch in a piece of Timber, and bind it on with an Iron which goes under the Ship ’ s Keel and comes tip on each Side of the Ship, where ’ tis Nailed strongly with Spikes and this they call a Stir - up

stoaked.c: STOAKED, when in a Ship the Water in the Bottom can ’ t come to the Well of the Pump, they fay, The Ship is a - stop or stoaked: So they fay also, The Limber - holes are stoaked, when the Wa - ter cannot pass through them; and that the Pump is floated, when something is got into it which choaks it up, so that it will not Work.

stocks.c: STOCKS; lb the Ship - Carpenters call a Frame of Timber, and great Polls made a - shore to build Pinnaces, Ketches, Boats, and such small Craft, and sometimes small Frigats: Hence we fay, a Ship is on the Stocks, when she is a Building.,

stolones.c: STOLONES, are the Suckers which spring up from the Root of any Tree or Plant; and Which, if not cut off, will hinder the Thriving of the Tree.

stomachusinanatomy.c: STOMACHUS, in Anatomy, is not the Sto - mach of an Animal, for that is called Ventriculw j but is properly the left or upper Orifice of the Ventricle, or Stomach, by which Meats are re - ceiled into it. To this Part descend Nerves from the eighth Pair and intercostal Nerves, and are mixed and interwoven with one another. The Greekj call it the Heart: Whence it is that a Pain which is sometimes felt in this Part, it corruptly called the Heart - burn; and the Regi - on of the Stomach whereabout is called also Scrobi - culus Cordis, or the Heart - Pit. It hath its Fi - bres Orbicular, that its Orifice may exactly diut or close upon the Meat and Drink received into the Stomach, to prevent Fumes coming up from thence to affedt the Head, and to hinder Concodtion.

stopper.c: STOPPER, is a piece of Rope ( in a Ship ) ha - ving a Wale - knot at one end, with a Larmier fpli - ced into it, and at the other end ’ tis made fail in the Place where ’ tis to be used. Its use is to flop the main Halliards, or the Cable. The Stopper for the Halliards is fastened at the Main - Knight, and it serves when they are Hoifing theMain - Yard, to flop it, while the Men that Hale may flay and reft a little. But ’ tis chiefly uled for the Cable, to flop it, that it don ’ t run out too fast: They bind the Wale - knot about the Cable with the Larmiers, and that flops it, so that it cannot flip away. This Stopper is fastened to the Bottom of the Bitts by the Deck. The Word is, Lay on the Stoppers. And a Ship is said to Hide by the Stoppers, when the Ca - ble is fastened or flayed only by them, and not Bit - ted; but this is not safe Riding in a ft less of Wea - ther.,

strabismussquinting.c: STRABISMUS, Squinting, is occasioned by the Relaxation, Contraction, Distortion, too great Length, or too great Shortriefs of the Muscles which move the Eye, Blanchard.

strait.c: STRAIT, or S freight, in Hydrography, is a narrow Sea ftiut up between Lands on either side, affording a Passage from one great Sea into ano - ther; as the Strait of Magellan, the Strait of Gi - braltar, &c.

strake.c: STRAKE, in the Sea Phrale, is a Seam between two Planks; as the Garboard - Jlrake is the first Seam next the Keel. They fay also a Ship heels a - strake, that is, hangs or inclines to one Side, the quantity of an whole Plank ’ s breadth.

strangury.c: STRANGURY, is a difficulty of Urine, when the Urine comes away by drops only, accompany ’ d With a constant Inclination of making Water.

strap.c: STRAP, in a Ship, is the Rope which is spliced about any Block, and made with an Eye to fatten it any where on occasion.

strata.c: STRATA. Dr. Woodward, in his Natural Hi - story of the Earth, observes, ( and that very truly ) That the far greatest part of the Terrestrial Globe, consists, from its Surface downwards to the greatest Depth we ever Dig or Mine, of several Layers or Strata of different kinds of Earthy Matter, lying one over another, without any regular Order. This disposition of the Earth into these Strata, had been before observed by Stem but the Observations and Deductions that Dr. Woodward made from them, are wholly New, very Numerous, and of great Importance.

stratarithmetry.c: STRATARITHMETRY, is the Art of Draw - ing up an Army or Battalion of Men, according to any Geometrical Figure assigned: And also of ex - pressing the just Number of Men contained in such a Figure, as they stand in Array, either near at hand, or at a distance.

stratificationorstratum.c: STRATIFICATION, or Stratum super Stratum, as the Chymifts call it, is putting different Matters Bed upon Bed, or one layer upon another, in a Cru - cable in order to Calcine a Metal or Mineral. Thus in Cementation ( which see ) there is first laid a Bed of Cement, then a Plate of Gold; then another Layer of Cement, and then another Plate of Gold; and this is done alternately, till the Crucible is full; which the Chymifts would express by fay - ing, Strati fie Gold and Cement in a Crucible.

stkeam.c: STKEAM - Arichor, is only a small one made fast to a Stream Cable for a Ship to Ride by in gentle Streams and in fair Whether, when they would only flop a Tide.

stretch.c: STRETCH j when at Sea they are going to sty - mmiv. Hoise the Yard, or Hale the Sheet, t they fay, Stretch forwards the Hale - Yards or Sheets; meaning that the part which the Men are to Hale by, should be put into their Hands, in order to their Hoifing or Haling.

stride.c: STRIDE, with the Writers of Natural History are the small Hollows, Channels or Chamfering s, which are found in the Shells of Cockles, Efcollops and other Shell - Fishes.
STRIDE, are the Lifts or Rays which run be - tween the Flutes, Chanels or Strives in Fluted Pillars,, These are in the Dorick, and in the lonick Order.

strikeasea.c: STRIKE, a Sea word variously used: When a Ship in a Fight, or on meeting with a Man of War, lets down or lowers her Top - fails, at least half Mast high, which they call Striking the Top - fails upon the Bunt, they fay, She Strides, mean - ing, he Yields or Submits, or pays heir Devoir to that Man of War as she passes by. When a Ship touches Ground in shoal Water, they fay also, she Strikes. When any Top - mast is to be taken down, the Word is, Strike the Top - majl: And when any thing is Let or Lowered, as they call it, down into the Hold, they call it Striking down into the Hold.

striking.c: STRIKING - ? UW, in a Clock, is that which by some is called the Pin - wheel; because of the Pins which are place upon the Round or Rim ( which in Number are the Quotient of the Pinion divided by the Pinion of the Detent - wheel ). In Days Clocks, the frfi or great Wheel is usually the Pin - wheel; but in Pieces that go Days, the second Wheel is the Pin - wheel or Striking - wheel.

structure.c: STRUCTURE, is the combination or result of all those Qualities or Modifications of Matter in any Natural Body, which distinguish it from others, and are what, in other Words, is called the Pecu - lar Form, or Texture of it. STRUMA. See Scrophula.

stylobatainarchitecture.c: STYLOBATA, in Architecture, is the Pedestal of a Column or Pillar.

styloceratohyoides.c: STYLOCERATOHYOIDES, are Muscles of the Os Hyoides, which draw upwards the Tongue and Larynx, as also the Jaws in Degluti - tion; whereby the Mafticared Aliment is not only compressed into the latter, ( the Fauces being then dilated ) but the Epiglottis is also depressed, and adequately covers the Rimula of the Larynx, by its Application to it; by which means the descent of the least part of the Aliment into the Aspera Artena is hindred which is a molt wonderful Mecha - nifm. The middle Tendon of the Digafiricus of the Lower - Jaw is transmitted through it. ’ Tis called also Stylohyoid ecus. styloglossum.c: STYLOGLOSSUM, is that Pair of Muscles which lift up the Tongue. They arise from the Appendix of the Os Styliforme, and are inferred about the middle of the Tongue.

stylohy.c: STYLOHY OIDiEUS. See Styloceratohyoides. STYLOPHARYNGiEUS, is a Pair of Muscles placed at the foot of the Procejfus Sty loides, that di - late the Gullet, and draw the Fauces upwards. They descend from an Appendix of a Bone in fa - fhion of a Pencil, and which reaches the hides of the Gullet.

stymma.c: STYMMA, is that thick Mass which remains after the Steeping of Flowers, Herbs, &c. and pr easing out their Oil. Blanchard.

sublimatecorrosive.c: SUBLIMATE Corrosive, is a Preparation in Chymistry, whereby Mercury is impregnated with Acids, and then sublimed up to the top of the Ves - sel: Thus performed. Pour on a Pound of good running Mercury, Ounces of Spirit of Nitre, fet the Matrass in Sand a little warmed, till the Mercury be all dissolved, evaporate the Dissolution, in a Glass, or Earthen Pan, till all the Moisture be carried off and then powder the remaining white Mass in a Glass Mor - tar, and then mix with it a Pound of Vitriol cal - cined white, and so much Salt decrepitated. Put this Mixture into a Matrass, whose Thirds at least remain unfilled fet the Vessel in Sand, and begin with a small Fire for three Hours, after which, that Fire must be encreased to a good strength: The Sublimate will adhere to the top of the Matrass, and there will be a Pound and three Ounces of it. The Red Scories at the Bottom, are useless, ’ Tis a more violent Efcharotick than the Lapis Infernalis, and inwardly taken, is one of the strongest Poilons in the World. Of this is made MercuriUs Dulcis. The Druggists sometimes fell a fort of it that is made of Arfenick.; but you may easily discover it by rubbing it with a little Salt of Tartar, for then it will turn Black, hut if it turn Tellow, ’ tis good.

subpoena.c: SUBPOENA, is a Writ whereby all Persons, under the Degree of Peerage, are called into Chancery, in such case only Where the Common Law fails, and hath made no provision so as the Party who in Equity hath Wrong can have no or - finary Remedy by the Rules and Course of the Common Law: But Peers of the Realm, in such Cafes, are called by the Lord Chancellor ’ s, or Lord Keeper ’ s Letters, giving notice of the Suit in - tended against them, and requiring them to ap - pear. The Tendon of this Muscle, together with the Supra and Infra Spina - tus, and Teres Minor, unite near their Insertions, and environ the Articulation of the Os Humeri with the Scapula, not Unlike the Ligamentum Catum of the Coxa, to prevent frequent Luxations: And by their successive alternate adding, the Arm is moved circularly.

sun.c: SUN, Our Excellent Sir Isaac Newton faith in his Principia, That the Density of the Sun ’ s Light ( which is Proportional to Heat ) is seven. times as great in Mercury, as with us; and therefore our Water there, would be all carried off, and boil a - Way: For he found by Experiments of the Thermo - meter, That an Heat but Times as great as that of the Sun Beams in Summer, will serve to make Water Boil. He proves. also, That the Matter of the Sun to that of Jupiter, is nearly as to i; and that the Distance of that Planet from the Sun, is in the fame Ratio to the Sun ’ s Semidiameter. That the Matter of the Sun to that of Saturn, is as to j and the Distance of Saturn from the Sun, is in a Ratio, but a little less than that, to the Sun ’ s Semidiameter. And Consequently that the common Centre of Gravity, of the Sun, and Jupiter, is nearly in the Superficies of the Sun; of Saturn, and the Sun a little within it. And by the fame manner of Cal - cubation, ft will be found that the common Centre of Gravity of all the Planets, cannot be more than the Length of the Solar Diameter distant from the Centre of the Sun: This common Centre of Gra - city he proves to be at reft; and therefore tfio ’ the Sun by reason of the various Position of the Pla - nets may be moved every way, yet it cannot re - cced far from the common Centre of Gravity. And this he thinks ought to be accounted the Cen - tre of our World. Boof. prop. ix. By Means of the Solar Spots it hath been dise - vered that the Sun revolves round his own Axis, without moving ( considerably ) out of his Place, In about Days. And that the Axis of this Moti - on is enclined to the Ecliptick, in an Angle of Degrees, Minutes nearly. Gregor. Aflronom. The Sun ’ s apparent Diameter being sensibly shorter in December than in June, as is plain and agreed from observation; the Sun mu ft be Proper - tionably nearer to the Earth in Winter than in Summer; in the former of which Seasons will be the Perihelion, in the latter the Aphelion And this is also confirmed by the Earth ’ s moving swiss - er in December, than it doth in June; as it doth about tt For since, as Sir Isaac Newton hath demonftra - ted by a Line drawn to the Sun, the Earth always describes equal Area ’ s in equal Times, when ever it moves fvvifter, it must needs be nearer to the Sun. And for this Reason there are about Days more from the Sun s Vernal Equinox to the Autumnal, than from the Autumnal to the Vernal. According to Mr. Cajjini, the Sun ’ s greatest distance from the Earth is, his mean Di - stance, and his least Distance, SemL Diameters of the Earth. And that the Sun ’ s Diameter is equal to Di - ameters of the Earth, and therefore the Body of the Sun, must, be icooqoo times greater than that of the Earth. Mr, A out assures us that he observed by a very ead Method the Sun ’ s Diameter to be not less than Minutes, Seconds in his Apogee, and not greater than Minutes Seconds in his Perigee. The mean Apparent Diameter of the Sun ac - cording to Sir Isaac Newton, is Minutes Seconds, in his Theory of the Moon, ' ' '. If you divide Degrees ( i. e the whole Ec - liptick ) by the Quantity of the Solar Year, it will Quote Minutes, Seconds Sc. which therefore is the Quantity of the Sun ’ s Diurnal Mo - tion. And if this Minutes, Seconds be divided by, you have the Sun ’ s Horary Motion, which is Minutes, Seconds, and if you will divide, this last by,, you will have his Motion in a Minute, Sc. And this way are the Tables of the Sun ’ s mean Motion, which you have in the Books of Astronomical Calculation, construed. The Sun ’ s Horizontal Parallax, Dr. Gregory and Sir Isaac Newton, makes but o Seconds. The fame learned Mathematician, at the end of his Aflronomite Pbyf S Geometr. Elem. hath a Com - palative Astronomy, where among the reft he con - sides what Phenomena would appear in the Pla - notary System, Sc. to an Eye placed at the Sun which are such as these: . That the Fixt Stars would appear in a Con -; cave Sphere, the apparent Centre of which, is the Eye of the Spedator. . He would distinguish the Planets from the Fixt Stars tho ’ they would appear to him to be placed among them by their Pericecal Revoluti - OnSjr ns, and by the Time of those, one Planet from another: And he would judge that Planet to be farthest off, whole Periodical Revolution was the longest; and so on in order for the reft, . To this Solar Oblerver ’ s Eye, the Planets would appear always direct, and never Stationary, nor Retrograde, as they do to an Eye at the Earth: And they would be found to return to the fame Eixt Stars again at Periods of very different lengths; and the Inferior Planets would sometimes cover the Superior ones. . If you suppose the Eye to be moved from the Centre of the Sun to its Surface, then by the Parallax of the Planets some better guess will be had of their Distances, than by the Observation of the different Velocity and Tardityof their Motion, could before be obtained: For to the Eye thus pla - ced, the Earths Horizontal Parallax will be Mi - nutes, equal to the Sun ’ s Semi - diameter, and con - sequently sensible enough. That of Saturn will be something above one Minute and an half, ( that Planet being times the Distance of the Earth from the Sun; and the Horizontal Parallax of Mercury, will be almost Minutes: And since these Parallaxes are sufficiently sensible, the Distant - ces of the Planets may be compared with the Sun ’ s Diameter, and with one another. . To an Eye thus placed all the Fixt Stars and Planets, will seem to revolve from East to Weft, in the Space of of our Natural Days: The North Pole of which Revolution, will be in that part of the Heaven, which we ( Inhabitants of the Earth ) call the loth Degree of Pisces, with or De - grees of North Latitude: Wherefore the Artick Pole Star will be at the d Flexure of Draco, and which will not be above Degrees from the Pole. The South Pole will be in Degrees of Virgo, with or Degrees South Latitude, near a Star of the fourth Magnitude, which in Cap. Hal - leys Catalogue, is in the first Oar of the Argo Navis. . The Planets thus seen from the Sun will ap - pear of Different Magnitudes: For the Diame - ter of Saturn, will subtend there but an Angle of Seconds: That of Jupiter near Seconds: That of Mars but Seconds: That of Venus Seconds: And the Diameter of Mercury o Seconds. But Mr. Hugens supposes the Diameters of the Superior Planets will be much larger; as making that of Jupiter, to subtend an Angle of almost Seconds; and that of the Body of Saturn with - out his Ring Seconds. . Of these fix Planets thus moving round the Sun, three will appear attended with their Satel - lites: Of which the Earth will have but one, which is the Moon; and who will appear at the greatest distance, not to be from the Earth above i o Minutes. Jupiter will appear with his Moons, or Sa - tellites; of which the outermost will never appear ver be above Minutes distant from the Primary Planet. Saturn will appear w ] th his Satellites ( if so many there be ) and the furhermoft of them will ne - ver be above Minutes distant from his Body: His Ring also will appear compassing roundthe Planet. The Paths, or Orbits of these Satellites being seen from the Sun sometimes more, sometimes less Oblique, will appear accordingly now broader, now narrower Ellipses; sometimes the Planes of these Orbits being produced, Will pass thro ’ the Sun: In which Case, the former narrow Ellipses will pass into Right Lines; which Will happen twice in every Revolution of the Orbit round the Sun if its Plane remain always parallel to its less; Whence the ’ Satellite will now appear to be cover - ed by the Primary Planet, and then the Planet by it; and sometimes will appear round the Planet, without its Disk, in an Ellipsis. ‘ . The Primary Planets, as also their Satellites; have not only rough and unpolished Surfaces, but also are so difform, that they have their Spots, which are places more or less obscure, ( ' and some - times more bright ) than the reft of their Disk: And these Spots, by the Rotation of the Planet, or Satellite, round its Axis, do describe Circles; and therefore these Ways, or Paths of the Spots, being seen from the Sun in the Plane of the Planetary Disk, will now appear Elliptical, and now strait Lines, ( as before the Paths of the Satellites Disk ) according as the Sun is elevated on either side - above the Plane of thole Circles; ’ or is found in it, as it is when it is in the Equinoiftial of that Planet. And if there be a Series, or Row, of thele Spots, ( as in the Belts of Mars and Jupiter ) these will appear in the form of Semi - Ellipses ( the one half being behind, or on the other side the Planes ) or will pass into straight Lines; will which also be the Cale of the outward Edge of the Ring of Saturn. But some of thele Spots will now and then be hid, and sometimes be visible for a long time, accord - ing as they are near to the Planets Pole, which is turned from, or towards the Sun. And this will be roost observable in Saturn, and in the Earth, in the others scarcely at all, because in them the Illustration of the Sun reaches to both their Poles. . Besides these fix primary Planets, and their o Satellites, which to our Solar Observator, will all appear to move within the Bounds of a Zodiack, scarce Degrees broad, and not much inclined to the Circle of the first Motion, all the fame way, and in Orbits nearly Concentrical to the Sun: There are also another kind of Bodies, whose Number is uncertain, which move round the Sun in very Eccentrical Orbits, and which are called Comets; and which sometimes come very near the Sun, and sometimes are vastly remote from him - These Comets do not move all in the fame Track ( altho ’ each one always keeps his own ) but some one Way, and some another, and mostly in Orbits very much enclined to the Ecliptick, and always in great Circles of the Sphere. Their Com, a or Tail ( to an Eye at the Sun ) will not appear oblong, or stretch out in length, as it doth to us, but every way diffused round the Head.

superfoetation.c: SUPERFOETATION, is when After one Con - caption another succeeds, so that both are in the Womb together: Sennertus makes mention of fre - quent Cafes of this Nature.

super.c: SUPER - INSTITUTION, one Institution upon another; as Where A is admitted and instituted to a Benefice upon one Tittle, and B. is admitted, in - ftituted, See. by the Presentment of another.
SUPER, is a Word used by the Auditors of the. Exchequer: In their Accounts they say, So inuch remains Infuper to such an Accountant That is. So much remains due on fetch an Ac - count.

superonerationepaftune.c: SUPERONERATIONE Paftune, is a Writ judicial, that lies against him who is impleaded in the County, for the over - burdening of a Com - mon with his Cattel, in case where he was formerly impleaded for it in the County, and the Cause is removed into the King ’ s Court at Westminster.

superparticularproportion.c: SUPERPARTICULAR Proportion, is when one Number, or Quantity, contains another once, and one such part, whose Numerator is i; then the Number so contained in the Greater, is said to be EO it in Super particular Proportion.

superpartientproportion.c: SUPERPARTIENT Proportion, is when one Number, or Quantity, contains another once, and some Number of Aliquot Parts remaining; as, j " f Sec.

superprerogativeregis.c: SUPER Prerogative Regis, is a Writ which lay against the Rings Widow, for Marrying without his Licence.

superstatuto.c: SUPER Statuto, is a Writ that lay against the King s Tenant holding in Chief, which alienateth the King ’ s Land without his Licence.

SUPER Statuto faElo pour Senejhnl & Adarfhal de Roy, Sec. is a Writ lying against the Steward, or Marfloal, for holding Plea in the Court of Free - hold, or for Trespass, or Contrail not made within the King ’ s Houfhold.

superstatutodearticulocleri.c: SUPER Statuto de Articulo Cleri, is a Writ a - gainst the Sheriff, or other Officer, that Diftrains in the King ’ s High - way, or in the Glebe - Lands, anciently given to Redtories.

superlativedegree.c: SUPERLATIVE Degree, in Grammar, is when an Adjettive hath joined to its Natural and Ordi - nary Signification, the Word most or very, as most Wife, very Good. SUPERPURGATION. See Hypercrttharfts.

supersedeas.c: SUPERSEDEAS, is a Writ in Divers Cafes, and signifies in general, a Command to stay, or forbear the doing of that which ought not to be done, or in appearance of Law were to be done, were it not for that whereon the Writ is granted, Thus,: A Man regularly, is to have Surety of Peace against him of whom he will Swear he is afraid, and the Justice required hereunto cannot deny it him: Yet if the Party be formerly bound to the Peace, either in Chancery, or elsewhere, this Writ lies to stay the Justice from doing that which otherwise he ought not to deny.

superstatutumed.c: SUPER Statutum Ed.. verfus Servants f La - borers, is a Writ lying against him who keeps my Servants, departed out of any Service against Law.

superstatutodeyork.c: SUPER Statuto de York., quo nul f era viteller, Sec. is a Writ that lies against him that uses Victualing either in Gross, or by Retail in a City, or Bo - rough - Town, during the time he is Mayor, &c.

supervisor.c: SUPERVISOR,, signifies a Surveyor, trover - seer: It was formerly, and is still among some a Custom, especially of the better fort to make a Su - servitor of a Will, but it is to little purpose: HoW - eyer the first might be good, that he Ihould Super - S U R,,;;: vise the Executor, and see the Will truly per - formed. - y

supinatorradiibrevis.c: SUPINATOR Radii Brevis, is a Muscle of the Radius, which ariseth partly Tendinous and Flefiiy. from the Superior and External part of the Vena, next the Radius, and passing obliquely transverse over that Bone, is so inferred to its Superior part below the Prominence of the Radius, where the round Tendon of the Biceps fendeth: It. helps with the Supinator Longus, to move the Radius out - wards.

supinatorradiilongus.c: SUPINATOR Radii Longus, is a Muscle of the Radius, which ariseth broad and fleffiy from the Superior and External part of the Os Humeri three Fingers breadth below the Termination of the Del - tides, and descending obliquely inwards, it gra - dually lessens it less, and becomes a flat, broad Tendon, which likewise grows narrower till it is inserted to the External and Inferior part of the Radius near the Carpus, it helps with Supinator Brevis, to move the Radius outwards.

supplantalia.c: SUPPLANTALIA, are Plaifters applied to the Feet; these for the most part are made of Leven, Mustard, Wild Radish, Salt, Sope,. Gunpowder Euphorbium, &c. they are called also Supply dane.

supplement.c: SUPPLEMENT of an Ark, in Geometry or Tri - gonometry, is the Number of Degrees that it wants of being an entire Semi - circle; as Complement signifies what an Ark wants of being a Qua - drant. SUPPLICAVlT, is a Writ issuing tit of the Chancery, for taking the Surety of Peace against a Man: It is directed to the Justices of Peace of the County, and the Sheriff, and is grounded upon the Statute, Anno E.. Cap.. which ordains. That certain Persons in Chancery, shall be assigned to take care of the Peace. This Writ was formerly called Breve de minis.

supportersinheraldry.c: SUPPORTERS, in Heraldry, are some kind of Beasts, Birds & c. which in an Atehietfement, ate drawn standing on each side of, and supporting the Shield, or Escutcheon ', None one under the De - gree of a Rjiight Banneret, can have his Arm drawn with Supporters.

suppository.c: SUPPOSITORY, is an oblong piece of a kind of Paste, of about a Fingers length, which in some Cafes is put Up into the Fundament, to purge the Patient; ’ tis usually compounded of Honey, Salt, Purging Powders, &c. Blanchard.

supraspinatus.c: SUPRA Spinatus. or Supra Scapularis, is a Muf - cle so called, because it is placed above the Spine of the Shoulder - blade: It ariseth fleftiy from the Superior part of the Basts Scapula, that is above its Spine; as also from the said Spine and Costa Supe - rior of the Scapula - from thence passing between the Procejfus Coracoides, and Anchor ef or mis, it grows less, and becoming Tendinous, marches over the Articulations of the Humerus, joining its Tendons with the Infrafpinatus, is inferred to the Head of the Os Humeri. The proper use of this Muscle, is to lift the Arm upwards towards the Occiput.

suralvein.c: SURAL Vein, is a Vein which runs down on the Calf of the Leg.

sur.c: SUR cut in vita, is a Writ that lies for the Heir of that Woman, whose Husband has alien - ted her Land in Fee, and die brings not the Writ Cut in vita, for the Recovery of her own Land: In this Case her Heir may have this Writ against the Tenant after her Decease.

surety.c: SURETY of the Peace, ( so called, because the Party that was in fear, is thereby secured ) is an acknowledging of a Bond to the Prince, taken by a competent Judge of Pvecord, for the Keeping of the Peace. This Peace may a Just ice of the Peace command, either as a Minister, when he is com - mended thereto by a higher Authority or as a Judge, when he doth it of his own Power, derived from his Commission. Surety of the good adhering, differs from this, j hat whereas the Peace is not broken without an Affray, or such like the Surety tf de bone gefiu may be broken by the Number of & Man ’ s Company, or by his or their Weapon and Hardness.

surface.c: SURFACE, ( the fame with Superficies ) is the bare outside of any Body and considered by it self, is Quantity extended in Length and Breadth only, without Thickness. There are Plane Surfaces, and there are Crooked or Curved ones. A Plane Surface or Superficies, is made by the Motion of a PJght Line always keeping in the fame Plane. A B Thus, if the Line A B be conceived to move ( with a Motion parallel to it self in its first situation ) in the fame Plane downward, and at last to stop in the Position E F, it will describe the Plane Fi - gure or Surface A BE, which is called a Parallel - logram. j As also the Two Plane Figures or Surfa - ces A B F and AS, which are called Triangles. Also, if the Right Line C A having one end as A fix ’ d as on a Center, be moved quite round in the fame Plane, till the Point C come to C again this Line will ' Ey its Motion describe a Plane Figure or Surface, which is called a Circle, as C E B A. Curved Surfaces, are Convex above or without and Concave below or within You may conceive them like the Tilt of a Boat or Waggon And such Surfaces may be generated either by the Motion of a Right Line on a Curve, or a Curve Line on a Right one, v. gr. In the Figure, Let S U R A b Let the Curve Line A a a C represent the Hoop keeping up the Cloth of a Waggon or Boat; and let the Line A B represent the Gunnel or the upper Edge of the Boats side, or the upper Rail of the Waggon. Tis plain that if you conceive either the Right Line A B to move up along the Hoop A a C till it come to the Top, and then down again on the other side till it come to the Bottom, it will by its Motion describe the Figure of the Tilt or curved Surface Abb Q a a A. And the very fame Figure would be produced by the Motion of one of the Hoops or crooked Line A a C, carried ( in a Position parallel to it self ) along the Edges of the Boat or Waggon.

How to change Customary - Measure into Statute - Meal Jure, and the Contrary. /; Say, As the Square of one fort of Measure, is to the Square of the other: So is the Content of the one, to the Content of the other. Thus, Suppose a Field Measured by a Perch of Foot contain Acres, How many Acres shall the fame Field contain by a Perch of Foot - j ? Say, If the Square of Foot, vi.,, give the Square of, vi., What shall Acres Cufiomary give ? Answer, - f Statute J. crcs

surveying.c: SURVEYING - SWe, the fame with Reducing - Scale.

survivorinlaw.c: SURVIVOR in Law, fignioes the longer Liver of two Joint - Tenants - or of any two Joined in the Right of any thing.

suspensionorsuspense.c: SUSPENSION, or Suspense, is a Temporal stop of a Mans Right; as when a Seigniory, Rent, & e. by reason of the unity of Possession thereof, and of the Land out of which they Issue, are not in else for a time, and tunc dormiunt, but may be revived or awaked, and so differs from Extinguifhmenr, which dies for ever. And sometimes this Word Sulpen - sion is used in Common Law, as it is inthe Canon Law, pro minori Excommuicatione.

suspensor.c: SUSPENSOR TeJUculi, the Name of a Muscle otherwise call ’ d Cremajler; which fee.

suspensokium.c: SUSPENSOKIUM, is a Ligament of the Penis, first discover ’ d by our Accurate M, r. Ccwper the Sur - geon Sf I S Y M geon. It ariseth from the Anterior Part of the Os Pubis, and fix ’ d to the upper part of the Do'r - sum Penis, on each side. its great Vein. It ’ s use is to assist the Mufculi Erigentes in their Action. S SUTURA also, is a connexion of the Sides or Lips of a Wound. This is of two forts: Acftual, which is done with a Needle of a triangular Point, a Pipe, or Cane, and waxed Thread: Firftinthe middle of the Wound you must few it together with a double Thred, and having made a Knot, cut it off; the reft of the Wound must be sewed up with single Thred; care must be taken that the Stitches are not fet too wide nor too close efpe - cially not too close, that there may be room for any corrupt Matter bred in the Wound to work out. The other fort of Suture, is much like the Way that the Skinners use to few Skins together: This is proper in Wounds of the Intestines, and in Cuts of the Veins and Arteries. Also the JunEiures of the Parts of the Shells of Fishes to one another, are call ’ d Sutures.

sutura.c: SUTURA OJJium, a Suture in the Juncture of the Bones of the Skull, like the Teeth of Saws meeting together. Those which join the Parts of the Skull to the Bones of the upper Jaw, are of forts; the ' franfverfalis, the Ethmoidalis, and the Sphanoidalis; which fee under those Words. The Sutures joining the parts of the Skull are: The Coronalis, Lambdoidalis, Sagit tails, and Squam - tnofa which fee.

swabber.c: SWABBER; the Title of an inferior Officer aboard a Man of War, whose Office it is to fee that the Ship be kept Neat and Clean; in order to Which, he is to fee her Washed well once or twice ' a Weak at least, especially about the Gun walls and Chains. He ought to burn Pitch or some such thing now and then between Decks, to pre - sent Infection: and to acquaint the Captain of such as are Nasty and Offensive.

swainmoteorswainimote.c: SWAINMOTE, or Swainimote, signifies a Court touching Matters ofForeft, and held by the Charter of the Forest thrice in the Year, before the Verdorors, as Judges. And it is as incident to a Forest, as Court of Pye - powder to a Fair.

swallow.c: SWALLOW - TW /, in Fortification, is a single tenaille, that is narrower towards the Place than towards the Country, See Queue dyronde.

sweep.c: SWEEP. The Seamen call the Mold of a Ship When file begins to compass in at the Rungheads, the Sweep of her; or the Sweep of the Futtock.

sweepingatsea.c: SWEEPING, at Sea, signifies dragging along the Ground, at the Bottom of the Sea, or Chan - nel, with a Tree - fluked Grapnel, to find some Uawfer or Cable, which is slipper from an Anchor.

swiftinmotion.c: SWIFT in Motion, a Planet is said to - be lo,. when by its own proper Diurnal Motion, he ex - ceeds, or moves further than his mean Diurnal Motion: Slow in Motion, is when his Motion hap - pens to be lels than his mean Motion.

swifters.c: SWIFTERS, in a Ship, are Ropes belonging to the Main - masts, and Fore - masts, and help to succour or strengthen the Shrowds and to keep the Masts stiff: They have Pendants fattened under the Shrouds at the Head of the Masts, with a double Block, thro ’ which the Swifter is reeved; which at the standing Part hath a single Block with a Hcok, hitched into a Ring at the Chain VP ale, and so the Fall being haled up, helps to strengthen the Mast, and it is belayed about the Timber - heads of the lower Rails aloft, m - I:, S WIFTING of a Boat, is compassing her Gun - Wile round with a good Rope, to II lengthen her in a Stress of Weather, that fire be not fluttered by the Violence of the Sea.

swifting.c: SWIFTING of a Ship, is either bringing her aground, or upon a Careen; for then they use to Swift the Masts, to ease and strengthen them, that all the Weight may not hang by the Head; which is done by laying fast all the Pendants of the Swifu ers and Tackles ( with a Rope ) close to the Mast, and as near to the Blocks as can be; and then to carry forward the Tackles, and there to Bowse, or hale them down, as hard and taught as is possible. ( So that the Sea Word of Command here, is, Ho l Bowse Men ! ) All this is done also to keep the Mast from rising out of the Step.

swiftingthecapstan.c: SWIFTING the Capstan - Bars, is ( training a Rope all round the outer ends of the Capstan - Bars, in order to strengthen them, and make them bear all alike, and together, when the Men have or work there

swing.c: SWING - WHEEL, in a Royal Pendulum - Clock, is that Wheel which drives the Pendulum: This Weel, in a Watch is called the Crown - wheel, as also in a Balance - Clock.

superficialfoumcau.c: SUPERFICIAL Foumcau,, a Term in Fortifica - tion, the fame with Caijfon, which is a Wooden Chest, or Box, with,,, or Bombs in it, and sometimes ’ tis filled only with Powder; and is used in a close Siege, by being buried under ground with a Train to it, to blow up any Long - ment that the Enemy shall advance to. There - fore they usually express it thus: “ After the Mine, “ or Fourneau, had destroyed the Bonette, a Caijfon “ was buried under the Ground thrown up, and “ the Enemy advancing to make a Lodgment “ on the Ruins of the Bonette i the Caijfon was “ fifed, and blew up the Post a second time.

sycosis.c: SYCOSIS, is an Excrefence of the Flesh about the Fundament; ’ tis also an Ulcer, so called from the Resemblance of a Fig; this is of two kinds one hard and round the other soft and flat: out of the hard issues a very small Quantity of glut - nous Matter; out of the moist proceeds a greater Quantity, and of an ill smell: These Ulcers grow in those Parts only which are covered with Hair the hard and round chiefly in the Beard; the moist for the most part in the Scalp. Blanchard.

syllepsisorconceptio.c: SYLLEPSIS, or Conceptio, ( in Grammar ) is when the Sense of an Exprefllon is to be conceived otherwise than is imported by the Words; and so the Conftruiftion is made accordingly as some de - fine ir. But VoJJius faith, ’ tis an Agreement of a Verb or an Adjecftive, not with that Word which is most near, but with that which is most Worthy, Honorable, Eftc. in any Sentence, as Be E Regina beati.

symmetry.c: SYMMETRY, is usually taken in ArchiteElurc, for the Proportion required, according to the Rules of Geometry, to make all the Parts of any Structure compleatly agree to, and with the Whole.

sympatheticalinky.c: SYMPATHETICAL Inky, are such as can be made to appear or disappear very suddenly by the Application of something that seems to work by Sympathy., / Thsr f S Y M S Y M There are some ways of preparing Inks of this Kind; which are really wonderful and surprising, as well as curious and diverting. The Experiments are these. i. That the first of these Liquors is a mixture of the Alkalizate, and fiery Salt of Quick - lime,, with the Sulphureous Substance of the Orpin, which is a kind of Arfenick. Take of good unslaked Lime, two dr three parts, according to the strength and goodness of the fame, and one part of Yellow Orpiment, ( which to powder, had best be wrapt up in a thick Paper, and so beaten, to prevent the dangerous Steams that may passed the Head ) both these being pow - der ’ d and mixed, put to them or x times as much Water, in Weight, as there was of Orpin: Stop the Viol well with Cork and a Bladder, and let it in warm Embers, or some such place; ha - king the Viol now and then for or Hours; then warily decant the clear part; or which is better, filtrate it. In the mean time burn a piece of Cork through - ly; and when it is well inflamed, quench it in common Water ( or which is better, Aqua Vita:, or Brandy ) and by this means reducing of it to a friable Coal, grind it with a sufficient quantity of fair Water, in ' which you have diflblved a little Gum - Arabicks and so it will make a Liquor as black as common Ink, which will serve very well to write any thing with. While these are doing, diflblve in three tithes as much distilled, or strong Vinegar, over warm Em - bers, a Quantity of Bed Lead, ( or Minium ), or of Saccharum Saturni, in three times as much Wa - ter, for or Hours, or till you find the Liquor have a very sweet Taste. This will likewise, as the first Liquor, be clear as common Water. All things being thus ready ( for you must be pretty quick at it ) write on a piece of Paper what you will, with this last Liquor, with a clean, or new Pen and when it is dry, nothing will ap - pear. Then over that place write with the Ink you made of the Cork, what you please; it will look just as if it had been written with common Ink, which let dry; then dipping a small piece of Rag, or a Sponge, in the first Liquor, rub it On the place written, and you will immediately see the Black Writing varnish, and that written with the Invisible Ink, appear Black and Legible, Take also a Book or Inches thick, and writ - ting on the first Blank Leaf with the last Liquor, or the Invisible Ink; or putting in there a Paper so written, turn to the other end of the Book, and rub there with a Rag dipt in the first Liquor, on that part that is as nearly as you can guess, oppo - site to the Writing, and leave also the Rag there: And over it clap a folded Paper, and nimbly hut - ting the Book, strike or good Stroaks on it with your Hand, and then turning it t ’ other side uppermost, clap it into a Press, or lay it between two Boards with a good Weight on it for a Quar - ter of an Hour ( or half that time will do ) then taking it out, you ’ ll find the Writing black and le - gisle, which was written with the Invisible Ink. This Process, Mr. Boyle communicated in his History of Cold, pag. a. and afterwards Lemery publiflied it in his Course of Chymijiry, with the Addition of the latter Experiment. By whole help we may endeavour at a Solution of these strange Experiments; ifweconfider, . That the Blackness of the Ink, which is the second Liquor, proceeds only from the porous, light, and sooty parts of the Cork; which are its Oily Parts very much rarified. . That the last Liquor ( or the Invisible Ink ) only the Parts of the Lead held up imperceptibly in the acid Liquor of Vinegar. Hence then, the Reason of the disappearing of the Ihk in the first Experiment, is from the pene - trating Parts of the first Liquor, which consisting of an Alkalizate Salr, and a penetrating Oil, or Sulphur, doth make a kind of Soap, which soon diflolves the rarity ’ d Fuliginosity of the Ink, as common Soap takes away grease Spots out of C loath s, CSV. And the Invisible Ink then appears black, be - cause the Edges of the acid Liquor that hold the Parts of the Lead diflblved, being now broken by its Conflid with the Alkali of the first Liquor; the Parts of the Lead, are, as it were, precipitated on the Paper, and so appear in their proper colour, ' which is Black. So that the Visible Ink disappears, because its Black Parts are diflblved; and the Invisible doth appear, because it ’ s diflblved Parts are revived, of restored. The Second Experiment slews the strange piercing Subtility of the first Liquor. You had best make all the Liquors in different Places, least they should mingle, and so spoil the Experiment, as I have known them fotnetimes do. ' Experiment the Third. Diflblve a little White, or Green Vitriol In Water; and then write with a clean Pen with the Solution, nothing will appear. Boil Galls in Water, and dip a Rag of Linneri in the Decodion, and with it rub the Place before written, and it will appear Black and Legible. But if you rub over it with a Feather, or a Rag dipt in Spirit of Vitriol, ( or its Oil ) the Letters will disappear again. V Dip another Rag in Oil o Tartar per Deliquium and rub on the Place, the Letters will appear again, but of a Yellowifli Colour. Lemery s Chymijiry, last Edit. pag.. REASONS. The Coagulum of the Vitriol and Galls, is the Cause of the firfl Blackness, ( as is sees in making common Ink, ) which the acid Spirit of Vitriol dis - solves, and so the Letters disappear: But the Oyl of Tartar breaking ( as it uses to do in all Precipitate - ons ) the force of this acid Spirit, rejlores the Coagu - lum; but spoils its Colour a little, by mingling it self with it.

sympathetickpowder.c: SYMPATHETICK Powder, is only ( said Le - very, ) Green, or Pp an Vitriol, opened by the Sun Beams Beams penetrating into it, and imperfectly calci - ning it: The Vitriol is usually exposed to the Sun ’ s heat in the Month of July, but some use only Pow - der of Vitriol. When they use it, they spread some of the Powder upon a Linen - cloth dipt in the Blood of any Wound, and then pretend, that if the Cloth be many Miles off the wounded Person, yet he ( hall be healed: but this is so far from being true, notwithstanding the vaunting Stories of Sir JQen. Digby and others, That ’ twill hardly have its EffeCt if done in the fame Rooih where the Patient lies and he is certainly very much wanting to himself, who will use no other help. Vitriol hath its Parts in continual Motion; and tis probable, many Effiuvia, may go out from it and some few of those, if Application be made to the Cloth, just by the Patient, may perhaps en - ter into the Wound, and help to stop the Bleeding, for Vitriol is a known Styptick but he that Will negleCt all other Means, and depend only on this may probably pay dear for his Credulity.

sympeps.c: SYMPEPS S, is a CoChon of those Humors, which are growing into an Impoftuine.

symphysis.c: SYMPHYSIS, is the joyning of two Bones of which neither has a proper distinct Motion: This is either without any Medium, or else with it, as with a Cartilage, or Grille, a Ligament, or Flesh, &c.

symptom.c: SYMPTOM, is a preternatural Disposition of the Body, occasioned by feme Disease; this is ei - ther a Disease caused by another Disease or else the Cause of a Disease proceeding from another Disease or else limply a Symptom: This last is either some Action of the Body hundred, or di - surbed, some fault of the Excrement, or change f the Natural Temper. Blanchard.

symptomaticalfevers.c: SYMPTOMATICAL Fevers, according to some are those which arise from the Inflammation and Putrefaction of Humors contain ’ d in foftie of the Bowels, of which kind are those Fevers that ac - company the Pleurifie, Inflammation of the Lungs, and Liver, Frenzy, Quinsie, and other Inflammati - ons, or Ulcers of the Internal of External Parts.

synactica.c: SYNACTICA, are Medicines that con trad any part. SYNALfEPHA, is a Figure in the Dimension, of Scanning of a Latin Verse whereby there is a Coalition of the two VoWels, or Diphthongs, one of which ends, and the other begins two contigu - ous Words in a Verse, fd that they make but one.

synarthrosis.c: SYNARTHROSIS, is a joyning of Bones by a Grille, and is of two forts, vi. Sutura, and Gomphojis, which fee.

sybjchysisingrammar.c: SYBJCHYSIS, in Grammar, is a confused and disorderly placing of Words in a Sentence.

synchysisadisease.c: SYNCHYSIS, a Disease, is a preternatural Confusion of the Blood, or Humors of the Eyes. Blanchard.

syncopalisfelris.c: SYNCOPALIS Felris, or the Swooning Fever is that in which the Patient often Swoons and Faints away. Blanchard.

syncopationaterminmusick.c: SYNCOPATION, a Term in Musick, which is when a Note of one Part ends and breaks off upon the middle of a Note of another part.

syncopeinmusick.c: SYNCOPE, in Musick, is the driving a Note, when some Shorter Note prefix ’ d at the beginning of the Measure, or Half - measure, is immediately Note equivalent to that which began the driving, to make the Number even, As when an odd Crot - chet comes before two, three, or more Minims, or an odd Quaver before two, three, or more Crotchets.

syncopeinphysick.c: SYNCOPE, in Physick, is a sudden Prostration or Swooning, with a very weak, or no Pulse, and a Depravation of Sense and Motion.

syncopeingrammar.c: SYNCOPE, in Grammar, is the taking away a Letter or Letters, out of the middle of a Word: As Dixti, for Dixijli, Eppoflum for flepofitum.

syndesmusorsyndefmous.c: SYNDESMUS, or Syndefmous, the fame with a Ligament.

syndrome.c: SYNDROME, is a Concurrence of several Symptoms in the fame Disease.

synecdocheatropeinbhctorick.c: SYNECDOCHE, a Trope in Bhctorick., where the Name of the Whole is put for a Part; or the Name of the Part for the Whole: As if we should fay, Europe for England, or England for Europe.

synecdocheingrammar.c: SYNECDOCHE, in Grammar, is when the Ablative Case of the Part, or the AdjunCt, is chan ged into the Accusative: As in that of Virgil. Deiphohum vidi lacerum crudditer Ora And in this: Flores infcripti nominee Begum.

synechphonesisorsyni.c: SYNECHPHONESIS, or Syni efls, is a Figure in Grammar, whereby two Vowels are contracted into one as in this Verse of Virgil. Seu lent fuerint Alvearia viminal text Where the ca in Alvearia, are contracted Into one Vowel. .

synedrenonta.c: SYNEDRENONTA, are common. Symptoms which accompany Diseases and yet neither flow from the Nature of the Disease, nor are necessary Concomitants of t; but do, notwithstanding, fig - nisi the Greatness, Continuance, &c. of the Dis - ease.

syngultusthehiccough.c: SYNGULTUS, the Hiccough, is a depraved Convulsive Motion of the Stomach, by which it endeavours to expel something that is hurtful, or offensive.

sinocha.c: SINOCHA, is a Continued intermitting Feverj this lasts for many Days with a great Heat, some - times Putrefactions qf the Blood: it is either Quo - tidian, Tertian, or Quartan. Blanchard.

synochus.c: SYNOCHUS, is a continued Fever without any Intermission, or Abatement of the Heat, which continues. for many Days: This is either simple,, of accompanied with PutrefaCtion. Blanchard.

synodameeting.c: SYNOD, A Meeting, or AfTembly of Ecclefi aftical Persons concerning Religion Of Which, there are four Kinds. . General, where Bishops,. &c, meet of a ll Na - tions; '. ' ‘ ' Q, i. Nati - S Y K S V N follow ’ d by two, three, or more Notes of. a great - ter Quantity, before you meet with, another sliort S YP . national, where those of [ one Nation only come together. . Provincial t where they of be only Pro - since meet, , Dioceftan, where those of bat one Diocese meet: See Convocation, which is the fame with Synod, only the one is a Greeks, and the other a Latine World. Cowel's Interpreter.

synodicalmonth.c: SYNODICAL Month, is the Space of Time, ( vi. Days, Hours, Minutes ) contained between the Moon s parting from the Sun at a Conjunction, and returning to him again during which time, she puts on all her Phases. And her

synodicalrevolution.c: SYNODICAL Revolution, is that Motion where - by her whole System is carried along with the Earth round the Sun.

synonomy.c: SYNONOMY, is when the fame thing is cx - prels ’ d by several Words that have but one and the lame signification: As if one should fay. He went away, he escaped, he fled.

syntasis.c: SYNTASIS, is a preternatural Distention of Parts,

syntectoe.c: SYNTECTOE, is a kind of Looseness that pro - ceeds from the melting away of the Substance of the Body, by a violent hot Distemper of the solid Parts such as sometimes happen in the Inflamma - tion of the Bowels, and in a vehement burning Fe - ver, Hectick, or Pestilential in which a fat Mat - ter, as it were mixt with Oil, or Grease, is voided by Stool.

syntenosis.c: SYNTENOSIS, is reckoned by some, to be the tJnition of one Bone to another, by a Tendon j as the Knee - pan to the Thigh - bone and Tibia.

synteretickmedicines.c: SYNTERETICK Medicines, are that part of Physick, which give Rules for the Preservation of Health.

syntexis.c: SYNTEXIS, is a Consumption and Colliqua - flon of the Body, in which first the Flesh is wafted, and afterwards the Substance of the more solid Parts. Blanchard.

synthesis.c: SYNTHESIS, is either the Frame and Structure of the whole Body; or more strictly, the Com - posture of the Bones. Tis also used in Mathema - ticks, in opposition to the Word Analysis; in which sense it signifies Composition, or the
SYNTHESIS is also used by the Grammarians, to signifie an Agreement of the Parts of a Sentence as to Sense, but not as to the Words.

syntheticalmethodofenquiry.c: SYNTHETICAL Method of Enquiry, or De - fnonftration in Mathematicks, is when we pursue the Truth chiefly by Reasons drawn from Princi - ples before established, and Propositions formerly proved, and proceed by a long regular Chain, till we come to the Conclusion: As is done in the Ele - ments of Euclid, and in almost all the Demonflrati - ons of the Ancients. This is called Composition, and is opposed to the Analytical Method, which is called Resolution; which fee.

synymensis.c: SYNYMENSIS, is taken to be the uniting of Bones together by a Membrane, as in Infants, the Bones of the Synciput, with the Os Frontis.

syphon.c: SYPHON, is a Tube, or Pipe of QJafs, or Me - tal, which is usually bent to an Acute Angle, and having One Leg shorter than the other; they are frequently to draw oft Liquors out of one Barrel, r Vessel, into another, without railing the Lees, V or Dregs, and are called Cranes, Sometimes Glass Tubes, or Pipes, tho ’ strait, are called iy - pons. For the Cause of the running of Water, or other Liquors, through Syphons or Cranes: See Hydrofta - ticks, Paradox.

syringe.c: SYRINGE, is an Instrument which is used in injecting Liquors into Wounds, Ulcers, or any diseased Parts of the Body.

syringomat.c: SYRINGOMAT, are Chirurgeons Knives, which they open Fiflulas with.

syringotomia.c: SYRINGOTOMIA, is the Incision of the Ft - tula.

syssarcosis.c: SYSSARCOSIS, is the Connexion of Bones by Flesh. Blanchard.

systeminmusick.c: SYSTEM, in Musick, is the Extent of a cer - tain Number of Chords, having its bounds toward the Grave and Acute, which hath been differently determined by the different Progress made in Mu - sick, and according to the different Divisions of the Monochord. The System of the Ancients, was composed of four T etrachords, and one Supernumerary Chord, the whole making Fifteen Chords.

system.c: SYSTEM properly is a regular orderly Collecti - on, or Composition of many things together. Thus the Solar System, is the Aggregate Union j or orderly Disposition of all thole Planets which move round the Sun as their Centre, in determin'd Orbits, and never deviate farther from him than their proper and usual Bounds. And a System of Philosophy, is a Regular Collection of the Principles and Parts of that Science into one Body, and a treating of them Dogmatically, or in a Scholaftical Method; which is called the System - matical Way, in contra - distinction to the Way of Eft - fay, wherein the Writer delivers himself more loosely, easily, and modesty. The Learned Dr. Hook., did in the Year at the end of his Attempt to prove the Motion of the Earth by Observation, promise that he would explain a System of the World, differing in many things from any then known, and yet exactly a - agreeable to Mechanical Principles. Which System he there says, depends on these three Suppose - tions, vi. First, That all the Heavenly Bodies have a gray vitiating or attracting Power towards their own Centres, whereby they attract not only their own Parts, and keep them from flying off from them, but also all other Celestial Bodies within the Sphere of their Activity. Secondly, That all Bodies put into a direct and simple Motion, will so continue to move forwards in a strait Line, till they are by some other more effectual Power bent or deflected into a Motion, which describes some Curve Line. Thirdly, That these attractive Powers are so much the more powerful in operating by how much the nearer the Body wrought upon, is to their own Centres. All which is abundantly confirmed in Sir Isaac Newton s Admirable Principia Philosophy Mathema - lcd

systoleinanatomy.c: SYSTOLE, in Anatomy, is the Contraction of the Ventricles of the Heart, whereby the Blood is forcibly driven into the great Artery. SYSTOLE SYS S Y Z

systoleingrammar.c: SYSTOLE, in Grammar, is pare of the Poetical Licence, whereby a long Syllable is made short: As in that of Virgil. - Tulerunt fajlidia Menses.

systyleinarchitecture.c: SYSTYLE, in Architecture, is a Building where the Pillars Hand thick, but not altogether so close as in the Pychnojlyle; the Inter - calumniation, or Di - stance between them, being only two Diameters of the Column.

syzygieinastronomy.c: SYZYGIE, in Astronomy, is the fame with the Conjunction of any two Planets, or Stars, Or when they are both referred to the fame Point in the Heavens; or when they are referred to tile fame Degree of the Ecliptick, by a Circle of Longitude putting through them both. H . j s he Vfesof the Astronomical Tables, in the Calculation of Eclipses, & d " DEforc I shew you the Method of the Calctila - tion of the Exadfc Time of the Eclipses of the Sun and Moon it will be proper to premise these Observations by way of Lemmata: As Mr PVhifton hath done in his PraleEl Afironom. I. That there is this great difference between an Eclipse of the Sun and of the Moon: That a Lunar Eclipfeisthe fame entirely, from what part of the Earth soever it be look upon, and doth not receive any alteration, from the divers Position of Places ofthe Surface of the Earth, for where there is a real Lofsor Deprivation of Light, ’ tis all one if you look upon it from the Equator, or from the Poles; for the Beginning, End, and Quantity of the Eclipse of the Moon depends on real Causes, and not only on the different Position of the Observer. But in theSun the Case is quite otherwise: A So - lar Eclipse, is not any real deprivation or loss of Light in him; ’ tis only a local interruption of the Sun ’ s Light to some particular Places, occasioned by the Interposition of the Moon ’ s Body. For in such Parts of the Earth, as have the Centre of the Moon ’ s Body interposed between them, and the Centre of the Sun; there may be a Total Solar Eclipse; whereas in Regions lying at some di - stance side - ways from thence, the Eclipse may be only Partial, and if they lie very remote, they may not see the Sun eclipsed at all. And there - fore Lunar Eclipses are of the greatest Use in the finding the Longitude of Places, the Observation of those of the Sun being useless for that Purpose. z. There are uni verbally considered, more So - lar than Lunar Eclipses, but there are more of the Moon in any one particular Place; for since the Earth ’ s Dis, is much greater than the Disk of its Shadow seen at the Moon; it must needs be that the Penumbra of the Moon, ( ball sal oftner into the broader Disk of the Earth while the Sun is eclipsed, than the narrower Moon can into the narrower Disk of the Earth ’ s Shadow, while Ihe is eclipsed. But since the Eclipses of the Moon will be all observable in the fame Place, as often as Ihe is never so little above the Horizon of that Place; whereas such of the Sun only, will be visible any where, as happen when the Moon is interposed, between that particular Place and the Sun: ’ Tis easily seen, that in particular Places, Lunar Eclipses mu ft be roost frequent. . Total Eclipses of the Sun are very rare, so that if you confider them with regard to any par - dicular Place, you will hardly have above two or three in the compass of an Hundred Years. The Reason of which, is, that the Vertex or Point of the Conical Shadow of the Moon ’ s Body, doth fall beyond the Earth ’ s Surface, and sometimes doth not quite reach it: Nor is that strange, when we take notice, thatthe Moon ’ s apparent Dia - meter doth so little exceed that of the Sun, that it can ’ t totally cover or obscure it, but only in some very Rare, Total, and Central Eclipses, nor in every Central one neither; For if no Eclipse happen when the Sun is in his Perigecum, and the Moon in her Apogstumr the apparent Diameter of the Sun will exceed the. Lunar one, and so the Eclipse will appear annular, or the Shadow of the Moon will be environed with a Ring of Light all round about it. . The Moon is never eclipsed by the very Sha - dow of the Earth it self, but only by that of the Earth ’ s Atmosphere. This was a Proposition perfectly unknown to the Ancients, but is fuss - ciently apparent and manifest, from the Conse - duration of Refra & ion. For those Rays of Light which are next the Earth, enter into its Atmosphere, and then go out of it again: But while they do thus pass out of a Rarer medium into a Denjer, they must by the known Laws of Refradfion, tend towards the Perpendicular; nor can it be otherwise when they go out of the Atmosphere again, for then they will recede from the Perpendicular; and as well in the former Case as in the latter, the Perpendicular being changed, they are inclined the fame way; that is, towards the Axis. And from this double Refrad & ion, when brought to Calculation,. it appears that those Rays of the Sun, which pass near the Earth, are so infietted, as to concur in a Point long before they reach, to the Distance the Moon is placed at. . In Lunar Eclipses, the consideration of Pa - rallaxes and Refractions hath no Place; but in So - lar one ’ s, tho ’ there be not much regard had to the latter, there must be the greatest to the former. The Reason whereof, is, that with regard to Refradfion and Parallax, the Shadow of the Earth in the fame Place of the Lunar Transit m aftedted after the fame manner, as the Moon her self would be in palling thro ’ it - y and so produces no difference in the Calculation. And in like manner in Solar Eclipses, the Refraction of ei - ther the Solar or Lunar Light, at the fame Ele - vation above the Earth ’ s Horizon, is still one and the fame; ( as by late Observation hath been af - certained ) as if both Luminaries had been at the fame distance from the Earth.
