There is usually a great Difference between the nearest approach of their Centres and the Moment of the Full or New Moon, and therefore between those Moments of Time, and the Time of the true Syzygy in the Moon ’ s Orbit, accounting from the beginning of Aries. For the Time of the Eclipti - cal Full or New Moon, in a Plane Normal to the Ecliptick: The Time of the nearest approach of their Centres, in a Plane nearly Normal to the Lunar Orbit: The Apparent Time of the Syzygy in the Lunar Orbit, where the Archs drawn from the beginning of Aries, to the Centres of the Sum and Moon, are equal, ! is obfervedVto happen in a Plane Normal, neither to the Ecliptick, nor the Moon ’ s Orbit, but in an intermediate one between both. The half therefore, of the Excels or Defed, of the least Distance of their Centres in the Ecliptical Syzygy, is. nearly equal to the Difference between the Time of the Full or New Moon in the Lunar Orbit, and that in the EcJiptical Orbit, and confequendy to the least Difference of their Centres, and this half Difference is called the Re - suction j which if taken, from the Time of the true Syzygy, accounted from the beginning of Aries, will give the Moment of the Ecliptical Syzygy; if added to it, the Moment of the nearest approach of their Centres. But it an - ciently signified the Reception and Entertainment of the King, or any other Lord and his Retinue; and frequently in the Doomsday Book, a Con - dition of Tenure was pro firm a per nnum diem, or pro firmaper unam noBem: And lb, because in the Saxon, and Part of the ATor man, Times, the Rent of Lands was paid in Provisions, Firm a signified the Profits and Rent of an Estate: But Henry II. for better Convenience, alter ’ d this Custom into ah equivalent of Money; which Pecuniary Rent was still call ’ d Firma Regis.

sailsandsailing.c: SAILS and Sailing of a Ship. In order to com - put the Force of the Water against a Ships Rud - der, Stem or Side; or the force of the Wind a - Painft her Sails, a late Author, whose Book is tinted at Parish y the French King ’ s express Com - and, and called the Theory of the Handling or Working of Ships at Sea, and lately Englished, pro - ceeds on this Foundation;. He considers all Fluid Bodies, as the Air or Water, cc. as being composed of little Bodies or Particles, which when they at upon, or move against any Surface, do all move parallel one to another, or strike a - gainst the Surface after the fame manner.. He considers that the Motion of any Body, with re - gard to a Surface on which it is to strike, rust be afterone of these three ways, either Perpendicular s Parallel or Oblique. In the first Case, let the Line D C, in Fig.. represent a Plain Surface, and let the Line A B be Perpendicular to it, describing the direct Impulse of the Body A upon it; ris plain here that the Body A strikes upon it with all its force, and this Force may be called Absolute, and may be expressed by the Line A B, which the moving Body A describes: And this Absolute Force will be greater or les s, according as the Body A moves Jmfter or flower. (. ) If the Motion of the Body a be Parallel to the Surface D C, then ’ tis plain the Line of Motion a b will not affedi the Surface at all, because it is no way opposed to it j nor can the moving Body strike upon it, or touch it. (. ) If the Line of Motion A D be Oblique to the Surface D C, so that the Angle of Incidence be ADC. then the Motion of the Body in the Line A D, may be resolved into two Forces, vift, into AE, or D B, and into A B, ( See Composition of Motion. ) But the Direction or Line of Moti - on A E, being Parallel to the Surface D C, cannot affedt it at all; so that the whole Motion of the Body A, iir that Oblique manner of Striking on the Surface, will be expounded by the Perpendicular Line A B. And if DA be made the Radius of a Circle, whose Centre is at D, BA will be the Sine of the Angle of Incidence ADC, and consequently, you may conclude that the Force of a Particle of Air or Water, as A, linking against the Surface DC, which may represent either a Sail, or the Rudder of a Ship, in the Oblique Di - section A D, will be to the Perpendicular Force there, as B A Is to D A: that is, as the Sine of the Angle of Incidence is to Radius. And since what is thus true of one Particle singly considered, will be true of all the Particles of any Fluid Body ColleEiively; it will follow, that the force of the Air r Water falling Perpendicularly upon a Sailor the Rudder, to the force of the fame in any Ob - pique Impingency, will be as the Square of the Radius, to the Square of the Sine of the Angle of Incidence: And consequently, that all Oblique Forces of the Wind against the Sails, or of the Water against the Rudder, will be to one another as the Squares of the Sines of the Angles of Incidence. Here is no regard had to the different Degrees of Velocity, with which the Wind or Water may impinge against the Sail or Rudder; but only of the Position of the Surface so truck, with regard to the Impinging Force: But when that Matter is considered, it will be found that the different For - ces then will be as the Squares of the Velocities of the moving Air or Water: That is, that a Wind that blows thrice as strong, or moves thrice as swift as another, will have nine times the force upon the Sail. And it being also, faith he, indifferent, whe - ther you confider the Motion of a Solid in a Flu - id, whose Particles are at reft, or of those Parti - cles moving all Parallel against a Solid that is. at reft, the Reciprocal Impreftions being always the fame: So that if a Solid be moved with different Velocities in the fame Fluid Matter ( as suppose Water, ) the different Refiftences which it will re - A civ " A S A Ceive from that Water, will be in the fame Proper - tion as the Squares of the Velocities of that Bo - Let H M represent a Ship, C D the Position of the Sail, AB the Course of the Wind blowing to - wards B. Draw B G Perpendicular to: the Sail D C, and G K Perpendicular to the Line of the Keel produced HMK. By what he hath said above, the Sail C D will bedriven by the Wind AB, according to the Di - section of the Line BG: So that if ( he could di - vide the Water every way with the fame Facility, as ( he doth with her Head, the Ship would go di - erectly to the Point G, along the Line B G. And if H K represent her direCt Course, Ihe would have got forward the length B K, and sideways Ihe would have gone the Quantity G K. But as her Length is much greater than her Breadth, so she will divide the Water, or make her way in it much more difficultly with her Side, than with her Head or Stem -, on which account, she will not run sideways solar as KG, but fall Ihort of it in Proportion to the said Difficulty of dividing the Water with her Side: That is, if the Resistance ihe finds in palling thro ’ the Water sideways, be to that of palling lengthwise, suppose as to i, then will not the Ship get sideways above a i oth part of the Line GK. Wherefore if KG can be found to G L, in the Ratio of the Resistance of the Side to that of the Stem, and the Line B L be drawn, the Ship will go to the Point L, along the Line B L, in the fame time as it would have gone to G, if it could have divided the Water every way equally. salutesalus.c: SALUTE, SALUS, was a Coin of Gold, Stampt by K. Henry. in France, after his Con - quest there, it had on it the Arms of England and France quarterly.

sanctuary.c: SANCTUARY, was formerly a Place Privi - leged by the Prince for the Safeguard of Mens Lives that were Capital Offenders: Our ancient Kings of England, permitted the San & aries to protect Tray tors, Murderers, &c. if within Days they acknowledged their Fault, and submit - ted themselves to Bamlhment: And during ' that time, if any Layman Expelled them he was Excom - tunicated, and a Clerk was made irregular by it. Bu after days, no Man might relieve them. Of these there were many in England, and one more famous than the reft, at St. John s at Beverly. How these were taken away by degrees, you may find by reading the Statutes of H.,. H... H.,. E... E... and ....

sand.c: SAND - bags, in Fortification, are Bags holding about a Cubick Foot of Sand or Earth: They are used for railing Parapets in haft, or to repair what is beaten down; they are souse when the Ground is Rocky, and affords no Earth to carry on their Approaches; because they can be easily brought on and off at pleasure: There are a lesser fort of these which hold half what the former do, which are placed upon the upper Talus of the Parapet, to cover those which are behind, and who fire thro the Embrafiures, or Intervals that are between them.

sapinfortification.c: SAP, in Fortification, is digging deep under the Earth, in order to pass under the Glacis, and to open a way to come under cover to the Passage of the Moat. When they are got near the foot of the Glacis, the Trench is carried on diredfly for - wards, the Workmen covering themselves as well as they can, with Blinds, Wool - packs, Sand bags, and Mantelets upon Wheels: When they are got to the foot of the Glacis, they make Epamments, or Traverses on each side to lodge a good Body of Men. The Sap is made or Fathom from the Saliant Angle / of the Glacis, where the Men are only co - ver ’ d sideways; wherefore they lay Planks over - head with Hurdles and Earth above them. When they have forced the Enemy to quit the Cover ’ d Way, the Pioneers make immediately a Long - ment, and cover themselves as well as they can born the Fire of the opposite Bastion.

saphetainarchitecture.c: SAPHETA, in Architecture, is the Board over the top of a Window, and placed Parallel, and opposite to the Window - board at the bottom.

sarplier.c: SARPLIER, otherwise called a Pocket, is a half Sack of Wooll, a Sack is Tod, a Sod Stone, and a Stone Pounds. This in Scotland is called Serpliath, and contains Stone.

This Water thus impregnated with Salt, they boil in Leaden - pans, wherein ( as above ) the Wa - ter Evaporating, leaves the Salt behind. At New c agile, Prejlon - pans, in Scotland, White - haven in Cumberland, and otherPlaces, they make Salt in great Plenty, by Boiling and Evaporating the Sea - water, and in the Operation they make use of Oxes Blood, as at Nantwyche. From Dr. Jack fin ’ s Account of the Salt - works and Springs in Ches hire, in the Philofiophical Trans - actions, I find that now they have changed their Leaden - pans into Iron ones, something better than Yard square, and about Inches deep; which are fet upon Iron - bars, and made up on all sides very close, to hinder the Flame or Smoak to break thro, with Clay and Bricks. Their Fewel is Staf - fordjhire Pit - coal. They never cover their Pans at all, during uhe whole time of boiling; and their Houses are like Barns, open up to the Thatch, with a Louvre - hole or two to carry off the Steam, which is so great, that probably it would warp Boards, and rust Nails so that no Timber - covering would last long; what Tiles would do, no one yet hath tried there. The Sweepings of such Salt as is filed and feat ter ’ d about on the Floor, takes up with it a good deal of Dirt, and is called Grey - Salt. This sells but at half the Price of white Salt, and is only used by the Poor to Salt Cheese, Bacon, Catts of Salt are made of the worst Salt, when yet wet - tisri from the Pans, ’ tis molded and made up with some Cummin - feed and Allies, and so baked into Lumps at the Mouths of their Ovens j they are only used in Pigeonhoufes. But Loaves of Salt are thefineft of all for Table use. At Droitwyche in Worceprfhire, they use no Blood, but only Whites of Eggs ( a quarter of one White to a Gallon of Brine ) to Clarify their Brine j and to Granulate it, they use no Ale, nor any thing else; this Salt is much whiter and better than the Che - shire Salt, and a Winehefier Bulhel of it weighs halse hundred Weight. The way of making Bay - Salt in France,. is deferibedin Philofiophical FranfiaBions, N.. with Figures. The Water is let in from the Sea into a first and second Receptacle, and then into a third, which is called the Marijk. In these Beds or Ma - arches the Water is not above an Inch and half deep each Bed of the Marijh is Foot long, and Broad. When it rains much on any day, no Salt can be made in or days after, and then they have Stops to hinder the Sea - water from coming into the Mari foes But if it rain for or days, they are necemtated to empty all the Water out of the Beds by a peculiar Channel, which can - not be opened but at Low - water. The hotteft Years make the most Salt, and in the hotteft part of Summer, Salt is made in France, even in the Night: Less Salt is made in Calm than in W ind W either, and the Well and North - eji Winds are best for that Purpose. The People draw the Salt every day, and each day more than an hundred Pound weight. It doth not appear by any Astronomical Ob - fervations, that Saturn, like the other Planets, which have Satellites, revolves round his own Ax - is; but the contrary seems to be the Case. For in Jupiter and the Earth, which do turn round their Axes, the Equatorial Diameters are longer than Polar ones, or their Axes, but no such thing hath been found in Saturn. Each Surface of the Ring of Saturn seems to be plain and smooth, without any such Mountai - nous Inequalities as the Earths Surface, and the Moons hath; because it is not liable, tho Ill - minated by the Sun, but only when the Eye is e - elevated some few Degrees above its Plane. ’ Tis either Fluid therefore like Water, or Polite, like Ice or Glass. If it be a Fluid, it moves round Saturn with a Circular Motion; but if it be of a Solid Substance, it is not yet determined, whe - ther it move round the Planet or not. And since the Figure of Saturns Ring is exa & ly Circular, it must have no Linen Apfidum, nor any Progression of it: But because the Plane of the Ring hath a large Elevation above the Plane of the Ecliptick, vi. making with it an Angle of Degrees, the Nodes will recede, but yet very slowly, according to the manner of the other Planets.

satellites.c: SATELLITES. Dr. Gregory, in his Excellent Astronomy, hath deuaonftrated, that if a Satellite describe an Elliptick Orbit round a Planet, placed in one of the Foci, of that ElUpfis the greater Axis, or the Line of the Apfes will with an Angu - lar Motion twice advance forwards, vi. in the Syzygies, and twice recede backward, vi. when in Quadrature to the Sun. And that this Force of Progression is near twice as great as that of the Recess, and therefore the Line of the Apfes in every Revolution of the Sa - stellite, will advance more forward than it recedes backward; and that by the Excess of this Progref - sion, the Apfes will move in Confepientia. p. If a Satellite move round a Planet in an Eccen - trick Orbit, the Eccentricity will be twice changed in every Revolution, and in each Revolution will be greatest, when the Satellite is in the Syzygies with the Sun, and least when it is in the Quadratures; and will be continually encreasing from the Quadratures to the Syzygies, and decreasing from the Syzygies to the Quadratures, p.. If a Satellite revolve round a Planet in an Or - bit, whose Plane is inclined to the Plane of the Or - bit of the Planet round the Sun, then will the Line of the Nodes move in antecedentia, with an unequal Angular Motion; swiftest when the Nodes are in Quadrature to the Sun, after this flower, and at last when the Nodes are in the Syzygies, will be quite at reft. I the intermediate Places between the Quadratures and Syzygies, the Nodes will re - cede flower; and in every Revolution of the Satel - lite, will either be Retrograde or Stationary, be carried backward, or move in Antecedentia, and in each Revolution will recede fafteft, all things con - Adered, when the Satellite is in the Syzygies, b. The Inclination also of the Plane of the Orbit of the Satellite, to that of the Planet, will be conti - nually changing, and will b q greatest when the Nodes are in the Syzygies with the Sun, and least cater is paribus when they are in the Quadratures, / ?.. And all the Inequalities in the Motions of the Satellites will be a little greater when they are in Conjunction with the Sun, than when they are in opposition to him, p..

saw.c: SAW, is an Instrument very well known in the general, as well as its use. But they reckon these several forts of Saws.. The Pit Jaw, which is used to Saw Timber and Boards, and to cut off Scantlings, Quarters or Battens from any piece of Timber. The Matter to be Sawed is sore - times lain over a Pit, and sometimes on great Trusses above ground.. The hKhip - Saw sufed by Joyners, to cut off such pieces of Stuff as the Hand - Saw will not easily notch thro. ’ Tis drawn by two Men, and theTimber is placed on Trusses, in order to be cut.. The Hand - Saw, which is to be used by a Angle Man, and usually with one hand.. The Frame - Saw, or Bow - Saw, is a Saw with Cheeks made to it, and with a twisted Chord, and Tongue in the middle to draw the upper ends of the Cheeks closer together, that the lower ends maybe farther asunder, ands ( train the Saw the straighten -. The Tendon - Saw, which is a thin Saw with a Back to it, to keep it from bending.. The - Compass - S aw, which is design ’ dtocut a Round, or a, ny Compass - kerf; wherefore its Edge must be made ? road, and the Back thin, and the Blade narrow, that the Back may have a wide Kerf to turn in, and so the easier follow the Edge.

scaleofmusick.c: SCALE of Musick, tho ’ we find mention of fe - veral Distances of Musick among the Greeks, yet I rather think them to be Leaps in a Angle part, than Concords in Composition. The Distances talk ’ d of a - long the Greeks, are the lst ' Second, the APovtSKcr third, the ai s t sage or fourth, the ai Ah or Afth, and Aiamua or eighth; But if these were dean d to denote the Concords, they were iri the wrong to place the fourth, and more so to place th second among them: Or if such were admit - ted, ’ tis a wonder that the sixth, which is known to be a Concord, was refused. But if they were used to Ihew the Distances, by which a Voice may rife or fall, it is no wonder that they left out the sixth and J event b ( being Distances not to be used with - out better Judgment and DeAgn thanthofe Times would admit of ) and made mention of the reft, as being common in their MuAck. The Scale of Musick among the Greeks, confi - sted but of fifteen Notes, or the Distances of two O Staves, viz. The first from their ( which I suppose was the Key of their Musick, ) to their and the second from their or Middle - Note to their or highest Note, by which I suppose they designed only the uttnoft Extent of a Angle Natural Voice. And their Seven Moods, so much talk ’ d of, were no more than the seven different Methods of al - vering their Tunes, by Flats and Sharps, placed ' at the beginning of a Lesson; which therefore they called [ MiaZoKii KfKTzi TVVOV. Besides the Names of their Notes in the upper O & ave, have no Affinity with the Names in the other; whereas in Guido Are sinus his Scale f Notes ( tho ’ our Modern Compofers in many Parts often exceed the Scale, both above and below ) and the Notes in every Gdtave begin with the fame Letter; that we may thereby more readily compute the Concords and Discords.

sparagescaragium.c: SPARAGE, Scaragium, otherwise called Efche - rage, Shewage and Scheawing; and in a Charter of PI.. to Canterbury, ' tis written Scewinga was for -, merly a kind of Toll or Custom, exadted by Her Majefties Sheriffs, &c. of Merchant Strangers for Wares Wares, ybeweJ or offered to Sale within their Pre - cinifts. This is now Prohibited by Statute, i p H.. c.. But the City of London doth still retain the Custom. Cowel ’ s Interpreter. The Officer that Colle & ed this Toll, was called the Scabaldue.

scalewilliam.c: SCALE, William I. appointed the Arms, which before him had been usually answered in Victuals, to be converted into Money numbred, and directed the whole in every County to be charged on the Sheriff, - who brought it into the Exchequer. adding, that the Sheriff fllould make the Payment, ad Scalam, i. e. as Gervafe of Tilbury expounds it, he should pay Pence over in every Pound to make up the full Weight, and nearly the Intrin - sick Value. And this was agreed oh, as an easie way to remedy the defedive Weight of Money, and to avoid the trouble of weighing all Money which was brought into the Exchequer.

sceppe.c: SCEPPE, an old Word, omitted in our Gloffa - ries, signifying a Bujhel.

scenographyckprojection.c: SCENOGRAPHY CK Projection, or Perfpe - dive, is the Transcription of any given Mag - nitude, into a Plane which intense & s the Op - tick Pyramid at a proper distance: For in Projection, there is to be confided,. The Object, or Foundation, or Ground of the Projedi - on, from whence the Pyramid, Cone, or Pencil of Pays go. (. ) The Eye of the Spedator, and the Plane Table, r Diaphanum,, which interfeds the Rays, some where between the Object and the Eye: And the Representation or Appearance of the Object in that Plane, is the Projection or Per fpeElive of the Object. This Plane is always sup - posed to be at Right Angles with the Horizon. And from hence it will follow, that (. ) A Point will be pro jaded there in the Diaphanous Plane, where the Optick Ray cuts it. (. ) That Right Line will be projeded where the Optick Triangle and the Plane do mutually Intersect each other.. That a Plane or Superficies will be represent - ted where the Diaphanous Plane cuts the Optick Py - rapid of Rays coming from that Surface. And that Representation of it called its Image.

schemeorseen.c: SCHEME, or Seen, in Architecture, is the Workmens word for the middle part of an Ellip - tic. Arch

schire.c: SCHIRE - MOTE, was anciently a Solemn Meeting of all the free Tenants and Knights in a - ny County, to do Fealty to the King, and Eied an Annual Sheriff. See Folkymote.

suchre.c: SUCH RE - WYRE, was an Annual Tax or Impo - sition, paid to the Sheriff of any County or Shire, for holding the Assizes or County - Courts.

scratch.c: SCRATCH - work, in Italian, Sgrafitti, was a way of Painting in Fresco, by preparing of a black Ground, on which was placed a white Plaster and this White being taken off with an Iron Bod - kin, the Bl ck appears t ro ’ the Holes, and serves for Shadows: This kind of Work is laftirig, but being very rough, isunpleafant to the fight. ’ Twas used ip Pome by Polidoro de Caravagio.

scutage.c: SCUTAGE, all Tenants who held from the King by Military Service, were either bound to at - tend Personally in Wars and Expeditions, or for default of such Service, to pay a Scutage or Cotxipo - sition in Money, which was Levied on every Scu - tum Mili tare, ot Knights Fee, and the Proportional Parts for the Kings Use. And the Barons and Knights, which then paid a Scutage to the King,, had a Power to Levy the fame Tax on those Te - nants who held from them in Military Ser - vice.

scutagio.c: SCUTAGIO hahendo, was a Writ that lay for the King, or other Lord, against the Tenant that held by Knight - Service, to serve by himself, or else to fend a sufficient Man in his Place.

sculpture.c: SCULPTURE, may be distinguished into three several Arts, each of which hath its Specifick Dis - ference. For ( faith Mr - Evelin in his History of Cha l cography ) besides Sculptura, as it relates to Chal ography, there is both Sculptura and C ( datura both Which, according to Quintilian, differ frOm the fir ft, with respect to the Matter, on or out of which any thing is wrought. For it was applied to cutting or carving in Wood or Ivory j and thew was called Tomice, and the Artifts hese ( lores j to working in Plaster, and then called Paradigramma the, and the Axtifts, Gypfochi; to Cutting or Carving in Stone, and then called Colaptice, and the Workmen Lithoxoi, nd lastly in Metals, Glyphice. And it may be described to be an Art, which teaches us to cut or take away all that is fuperflu - ous of the subject Matter, reducing it to that Form or Body, which was designed in the Mind of the Ary tis.

scyre.c: SCYRE - GEMOTE, was anciently a Court held twice a Year ( as the Sheriffs turn is now, ) by the Bishop of the Diocese and the Ealderman i. e. in such Shires as had Ealdermen ) and by the Bishops and Sheriffs, in such as were committed to the Sheriffs that were immediate to the King; where both the Ecclesiastical and Temporal Laws were given in Charge to the Country.

sealer.c: SEALER, is an Officer in Chancery, appointed by the Lord Chancellor, or Keeper of the Great Seal, to Seal the Writs and Instruments there made in his Presence.

sectacurl.c: SECTA Curl, is Suit and Service done by Te - nants at the Court of their Lord.

sectaschirarum.c: SECTA Schirarum ( Hundredorum, was the At - tendance, Suit and Service done by Tenants in the County and Hundred Courts; and Quietos else de hac Secla, was a Privilege to be exempt from such Customary Service.

sectionsconick.c: SECTIONS Conick, fee ConickSeBions. SECTIONES Secjuentesy is a, Term in Conicks, arising thus: Let there be two Right Lines, asa, CD, mutually interfeeding each other in E; which point E, isfuppofed to be the Common Centre of the opposite Hyperbolick Sections, FG, HI, and whose common Asymptotes the proposed Lines A B, CD, also are. In this particular Case, the Sections G F, and H I, are called SeSliones Sequen - ces, because they are placed following one ano - ther in the Contiguous Angles of two Interfering Right, Lines. And if the determinate Diameter HG, f one of the SeBiones Sequent es ( which is coincident with the supposed Indeterminate Diameter of its Oppo - site ) be equal to the Vertical Tangent K L, apply - ed between the Alymptotes in the Point G, of the Diameter GF, then Apollonius calls such Sections Conjugate Sections.

segments.c: SEGMENTS, on Gunter ’ s Sector there are usu - ally placed two Lines, called Lines of Segments s they are numbred with,,,,,, and lie between the Lines of Smw, and those of Superficies They represent the Diameter of a Circle so divi - ded into parts, as that aright Line drawn thro those parts, and normal to the Diameter, shall cut the Circle into z Segments, of which the greater shall have that Proportion to the whole Circle j as the Parts cut have to. Their tiles are, I. To divide a given Circle into z Segments, which shall have a given fiatio, which is done by opening the Seder, and applying the given Circles Diame - ter in the Points of in these Lines j for then a Parallel taken from any Points proportional to the greater Segment required, shall give the depth of the greater Segment, accounted on a Diameter biifeding the Segment, Z. To find the Proportion between the Circle and an / given Segments of it. Open she Seder, as before, and then take the depth of the greater Segment, and apply Parallel to the Diameter, and the Points where it fits in exact - ly, willfhew the Proportion to. Seeing. The Sense of Seeing is probably caused thus; the Rays of Light exhibiting all Colours, fall upon the bottom of the Eye, and there cause or excite Vibrations in the Tunica Retina; Which Vibrations being communicated, or propagated a - long the Solid Fibres of the Optick Nerves into the Brain, do there cause that Sensation, which we call Vision or Seeing. For because dense Bo - dies conserve their Heat along while, and the Den - sest, the longefttime, the Vibrations of their Parts are of a lasting nature, and therefore may be pro - pacated along solid Fibres of Uniform Density to a great distance, for conveying into the Brain, the Impreflions made upon all the Organs of the Sense. For that Motion which can continue long in one and the fame part of a Body, can be propagated a long way from one part to another, supposing the Body Homogeneal, so that the Motion may not be reflected, refracted, interrupted, or disordered by a - ny unevenness of the Body. Newton ’ s Opticas, Book. The fame Author renders it probable, that the Species of Objects seen with both Eyes, are united in that Place where the Optick Nerves meet and joyn, before they come into the Brain: The Fi - bres on the right side of both Nerves uniting there, and after Union, going thence into the Brain in the Nerve, which is on the right side of the Head j and the Fibres on theleftfide of both Nerves uni - ting in the fame place, and after Union going into the Brain in the Nerve, which is on the left side of the Head: And these two latter Nerves meet and unite in the Brain, in such a manner that their Fi - bres make but one entire Species or Pidure: Half of which, vi. that on the right side of the Sense - rium, comes from the right side of both Eyes, thro the side of both the Optick Nerves, to the Place where these Nerves meet, and from thence on the right side of the Head into the Brain: But the other half, vi. that on the left side of the Sense - rium, comes in like manner from the left side of both Eyes. For the Optick Nerves of such A - animals as look the fame way with both Eyes, ( as of Men, Dogs, Sheep, Oxen, &c. ) meet before they come into the Brain j but the Op - tick Nerves of such Animals as do not look the SER S E R fame way with both Eyes ( as of Fifties, and of the Chamcelion, do not so meet and unite. If I am rightly informed. , Wlaeii a Man in the dark, presses either corner of his Eye with his Finger, and at the fame time turns his Eye a contrary way, he will fee a Cir - cle of Colours, like those in the Feather of a Pea - cock ’ s Tail; which variegated Circle of Colours, seems to arise from the fame kind of Motions ex - cited in. the bottom of the Eye by the Pressure f the Finger, as at other times are excited thereby Light for causing Vision. And when a Man by a stroke upon his Eyes fees a Flafli of Light, are not the like Motions excited in the Retina by that Stroke ?

seignourage.c: SEIGNOURAGE, H.. Stat.. c. i. seems to have been a Royalty or Prerogative of the Prince, whereby he challenged allowance of Gold and Silver brought into the Mass for his Exchange for Coin. Out of every Pound Weight of Gold, the King had for his Coin five Shillings, out of which he paid to the Master of the Mint for his Work, sometimes Shilling, and sometimes Pence. Upon every Pound Weight of Silver the Seignourage, answered to the King, in Ed. ' s time was eighteen Penny - weight Were, which about that time vamounted to about a Shilling, and out of which he paid sometimes, sometimes Pence to the Mint - master. In H. the th ’ s time, the King ’ s Seignourage for every Pound Weight of Silver was Pence.

sellinarchitecture.c: SELL, in Architecture, is the Term both for the lowest piece of Timber in a Timber - building, or for that on which the whole Superftrucfture is ere & ed; and alfofor the bottom - pieces in a Win - dow - frame; the former is called a Ground - fell, the latter a Window - fell.

semesumm.c: SEME, Summ t is an Horse load, a ' Seme of Corn is Bufhels.

seneschal.c: SENESCHAL, was the Word anciently for the Chief Steward or Head Bailiff of a Baron, that kept his Courts, and managed his Demesne lands, and hath beenthe Tide of the Lord High Stew - ard, and of the Steward of the King ’ s Houftiold, ? c.

septuagesima.c: SEPTUAGESIMA, is always the third Sunday before Quadragesima exclusive; from which, until the Otftaves after Eajler, Marriage is forbidder by the Canon - law. It takes its name from its being above Days before Eajler.

septummedium.c: SEPTUM Medium, is properly theinfideof the left Ventricle of the Heart, because its Fibres are continued with the Fibres of the opposite side of tbe fame Ventricle; it divides the left Ventricle of the Heart from the right.

sequelcause.c: SEQUEL Cause, is the Process and depend - ding Issue of a Cause or Trial.

sequelmolendini.c: SEQUEL Molendini, sowing Suit to a par - dicular Mill, or being bound to grind Corn in that Place only; which formerly was a Duty and Ser - vice laid upon many Tenants; wherefore Conci - dere Sequelam Molendini, was to grant all the Toll and Profits arising from such Customary Rights.

sergeant.c: SERGEANT, is a word diversly used in our Law, and applied to sundry Offices and Callings. A Sergeant at Law, or of the Coif, is the greatest Degree taken in that Profession, as that of a Do - ctor is in the Civil Law. Asthefe are the most Learned and Experienced, there is one Court ap - propriated to Plead in by themselves, which is the Common - fie as, where the Common Law of Eng - land i most stri & ly observed. - But tho ’ they have this Court to themselves, they are not prohibited Pleading in other Courts; where the Judges ( whomuft be first Sergeants ) call them Brothers, These Sergeants are call ’ d by the Kings Mandate, or Writ directed to them, and commanding them, under a great Penalty to take upon them that Degree by a Day Assigned. Out of these one is ( more maybe ) made the Kings Sergeant, t Plead for him in all Causes, efpedaily in Treason.

sergeantatarms.c: SERGEANT at Arms, is an Officer appointed to attend the Person of the King, An. H.. c.. to Arrest Traytors, c. and Persons of Quality Offending, and to attend the Lord High Steward when he fits in Judgment on any Traytor, c, By the Stat. Richard. c,. There cannot be a - above in the Realm. Two of these by the King ’ s Allowance attend the two Houses of Parliament. The Office of him in the House of Commons is to keep the Door, and to execute such Commands as the House ( hall direct, especially as to the apple - pension of Offenders, c. Another of these attends on the Lord Chancel - lor or Keeper in the Chancery, and one on the Lord High Treasurer, one to attend on the Lord Prefi - dent of Wales, and another on the Lord President of the North. Another fort of Sergeants, are chief Officers executing several Functions in the King ’ s Household; of which you may find many in Star. H.. c.. There is alfoan inferiour kind of Sergeants of the Mace, whereof there is a Troop in the City of London, attending the Lord May - or -

sergeantry.c: SERGEANTRY, was a Service formerly done for the holding of Lands, and was either Grand Ser - jeantry, which was some Honourable Military Ser - vice paid only to the King; as to carry his Banner, bear his Sword, c. Or Petty - Serjeantry, which was some less Noble Service paid to the King, or any other Lord. Some will have Grand Serjean - try, to be where a Man holds Lands of the King by Service, which he ought to perform in Person, and Petty Serjeantry, to be where he holds his Lands of the King, to yield him Yearly some small thing towards his Wants.

service.c: SERVICE - Royal, was the Rights and Preroga - tives that within such a Mannor belonged to the King, if Lord of it; and were generally rec - zoned to be these.. Power of Judicature in Mat - ters of Property.. Power of Life and Death in Criminal Causes.. A Right in Ways and Strays.. Affeffments.. Minting of Money.. Assize of Bread, Beer, Weights and Mea - fures.

SERVICE, ( which is sometimes called Ser - age ) is divided into Personal and Real, and into Military and Base; as also into Intrinfick. and Ex - trinfick. Intrinfick Service they reckon due to the Capital Lord of the Mannor. Service is again di - vided into Frank and Base, the one is ter med Libe - rum Servitium, the other Villenagium. ’ Tisalfo di - vided into Continual or Annual, and into Casual or Accidental; the former being the Seisin of Rent, and the latter Seisin of Reliefe.
SERVICE, in a Legal Sense, is a right by which one thing isfubjedt to another thing or Per - fon. And of these some are,

servicespredialorreal.c: SERVICES Predial or Real, which are Rights that one Estate sometimes owes another And these Predial Services, they reckon to be some Ruftical or Rural; such as the Right of Riding or Walking, or going with a Carriage thro ’ another Mans Ground; S I G V - -, ' C Ground j theRightof drawing Water, orbring - ing it thiyb ’ his Ground, He. And feme Services xare called Urban, which are the Rights that are preferred to Mens Houses, built contiguous to one another, He.

services.c: SERVICES Per final, are those Services which are due from a Thing to a Person - and of these they account by name, vi. VfufruB, Vfe and Habi - tation but there are very many and various ones which have no distend: Names.

servitiumregale.c: SERVITIUM Regale, Royal Service, are the Rights and Prerogatives that within such a Mannor belong to the King as Lord of it; and these are generally reckon ’ d. As,. Power of Judica - ture in Matters of Property.. Power of Life and Death in Cafes of Felony and Murder.. A Right in Waifs and Strays.. Alignments., Minting of Many. And Assize of Bread and Beer, Weights and Measures. All these entire Privileges were annexed to some Mannors, in their Grants from the King, and were sometimes conveyed in the Charters of Do - nation to Religious Houses.

servitorsofbills.c: SERVITORS of Bills, are such Servants or Meffengers of the Marshal of the Queen s - bench, as were sent abroad with Bills or Writs, to Summon Men to that Court. They are now commonly called Tip - Jlaves.

sesamoidta.c: SESAMOIDTA Of a, the Use of these Bones, which are placed at the Articulations of the Bones of the Fingers and Toes, is that they may serve as so many Pullies about which the Tendons pass, at some distance from the Centre of the Articulation, whereby the Directions of the Motions of these Tendons are kept always at the fame distance from the Centre of Motion of the Articulati - on.

sewers.c: SEWERS, are Passages, Canals, or Gutters to carry Water into the Sea or some River. And therefore the Commissioners of the Sewers are such Persons, as by Authority under the Great Seal of England, do fee Ditches and Drains in Marlhes and Fenny - places, well kept and maintained for the better preserving the Grass upon the Lands for feeding of Cattle, He. by conveying the Water off the Ground into the Sea or River.

sextaryofwheat.c: SEXTARY of Wheat or other Corn ( from Sexta - yius ) was that quantity anciently which we now call a Quarter, containing a Bushel. In some Countries ’ tis called a Same.

shaft.c: SHAFT, is the hollow Entrance into a Mine which is funk, or dug to come at the Ore. In the Tin mines, after this is funk about a Fathom, they leave a little long square Place, which is called a Shamble.

shelf.c: SHELF, is what the Miners ( especially in the Tin - Mines, ) call the FaJI - Country, by which they mean an Imaginary Surface of the Earth, which at the Concussion of the Waters in the general De - luge of Noah, was never moved and to the Shelf, they think all the Loads or Mineral Veins at first lay even and parallel; tho ’ after the Flood they were tome elevated, some depressed, He. And by Shelf now they mean that hard Surface or Coat of the Earth which lies under the Mold, usually about a Foot deep; for they suppose, that since the Flood the Earth hath gotten a new Coat of Vege - table Earth, or such as is made by the Corruption of Vegetables and Animals.

shriveorsheriff.c: SHRIVE or Sheriff, Vice - Comes, is the Chief Officer of the King in any Shire or County, for - merly the Sheriff was chosen by the People in the County - Court by Vote, as the Knights of the Shire for Parliament now are; but now the She riff is nominated by the King. Camden in his Britannia, describes this Office, and the Antiqui - ty and Authority of this Officer. See Co. Rep. lib.. And Spelmans Glossary under the word Vice - Comes. His Oath is extant in Reg. Orig. sol. i.

sheriff.c: SHERIFF - TOOTH, seems anciently to have been a Tenure by the Service or Duty offprovi - ding Entertainment for the Sheriff at his County - Turns or Courts. For it appears by Rule / s Place - ta Parliament, sol.. that in Derbyfbire the King ’ s Bayliffs did formerly take Pence of every Bovate of Land, in Name of Sheriff - tooth.

shillingsolidus.c: SHILLING, Solidus in the Latin is a word of very uncertain Signification, and differs almost in every Nation. But the word Scylling or Shilling in England, never signified any thing but d. with the Saxons, and id. ever since. When it first went for d. ’ tis hard to find: But there was no Penny Piece of that name Coined in England till. and then Stow calls them Groats tho ’ Fa - bian mentions them under the name of Shillings In H.. there were Penny Pieces struck, but they were called T efions.

shinglingtongs.c: SHINGLING Tongs, are used in the Finery of an Iron - forge, to take out the Loop, in order to bring it under the Hammer into a Bloom.

should.c: SHOULD, is the Miners Term in the Tin Mines, for such Fragments of Ore, which by Rains, Cur - rents of Water, He. are torn off from the Load or Veins of Ore. These are walht down from the Mountains, and by finding of them, they guess whereto look for a Load of Ore. Sometimes ’ tis called Squod, sometimes Squad.

shortsails.c: SHORT Sails, in a Man of War, are the fame with the Fighting - fails, and are the Fore - said Main - sail and Fore - topsail These are all that are used in a Fight, left the reft should be fired or spoiled: And besides they would be troublesome to handle and would hinder the fight and use of Arms. When a Ship gives Chafe to another, if the Chafe hath a mind to fight, they fay, the Chafe Jirips her self into her short or Fighting - fails; that is puts out her Colours in the Poop, her Flag at the Main - top, and her Streamers or Pendants at her Yard - arms j Furls her Sprit - fail, Peeks her Mizqn, and Slings her Main vard, and when the Chafer fees this, he is to prepare for an Engagement.

signals.c: SIGNALS, are Signs made at Sea by the Ad - moral or Commander in Chief of any Squadron of Ships, either in the Day or by Night, either for Sailing or Fighting, or for the better Security of the Merchants Ships that are under the Convoy of Her Majefties Men of War. These Signal s are appointed and determined by Order of the Lord High Admiral, and are as follows:

SIGNALS used when a Fleet Sails in a Fog. . If the Admiral would have them weigh, he fires o Guns, which every Flag - ship is to an - fwer. . To make them Tad he fires Guns; which are to be answered by the Flag - ships, and then the Leewayd - ma: Ships, and Stern - most Ships must Tack first. And after they are about, to go with the fame Sail they Tack ’ d with, and not to lie by, gxfie - dting the Admiral to come a Head: And this is to avoid the Danger of running thro ’ one another in thick Weather. . When the Admiral brings to, and lies with his Head - fails to the Mast -, if with the Star - board Tack Aboard, he fires Guns; but if with the Lar - board Tack Aboard, Guns, which the Flag - Ships are to answer. And after the, if he makes Sail, he fires o Guns, which the Flag - ships must answer; and then the Head - most and Weather - most Ships are to make Sail first. . If it grow thick and foggy Weather, the Ad - moral will continue Sailing with the fame Sail fet that he had before it grew foggy, and will fire a Gun every hour; which the Flag - ships must an - fwer, and the private Ships must answer by firing of Muskets, beating of Drums, and ringing of Bells. But if he be forced to make either more or less Sail than he had when the Fog begun, he will fire a Gun every half hour, that the Fleet may difeerri whether they come up with the Admiral, or fall a Stern of him; and the Flags and private Ships are to answer, as before. . If any one discovers Danger which he can a - void by Tacking and hanging from it; he is td make the Signal for tacking in a Fog; but if he should chance to fir ike andftick fast, he is to fire Gun after Gun, till he thinks the reft have avoided the Danger. B. When t SI G S I G . When the Admiral would have the Fleet to Anchor, he fires z Guns, which the Flags are tb answer; and after he hath been half an hour at an Anchor, he will fire a Guns more, to be answer - ed by the Flags, as before, that all the Fleet may know it.

SIGNALS for calling Officers on Board the Ad - moral . When the Admiral puts abroad a Union - Flag in the Mizen - ftirouds, and fires a Gun, all the Captains are to come Aboard him: And if with the fame Signal there be also a Weft made with the Ensign, then the Lieutenant of each Ship is to come on Board. . If an Ensign be put Aboard in the fame place, all the Matters of the Ships of War are to come on Board the Admiral. : If a Standard on the Flag - staff be hoisted at the Mizen - top - mast - head, and. a Gun fired, then all the Flag - Officers are to come Aboard the Admiral. If the Englijh Flags only, then a Stan - dard in the Mizeii - shrouds, and fire a Gun: If the Flags and Land General Officers, then the Ad - moral puts Aboard a Standard at Mizen - top - mast - head, and a Pendant at Mizen - peek, and fires a Gun. . If a Red Flag be hoisted in the Mizen - ftirouds, and a Gun sir'd, then the Captains of his own Squa - iron are to come on Board the Admiral; and if with the fame Signal there be also a Weft with the Ensign, a Lieutenant of each Shipmuftgoon Board. . If he hoist a White Flag, as before, then the Vice - Admiral, or he that Commands in the second Post, and all the Captains of his Squadron are to go on Board the Admiral. If a Blue Flag, cc. then the Rear - Admiral, and the Captains of his Squadron must come on Board; and if there be a Weft, as before, the Lieutenants. . When a Standard is hoisted on the Ensign - staff, and a Gun fired, the Vice and Rear - Admirals must both come on Board the Admiral ’ s Ship. . When the Admiral would speak with Cap - tains of his own Division, he will hoist a Pendant on the Mizen - peek, and fire a Gun; and if with the Lieutenants, a Weft is made with the Ensign, and the fame Signal. For whenever he would speak with Lieutenants of any particular Ship, he makes the Signal for the Captain, and makes a Weft also with the Ensign. . When the Admiral would have all the Tenders in the Fleet come under his Stern and speak with him, he hoist a Flag, striped Yellow and White, at the Mizen - peek, and fires a Gun. But if he would speak with any particular Ships Tender, he makes a Signal for speaking with the Captain ihe tends upon, and cl Weft with his Jack. . If all the Pinnaces and Barges are to come on Board, Manned and Armed, the Signal is a Pendant on the Flag - staff, hoisted on the Forc - top - mast - head, and a Gun; and if hd would have them Chafe any Ship, VeffelorBoat in View, he hoist the Pendant, and fires a Guns. The Signal for the Long - coats to come on o. w v Board him, Man d and Armed, is the Pendant hoi - sted on the Flag - staff at the Mizen - top - mast - head, and a Gun; and if he would have them Chafe any Ship, Vessel or Boat in open view, without coming on Board him, he hoist the Pendant, as aforesaid, and fires Guns. When the Admiral would ha call the Boats in the Fleet come on Board hint, And and Arm ’ d, he hoist a Pendant on the Flag - staff, both on the Fore - top - mast, and Mizen - top - mast - head, and Fires Gun; but if he would have them Chafe, he hoist his Pendants, as before, and Fires Guns., . When the Admiral would speak with the Vi & ualer, or his Agent, he puts ah Englijh Ensign in the Mizen - top - most - shrouds; and when with him that hath charge of the Gunner ’ s Stores, he will spread an Ensign at his Main - tOp - fail - yard - arm. SIGN ALS for managing a Sea - fight. When the Admiral would have the Fleet form a Line of. Battle, one Ship a head of another, he hoist an Union - flag at the Mizen - peek, and Fires a Gun, and every Flag - ship does the. fame. ' But when they are to form a. Line of Battle, one a breast of another, he hoist a Pendant with the Union - flag, &c. . When he would have the Admiral of the White, or he that Commands in the Second Post, and his whole Squadron, to Tack and endeavour to gain the Wind of the Enemy, he spreads a White Flag under the Flag at thd Main - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun; and when he would have the Vice - Admiral of theBlue do so, he doth the fame with a Blue Flag. . If he would have the Vice - Admiral of the ' Red dose, he spreads a Red Flag from the Cap on the Fore - top - tast - head, downward on the Back - lay: If the Vice - Admiral qf the Blue is to do o, he spreads a Blue Flag, &c. and Fires a Gun. If he would have the Rear - Admiral of the Red do so, he hoist a Red Flag at the Flag - staff at the Mizen - top - mast - head; if the Rear - Admiral of the White ’ a White Flag; if the Rear - Admiral of the Blue, a Blue Flag, and under it a Pendant of the fame Colour, with a Gun. . If he be to Leeward of the Fleet, or any part of it, and he would have them to bear down into his Wake or Grain, he hoist a Blue Flag at the Mizen - peek, and Fires a Gun. . If he would be to Leeward of the Enemy, and his Fleet, or any part of it be to Leeward of him; in order to bring these Ships into the Line, hebears down with a Blue Flag at the Mizen - peek, under the Union - flag ( which is the Signal for Bat - tle ) and Fires a Guri; and then those Ships which are to Leeward of him, must endeavour to get into his Wake or Grain, according to their State - on in the Line of Battle. . When the Fleet is Sailing before the Wind and he would have him that Commands in the second Post, and the Ships of the Star - board Quar - ter to clap by the Wind, and come to the Star - board Tack, he hoist a Red Flag on the Mizen - top - mast - head, but a Blue one, if he would have Ships of the Lar - board Quarter come to the Lar - board - tack, With a Gun. If the Van are to Tack first, he spreads the.. Union - flag at the Flag - staff on the Fore - top - m aft - head, and Fires a Gun, if the Red Flag be not a - broad; but if it be, then he lowers the Fore - top - fails a little, and the Union - flag is spread from the Cap of the Fore - top - mast downwards j apd every Flag - ship doth the fame. . If ' " " " ' ' . If the Rear be to Tack first, he hoist the Union - flag on the Flag - staff at the Mizen - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun, which all the Flag - ships are to answer. . If all the Flag - ships are to come Into his Wake or Grain, he hoist a Red Flag at his Mizempeek, and Fires a Gun, and all the Flag - ships must do the fame. . If he would have him that Commands in the second Port of his Squadron to make more ‘ Sail ( tho he himself shorten Sail ) he hoist a White; Flag on the Ensign - staff: But if he that Com - lands in the third PoftbetO do so, he hoist a Blue Flag at the fame Places, and Fires a Gun, and all theFlag - ships must make the fame Signal. . When ever he hoist a Red Flag on the Flag - staff at the Fore - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun, every Ship in the Fleet must use their utmost en - devour to engage the Enemy, in the Order pre - ascribed them. a. When he hoist a White Flag at his Mizen - peek, and Fires a Gun, then all the small Frigats of his Squadron that are not of the Line of Bat -. tie, are to come under the Stern. . If the Fleet be Sailing by a Wind in the Line of Battle, and the Admiral would have them brace their Head - fails to the Mast, he hoist up a yellow Flag on the Flag - staff, at the Mizen - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun which the Flag - ships are to an - fwer, and then the Ships in the Rear must brace first. . After this, if he would have them fall their Head - fails and stand on, he hoist a yellow Flag on the Flag - staff at the Fore - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun; which the Flag - ships must answer, and then the Ships in the Van must fall first, and stand on. If when this Signal is made, the Red Flag tthe Fore - top - mast - head be abroad, he spreads the Yellow Flag under the Red. . If the Fleets being near one another, the Admiral would have allour Ships to Tack together, the sooner to lie in a posture of Engaging the Ene - my, he hoist a Union - flag on the Flag - staves, at the Fore and Mizen - top - mast - heads, and Fires a Gun, and all the Flag - ships in the Fleet are to do the fame. . The Fleet being in a Line of Battle, if he would have the Ship that leads the Van, hoist, lower, fet, or hall up any of his Sails, the Admi - ral spreads a Yellow Flag under that at his Main - top - m aft - head, and Fires a Gun; which Signal the Flag - ships are to answer, and then the Admi - ral will hoist, lower, fet, or hall up the Sail, which he would have the Ship that leads the Van do; which is to be answered by theFlag - ships of theFleet, . Whenthe Enemy runs, and he would have the whole Fleet follow them, he makes all the Sail he can after them himself, takes down the Signal for the Line of Battle, and Fires Guns out of his Fore - chafe, which the Flag - ships answer, and then every Ship is to endeavour to come up with, and Board the Enemy. . When he would have the Chafe given over, he hoist a White Flag at the Fore - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun. . If he would have the Red Squadron draw into a Line of Battle, one a breast of another, he putsabroad a Flag, striped Red and White on the Flag - staff, at the Main - top - mast - head, with a Pen - dant under it, and Fires a Gun: If the White or fe - cond Squadron are to do so, the Flag is striped Red, White and Blue; if the Blue or third Squadron are to do so; the Flag is a Genoue c Ensign and Pen - dant. Eut if they are to draw into a Line ossa - tie, one a Head of another, the fame Signals are made without a Pendant. ao. If they are to draw into a Line of Battle, one a Stem of another, with a large Wind, and he would have the Leaders go with the Star - board - Tacks Aboard by the Wind, he hoist a Red and White Flag at theMizen - peek, and Fires a Gun: But if they should go with the Lar - board - tacks A - board by the Wind, he hoist a Genou / e Flag at the fame place; which Signals must be like others, answered by the Flag - ships.

signalsbyday.c: SIGNALS by Day, when Ships are at an An - chor, in weighing Anchor, Sailing, He. When the Admiral or Commander in Chief “ would have the Fleet prepare for Sailing, he first loofes his Fore - Topsail, and then the whole Fleet are to do the fame. . When he would have them Unmoor, he loo - fes his Main - top fail, and fires a Gun; which in the Royal Navy is to be answered by every Flagg Ship [. B I Be S I G . When he would have them Weigh, heloofes jhis Fon - top - fail, and Fires a Gun, and sometimes hawls home his Sheets; the Gun is to be answered by every Flag Ship, and every Ship to get to Sail as soon as it can. If with the Leeward side, the Stern - most Ship is to weigh firfl. . When the Admiral or Commander in Chief would have the Weather - most and Head - m oft Ships to Tack first, he hoist the Union - flag at the Fore - top - mast - hcad, and Fires a Gun, which each Flag Ship must answer. But if he would have the Sternmost and Lee - ward - most Ships to Tack first, he hoist the Union Flag at the Mizen - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun. And when he would have all the whole Fleet Tack, he hoist an Union, both on the Fore and Mizen - top - mast - heads, and Fires a Gun. . When in bad Weather, he would have them Wear and bring, to the other Tack -, he hoist a Pen - dant on the Ensign - staff, and Fires a Gun: And then the Leeward - most andStern - most Ships are to Wear first, and bring on the other Tack and lie by, or go on with an easie Sail till he comes a Head. Every Flag is to answer with the fame Sig - nal. - If they are lying by, or Sailing by a Wind, and the Admiral would have them bear up and Sail before the Wind, he hoist his Ensign, and fires a Gun, which the Flags are to answer. And then the Leewardemoft Ships are to bear up first, and to give room for the Weather - most to Wear, and Sail before the Wind with an easie Sail, till the Admi - ral come a Head, But if it should happen when the Admiral hath occasion to Wear and Sail before the Wind, that both Jack and Ensign be abroad, he will hall down the Jack before he fires the Gun to wear, and keep it down till the Fleet is before the Wind. . When they are Sailing before the Wind, and he would. have them bring to with theStar - board Tacks Aboard, he hoist a Red Flag at the Flag - staff, on the Mizen - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun; but if they are to bring too with the Lar - board - tack, he hoist. Blue Flag at the fame Place, and Fires a Gun. Every Ship to answer the Gun. . When any Ship discovers Land, he is to hoist his Jack and Ensign, and keep it abroad till the Admiral ' or Commander in Chief Answer him by hoisting his; on fight of which he is to hall down his Ensign. . If any discovers Danger, he is to Tack, or bear up from it; and to aw Jack abroad from the Main - top - mast Cross - trees downward upon the Back - flay, and Fire two Guns: But if he should strike or slick fast, then besides the fame Signal with his Jack, he is to keep Firing till he fees all the Fleet observe him, and endeavour to avoid the Danger. ic. When any fees a Ship or Ships more than the Fleet, he is to put abroad his Ensign, and there keep it, till the Admiral ’ s or Commander ’ s is our, and then to lower it as often as he fees Ships, and to Hand in with them, that so the Admiral may know which way they are, and how many: But if he be at such a distance that the Ensign can ’ t well be discovered, he is then to lay his Head towards the Ship or Ships so deserved, and to brail up his low Sails, and continue hoisting and towering bis Top - fails, and making a Weft S I G with his Top - gallant - fails, till he is perceived by the Admiral. . When the Admiral would have the Vice Admiral, or he that Commands in the second Post of the Fleet, to fend out Ships to Chafe, he hoist a Flag, Striped White and Red, on the Flag - staff, at the Fore - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun. But if he would have the Rear - Admiral do Jo, he then hoist the fame Signal on the Flag - staff at the Mizen - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun. x. When the Admiral would have any Ship to Chafe so Windward, he makes a Signal forfpea - kingwith the Captain, and hoist a Bed Flag in the Mizen - shrouds, and Fires a Gun. But if to Chafe to Leeward, a Blue Flag and the fame Signal is made by the Flag in whose Di - vision that Ship is. When he would have them give over Chafe, he hoist a White Flag on his Flag - staff at the Fore - top - mast - head, and Fires a Gun: Which Signal is to be made also by that Flag Ship, which is nearest the Ship that gives Chafe, till the Chafing Ship lees the Sig - nal, . I Case of Springing a Leak, cr any other Difaftcr that difabks their Ship from keeping Company, you are to hale up your Courses, and Fire two Guns. . When any Ship would speak with the Ad - moral, he must spread an Englijh Ensign from the Head of his Main or Fore - top - mast downwards on the Shrouds, towering his Main or Fore - top - fail, and Firing Guns till the Admiral observe him: And if any Ship perceives this, and judges that the Admiral doth not, that Ship must make the fame Signal, and make the best cf his way to ac - quaint the Admiral therewith, who will answer by Firing one Gun. . When the Admiral would have the Fleet to prepare to Anchor, he hoist an Ensign striped Red, Blue and White on the Ensign - staff, and Fires a Gun; and every Flag - Ship makes the fame Signal. . If he would have the Fleet Moor, he hoist bis Mizen - top - fail with the Clew - lines haled up, and Fires a Gun. . If he would have the Fleet Cut or Slip, he loofes both his Top fails, and Fires two Guns; and then the Leeward Ships are to cut or flip first, to give room to the Weather - most to come to Sail. So if he would have any particular Ship to cut or flip, and to Chafe to Windward, he makes the Signal for speaking with that Ship, hoist a Bed Flag in the Mizen - shrouds, and Fires a Gun: But if the Ship is to Chafe to Leeward, he hoist a Blue Flag, as before. . If he would have the Fleet Exercise their Small Arms, he hoist a Red Flag on the Ensign - Staff, and Fires a Gun but if the great Guns, then he puts up a Pendant over the Red Flag.

signalsbynight.c: SIGNALS by Night, to be observed at an An - chor, in Weighing, Anchoring and Sailing. . When the Admiral would have the Fleet to Vnmoor and Ride short, he hangs out Lights one over another in the Main - top - mast - shrouds, over the constant Light in the Main - top, and Fires z Guns, which are to be answered by the Flag - Ships; and each private Ship hangs out a Light in the Mizen - shrouds. N. B, / S I G S I G N: B. All Guns firdfor Signals in the Night, must be Fir ’ d on the fame side, that they may make no alteration in the Sound. . When he would have them Weigh, he hangs a Light in the Main - top - mast - shrouds, and fires a Gun, which is to be answered by all the Flags; and every private Ship must hang out a Light in his Mizen - shroud. . When he would have them Tack., he hoist Lights on the Ensign - staff, one over another, above the constant Light in his Poop, and fires a Gun; which is. to be answered by all the Flags And e - very private Ship is to hang out a Light extraordi - nary, which is not to b ? taken in till the Admiral ' takes in his. After the Signal is made, the Leewatd - most and Stern - moss Ships must Tack assist as they can; and the Stern - most Flag - Ship, after he is about upon the other Tack, is to ' lead the Fleet, and him they are to follow, to avoid running thro ’ one another in the dark. . When he is upon a Wind, and would have the Fleet ' Wear and bring to on the other Tack, he hoist up onp Light at the Mizen - peek, and fires Guns; which is to be answered by the Flag - Ships, and every private Ship must answer with one Light at the Mizen - peek. The Stern - most and Leeward - most Ships are to bear up, fofoonas the Signal is made. . When he would have them in blowing Wea - ther to lit a try, Short, or a Mull, or with the Head - fails braced to the Majl, he will shew Lights of e - qual height, and fire Guns; which are to be an - swerd by the Flag - Ships and then every private Ship must shew Lights. And after this, if he would have them to make Sail, he then fires Guns; which are to be answered by all the Flags, ' and then the Head - mo ft and Weather - most Ships are to make Sail first. . When the Fleet is Sailing large, or before the Wind, and the Admiral would have them Tring too, and lie by with their Star - board Tacks A - board, he puts out Lights in the Fore - shrouds, and fires Guns but if with the Lar - board Tacks Aboard, he fires Guns, which are to be answered by the Flag - Ships, and every private Ship must shew Lights. The Wind - most Ships must bring too first. . Whenever the Admiral alters his Course, he fires Gun ( without altering his Lights, ) which is to be answered by all the Flag - ships. .. If any Ship hath occasion to lie Short, or by, after the Fleet has made Sail, he is to fire Gun, and shew Lights in his Mizen shrouds. . When any one first discovers Land or Dan - ger, he is to shew as many Lights as he can, to fire Gun, and to Tack, or bear away from it. And if any one happen to spring a Leak, or any be disabled from keeping company with the Fleet, he hangs out. Lights of equal height, and sire Guns till he is relieved by some Ship of the Fleet. i o. If any one discovers a Fleet, he is, to fire ' Guns, make false Fires, put one Light out ofthe Main - sop, on the Poop, to Steer after them, and to continue firing Guns, unless the Admiral call him off, by Steering another Course, and fire Or Guns, for then he must follow the Admiral. . When the Admiral Anchors he fires Guns, '. a small space of Time one from the other, which are to be answered by the Flag - ships j and every private Ship must shew Lights, . When the Admiral would have the Fleet to Moor, he puts a Light on each Top - mast - head, and fires a Gun; which is to be answered by the Flag - ships, and every private Ship is to shew one Light. . If he would have them lower their Yards and Tep - masts, he hoist one Light upon his En - sign - staff, and fires one Gun; which is to be an - swerd by the Flag - ships, and every private Ship must shew Light. And when he would have them Hoijl their Yards and Top - masts, he puts out Lights, one under the other, in the Mizen - top - mast - shrouds, and fires Gun; which is to be answered by the Flag - ships, and each private Ship must shew Light in the Mizen - shrouds. . If any strange Ship be discovered coming into the Fleet, the next Ship is to endeavour to speak with her, and bring her to an Anchor, and not suffer her to pafsthro ’ the Fleet. And if any one discovers a Fleet, and it blow so hard that he cannot come to give the Admiral notice timely, he is to hang out a great number of Lights, and to continue firing Gun after Giln, till the Ad - moral answers him with one. . When the Admiral would have the Fleet to Cut or Slip, he hangs out Lights, one at each Main - yard - arm, and at each Fore - yard - arm, and fires Guns; which are to be answered by the Flag - ships, and every private Ship is to shew one Light.

signet.c: SIGNET, is one of the King ’ s Seals, where - with his private Letters are Sealed, and is always in the Custody of the King ’ s Secretaries; and there are Clerks of the Signet Office always at - tending.

silver.c: SILVER, of the ways of Smelting and Rest - ning of Silver, I find these Accounts.. Front Mr, star, at the end of his Catalogue of English Words about the Silver Mines jn Cardigan / hire in hPales. The Mine first beaten into small pieces, is brought from the Mine to the Smeking - house, and there melted with black and white Coal, i. e. with Charcoal and Wood flit into small pieces, and dr - ed in a Kiln for that Purpose: And they use both Wood and Coal, because the Coal alone makes too violent a Fire, and the Wood alone too gentle. After the Fire is made, the Mine is cast on the Coals, and so again. Mine and Coals interchange - ably. The Mine, when melted, runs down into the Sump, which is a round Pit of Stone lined with Clay within; thence ’ tis laden out and call into long square Bars with smaller ends, fit to lift and carry them by. These Bars they bring to the Refining Furnace, which is covered with. thick Cap of Stone, bound about with Iron, and moveable, ther ft ? they may lift it up, and make the Test at the bottom anttfi ' ( as they do at every Refining. ) In the middle of the Cap there is a hole, in which the Bar of Sil - ver hangs in Iron - slings above the Furnace, that so it may be letdown by degrees as it melts off. Be - sides this Hole, they have another in the side of the Furnace, Parallel to the Horizon, and bot - tom ’ d with Iron; at which Hole they thrust in ano - ther Bar. The Tejl is of an Oval Figure, and fits at the bottom of the Furnace. The Fire is put in by the side of the Bellows, when the Furnace is come to a true temper of Heat, the Lead conver - ted into Litharge, is blown off by the Bellows, the Silver subsiding to the bottom of the Test. As soon as all the Glut fas they call it ) cf Li - charge is blown off, the Silver in the bottom of the Cuple or Test grows cold, and the fame degrees of Heat will not keep it melted, as before. The Cake of Silver after it grows cold, springs or rises up into Branches ( faith Mr. R, but I question his Information as to this Point. ) The Test is made of Marrow - bones, burnt to small pieces, then Powdred and made into a Past with W aten The Test is about a Foot thick, laid in Iron: After the Cake of Silver is taken out, that part of the Test which is difcoioured, they mingle with new Ore to be melted; the reft they Pound and Pow - der, and use again for another Tfti The The Litharge is brought to a Reducing Furnace, and there with Charcoal only melted into Lead. The Litharge is cast upon the Charcoal in the Bing of the Furnace; and as the Charcoal burns away, and the Litharge melts, more Charcoal is thrown on, and Litharge put upon it, as at first Smel - ting. Another Furnace they have, which they tall an Almond Furnace, in which they melt the Slugs ( or Refuse of the Litharge ) not Stamped or Pounded, with Charcoal only. The Slugs or Cynders of the first Smelting, they beat small with great Stamps, lifted up by a Wheel moved by Water, and falling down by their own Weight. First they are Stamped with dry Stamps, then lifted with an Irop. - ficve in Wa - ter. That which lies at the bottom of the Sieve is returned to the Smelting - furnace, without more a - do; that which swims over the Sieve is beaten with wet Stamps. What hath pass ’ thro ’ ’ the Sieve, and also what after being beaten with the wet Stamps, passes thro ’ a fine Grate, or Strainer of Iron, goeth to th e Buddie; which is a Vessel made like a shal - low Tumbrel, and Hands a little shelving. On this the Matter is laid, and Water runs con - slantly over it, the Matter being moved to and fro with an Iron - rake; by which means the Earth and Dross being carried off by the Water, the Me - tal remains behind. That which is thus Buddled, they lue with a thick Hair - sieve, close wrought in a Tub of Wa - ter, rolling the Sieve about, and inclining it this way and that with their Hands. - The light part Which swims at top of the Sieve, or rather over it, is returned again to the Buddie; and that which subsides goes to the Furnace to be Smelted a - gain. They have also an AjJ'ay Furnace, wherewith they try the Value of the Metal, or what Proper - tion the Lead bears to the Silver; which they do by gutting off a piece from every Bar, and melting it in a small Cupel: First they weigh the piece cutoff,, and then after the Lead is separated, the Silver. A Tun of Metal sometimes will yield,, and if rich, Pound Weight of Silver. All Lead Ore dig ’ d in England, hath a Proper - tion of Silver mixtwichit; but feme so little, that it will not quit Cost to Refine it. At the first Smelting they mingle several forts of Ore together, some Richer, some Poorer, else they will not melt To kindly. The Silver made. here is exceeding good and fine. These fix Moon - tains in Cardiganshire, not far from one another, af - ford Silver Ore; Lai about, Geginnon, Comjomlack., Gedarren, Bromefloid and Summer. But when Mr. Bay was there, they dig ’ d only at T la - bout. Their way of Digging and Colle & ing the Ore, was thus They sink a Perpendicular square Hole, or Shaft, the sides of which they strength - en round from top to bottom with Wood, that the Earth may not fall in. The Transverse pieces of Wood, they call S temples; and on these, catch - ing hold with their Hands and Feet, they descend without using any Rope: They dig the Ore thus; one holds a little Pique, or Punch of Iron, having a long Handle of Wood, which they call a Gad; and another With a great Iron - fledge drives it into the Vein. The Vein of Metal runs Ears. and Weft; it rises North, and / uorflopesto the South. There is a white Fluor about the Vein, which they call Spar, and a black one, which they ' call Blinds: This last covers the Vein of Ore; so that when it ap - pears, they are sure to find Ore. There are several Silver Mines at Schemnit in Hungary, the chiefeft of which are mndfehacht and Trinity. Of which Dr. Edward Brown gives us this Account in Philojophical TranfaEtions, No.. Trinity Mines are Fathom deep, built and kept - pen with Under - work at a great Ex: pence. Much of this Mine being in an Earthy Soil, its Ore is much esteemed. Diverse Veins lie North, and o - thers run to the North - east. The blackifti Ore is esteemed the best much of it hath a mixture of a. yellow shining Substance, called Marchafite; which if not in too great quantity, disposed the Ore to Fluidity, and makes it melt and run the better. There is often found growing to the Ore a red Substance, called Cinnabar this Substance, ground with Oil, makes a Vermillion equal to, sis not exceeding that Cinnabar which is made by Sublimation of Mercury and Sulphur. An hundred Pound Weight of Ore sometimes yields but half an Ounce, or an Ounce of Silver; sometimes,,, and Ounces. There is an Officer in the Works, whom they call the Probcirer or Ejjayer, who proves the Rich - ness of the Ore, thus: Of all forts of Ore he takes the fame quantity, and having first dried, burned, and powdred them, then he gives an equal Propoi - of Lead to all, Melteth and Purifieth them; and then by exa ( ft Scales he takes notice of the Proper - tion between the Ore and the Metal contained in it, and reports it to those concerned in the great Melting - furnaces. If the Ore be found to hold Ounces and half, or more of Silver in an Pound Weight, they ordinarily mek it, without any previous Pre - pacation by the help of Iron Stone ( which by the by is not Iron Ore, but a Stone found thereabouts, of which the Livered - colour is the best. J Ifys, ( which is a fort of Pyrites ) and Slacken ( a Scum or Lake taken off the top of the Pan -, into which the melted Mineral runs, and is a Substance made out of the former, melted byFufion ) which are thrown with it into the Melting - furnace. If the Ore be pourer, holding but Ounces in Pound Weight, or less. - Then tis first pounded and waffl ’ d, till it become riches, or hath a greater Proportion of Metal, with refpetft to the Ore, much of the Earthy Parts being washed away. Then ’ tis thrown into the Furnace with the for - mer Materials; and the Marchafite, which remains still with it, as sinking always to the bottom with the Silver in the Wash - works, helps to quicken the Fusion of the Ore. Whatever is melted in the Melting - furnace, is let out thro ’ an hole at " the bottom thereof into the Pan, which is placed in the Earth before it. And thus exposed, it immediately acquires an hard Scum, Dross, Loaf or Cake; which being taken off from the top, the Metal remaining becomes the purer; to which is added Lead, and after some time the melted Metal is taken out. Then being again melted in the Driving - furnace ( as they call it, ) the Lead, or what else remains mixt with the Silver is driven off by the Blast of two great Bel lows, and runs over in the form of Litharge. That which first comes over is the FFhite, and that which is S I L S I N is last, being longer in the Fire, is Red; the former is called Litharge of Silver, the last of Gold but are both blown off the fame Metal. Most of this Schemnit Silver Ore holds some Gold, which is separated from the Silver by Gra - nutation and Dissolution in Aqua Fort is. When Silver is generated ( as ’ tis in some Places of America, and perhaps elsewhere ) in Rockey Stones, abounding with Bituminous Mixtures, so as that it can ’ t be forced from its Impuri - ties by the violent way of Melting; tho ’ Lead, and even Artificial Salts or Fluxes be added. In this Case the Use of Quicksilver hath been found most advantageous. The way of applying it is thus: They Calcine the Ore, first ’ broken into small pieces, in a Reverberatory Oven; but with a mo - delate Fire for fear ofFufion, and driving away into the Air part of the Metal. This Calcination frees the Mineral from such Mixtures as would hinder the Power of the Quicksilver upon it, and also renders the Ore more tra & able and pliant un - der the Milftone; where ’ tis reduced to a fine Powder, before the Application of the Mercury upon it. For ! the Ore being Ground, Calcined, Powder ’ d, and finely lifted, they divide it into fe - veral heaps, and then by lesser Effaysthey find how much Silver is contained in each heap; where ’ tis very ordinary to find not above Ounces in Pound Weight, sometimes iz; but if it arises to, ’ disesteemed a very rich Vein: Yet sometimes there are great MafTes found of pure Silver, which they call Virgin Metal - Then proportionable to the quantity of Silver in each heap, they besprinkler them with Quicksilver, and that not all at once, but at several times, stir - ring the Ore up and down. If the Mercury give Signs of its being Hoc ado ( as they call it ) i. e. if it appear mortified; not in small and clear Spherical Figures ( which is a good Prognoftick ) but in the form of long Worms, of a wan, pale, dark and Leadifh Colour f which indicates that the Ore a - bounds with Lead, &c. ) it is cured by certain Magiftrals, which have for their Balls or Master Ingredient, Calcined Copper mingled with Salt. The heaps of Ore being thus mingled with Quicksilver, are often stirred about, the better to incorporate the Mercury and Silver. They seem to have only Conjectural Signs to know when I the Qiiickfiliver hath done its Office in separating the Silver from these Hetcrogeneal Substances; which occasions by its uncertainty great Losses, e - specially when they Work this way on Gold. But when by the Colour of the Mercury, Coagulated by the Silver in clear Massy Lumps, they cone - cure the Work done, they wall it by means of three Vessels, standing in order, one under another: So that the Matter in the first and highest, being worked and stirred about with a Molinet, all the Dull of the Heterogeneous Matter that imbody not with the Mercury, is carried away together with the Water into the other Vessels, and from thence is quite thrown out by the continual Cur - rent of the Water: While the Silver in clotted Lumps ( called Fellas ) is by the Weight of the Mercury carried down to the bottom of the Tubs. Then the Mercury, with the Silver is taken out of the Vessels, and diligently squeezed in strong course Linen - cloths, and even with Strokes of a Beetle, that the Quicksilver may be separated as much as may be from the Silver. And this Mass is afterwards reduced in Molds of the stipe of the Indian Pine - apple, into a Piramidal or Conical Fi - gure, which they call Pineas de la Plata: They are thus fafliionfed for the easier placing them round the edges of a great Earthen, Vessel of the form of a blind, Alembick: Round about the top of which a Fire is made, did then all the reft of the Mercury forthwith abandons the Silver and falls to the bottom; from whence its recovered and kept for the like use again. The Silver last of all is melted down with Li - ga, as ’ tis called, which the Ring of Spain al - lows, by which he returns to the People in Copper the fifth part, which they allow him of all the Sil - ver. sines.c: SINES on the Plain Scale, Gunter's Scale, find almost all Scales have a Line, called the Line of Sines. This on the Senior is double, one on each Leg, and hath there many excellent Uses; some of which are these: . The Radius of a Circle being known to find the Sine of any Arch or Angle. Fit in the Radius between and in the Lines of Sines, and the Parallel distance between the Numbers of Degrees, anfweringtd any Works or Angles, will give their Sines. Thus the Parallel Distance between,,, c. will give the Sinesof o... &c. And vice versa, from the Sine given you may find the Radius, by fitting the Sine into the Sector Parallel - wife, between the Numbers expressing its Degrees. For then the Parallel Distance between and, will be the Radius fought. a . The fiadius of a Circle being given, and any Bight Line less than it, to know of what Arl it may be the Sign. Apply in the Radius between and, in the Lines of Sines, andtakingthe Length of the Line in the Compasses, carry it Parallel to the Radius, till it fall exactly on like Sines on each side; and the Degrees and Minutes where it fits, shall give you the Sine it represents.
