skin.c: SKIN: As soon as the Cuticula or Scarf - skin is separated from the Cutis or true Skin of a humane Body, there are these three parts appear first, an Infinite number of Papilla Pyramidaies, which are the ends of all the Nerves of the Skin, each of which are enclosed in two or three Covers ef a Pyramidal Figure. Between these Papillae are m infinite number of holes, which are nothing hat: the Orifices of the Excretory Vessels of the Miitmy Glands underneath. Secondly, There appears a Web of Nervous Fi - bres, and other Vessels, differently interwoven: This is always covered with a Mucous SubSaacCj serving to support and moisten the Papilla: Pyrdmi - dales. And this is the parenchyma, or that part of the Skin that Pai chmetit is made of. The third part is an infinite number of MHHmy Glands, about whom there is much Fat lifaatly: These Glands separate the Matter by Sweatand ln - sensible Perspiration. Each Gland receives a Nerve and Artery, and fends out a Vein, and an Exeratmy Dutt; which last passes thro ’ the other two Parts to the Cuticula, in order to moisten it and the Pa - pillar Pyramidaies, left they ihould be so dry as to hinder theSenfe of Feeling; and also to discharge that Matter out of the Body. The use of the Skin is to cover and wrap sp all the Parts of the Body, to be the Organ of Touching or Feeling, and to be the Emun & any of the whole Body. For thro ’ the Glands of the Skity pass not only such Particles of the Vessels, as de - may, by reason of the continual Motion of the Blood, but likewise the greatest part of the Li - quors which we drink; which having perform'd part of their Office, in conveying the Aliments Into the Blood, are in the next place to dissolve the Sa - line and Terrestrial Particles to be carried off thro ” the Glands of the Skin and Kidneys, Sanflorinsosm - putes, that about Ounces a Day are thus carry - ed off thro ’ the Cutaneous Glands: So that if a Man ’ s Body be supposed to weigh Pound, in r Days he may perspire a Quantity equal to the weight of his whole Body. Keifs Axau - my. Above the Cutis or thick Skin of the Bo - dy lies the Cuticula or Scarf - skin, and is com po - led of several Plates of small Scales, which cover one another, more or less, or lie thicker, accord - ding as it is thicker in one part of the Body tnzm in another: Between these Scales the Excretory DuEls of the Miliary Glands of the Cutis, or thick Skin, open. L ewenhoeef reckons, that round about one Cuticular such Dudts may lie, and that a Grain of Sand will cover of these Scales: So that one Grain of Sand will cover Orifi - ces of these little Dudts; and yet into every oaeof these Miliary Glands an Artery, Vein and Nerve do certainly enter. These Glands secern the Sweat, and what goes off by insensible Perspiration: Asd they must be very many in number, since, as S an & or; us observes, Ounces of a Fluid Matter passes in hours time. Next under the Scarf - Skin lie the Papilla Pyramidaies, which also arc prodigiously numerous, being the Extremities of all the Nerves of the Skin, and do more immedi - ately serve for the Sense of Feeling, and to con - very the Impulse recti ved, by means of the Nerves to the Brain. About these the Nerves and all - ther Vessels make a fine Web, all covered over with a Mucous Substance, to moisten these Pa - pillar Pyramidaies; and then under these the Milia - ry Glands are placed, protruding their Secretary Dufls up to the Surface of the Scarf - skin; on which there are many Parallel Lines, and these In - terfered by others, and in each Intersection there is an Hair ' usually placed. The Scales of the Scarf / S O L Scarf - skin defend the Orifices of the Excretory Du ts of the Miliary Glands, and hinder Objects from making too exquisite and painful an Impref - sion upon the Nerves, and so to save them - from External Injuries. The Skin it less is designed to Enwrap the whole Body, and to sustain the Bafillte Pyramidales in their places, and the Milia - ry Glands from being disordered; also to receive the Impression of External Objects, and to be the Organ of the Sense of Touching and Feeling.

sledge.c: SLEDGE, is a large Smith ’ s Hammer to be u - fed with both Hands: Of this there are two forts, T / je uphand Sledge, which is used by Under Workmen, when the Work is not of the largest fort: This is used with both the Hands before, and they seldom raise it higher than their Head. But the other, which is called the About - jledge, and which is used for Battering or drawing out the lar - gest; Work, is held by the handle with both hands, and swung round over their Heads, at their Arms - end, to strike as hard a blow as they can. a SLOOP, is a Vessel of the Shallop - kind. In our Navy such attend upon the Men of War. They are usually about o Tun, and carry about Men.

sovereign.c: SOVEREIGN, was a Piece of Gold Coin, Current at Shillings and Pence, in H.. When by Indenture of the Mint, a Pound Weight of Gold of the old Standard was to be Coined into Soveraigns. In H.. Soveraigns were Coined at Shillings, and half Soveraigns at Shillings. In, Ed.. Soveraigns were Coin - ed at Shillings a piece, and in E., at Shillings; and also in Elig.

spigurnel.c: SPIGURNEL, was anciently ( Spigurnellus ) he that had the Office of the Efpigumantia, or Sealing of the King ’ s Writs. This Word Spelman and Du Frefhc recite, without interpreting it. But it seems to be taken from the Saxon, Span an, which signifies to flout up. Seal or Secure. Kenneth GloJJ. in Par set. Antiquit.

spiritualities.c: SPIRITUALITIES of a Bishop, are such Pro - fits as arise to him from the Benefit of his Jurifdi - session in his Diocese, and not as a Baron of the Parliament, such as those of his Vifitations, Infti - tutions, Ordinations, &c.

spiralline.c: SPIRAL Line. See bn this Subject further. Stephana de Angclis de Infinitis Spiralihus inner - sis, &c. Petavii. II. Bullidldi Demonfly ationes Nova de Spiralis bus,

spleen.c: SPLEEN. The Vessel which in Beasts they call the Milt, is situated in the left Hypochmdrium, un - der the Diaphragm, between the Ribs and the Sto - mach, above the left Kidney it is tied to the Pe - ritoneum, to the Diaphragm, and to the Omentum, ' Tis of a blewilh or leaden Colour, of an Oblong Figure, thick at the edges, and not thin as the Li - ver, it hath two Membranes, the External comes from the Peritoneum. The Internal Membrane is finer and thinner than the External; for if you blow into the Splenick Artery, the Air will pass thro ’ the one, but not theothei. Its Fibres are not regularly woven, as those of other Membranes seem to be, but they come from innumerable Points, as fladii from so many Centres; and the Fibres of one Point are regularly woven with the Fibres of the Points surrounding it. It receives Veins, Nerves and Arteries from those that enter the Spleen. The Substance of the Spleen is not only kept together by its two Membranes, but also by inn - mirable Fibres which come from the Points of the Internal Membrane, and are inserted in the Points of the opposite side of the fame Membrane, and Expansion of the Extremity of these Fibres seem to compose the Internal Membrane. The Spleen is Composed of an Infinite number of Membranes, which from little Cells and Cavities of different Figures and Bigneffes, which Commu - nictate with one another, and are always full of Blood. At the Extremities of the Blood Vessels in the Spleen of Sheep, we find several white soft Specks, which Malpighius calls Glands. The Spleen hath Arteries from the Cceliaca, whose Capillary Branches make frequent Inofcu - Iations upon the Membranes of the Cells. Its Veins, whose Extremities communicate with the Cavities of the Cells, as they come out of the Spleen, unite and make the Ramus Splenicus of the Porta, which carries the Blood from the Spleen to the Liver. These with its Nerves, which are con - fiderable, from the Plexus Splenicus, are equally di ffributed thro ’ the whole Substance of the Spleen, being all included in a common Capsula. There are like wife a few Lympbadck Vessels which arise from the Spleen, and discharge themselves into the Lum bary Glands. The time Use of the Spleen is yet uncertain the Ancients thought it to be the Receptacle for the Melancholick Humour. - Some since considering that in the Spleen there are a great number of Membranes and Fibres, and also many Nerves, have thought that the Blood is attenuated, and be - comes more Spirituous in the Spleen: And considering that the most of the Blood in the Li - ver comes immediately from the Spleen and Omentum, they think that one funfifiies the Oleaginous, the other the Spirituous part of the Bile..: / SPOT !

squadronofships.c: SQUADRON of Ships, isaDivifion, or pay: of a Fleet, Commanded by a Vice or Rear Admi - ral, or some other Commander or Commadore, as they call it; but the Number of Ships in it is un - certain,

squadron.c: SQUADRON, is a Body of Horse, whose Number is not fix ’ d; but usually is from one to Men, according to the General ’ s Pleasure, the Strength of the Army, and as Occasion serves. Usually a Squadron confiftsof Troops, each of Men, and it never exceeds Men. Because a greater Number than that can ’ t be advantageously Ported, nor have room to at in narrow Ground, Woods, Marjhes, Defiles, See. The Eldest Troop takes the height of the Squadron, and the Second the Left, and the youngest in the Centre. A Squa - iron is always drawn up deep, or in Ranks, with the length of a Horse between each Rank. The Standard is always in the Centre of the first Rank.

squarebattel.c: SQUARE Battel, or Battalion of Men, is one / that hath an equal number of Meft in Rank and. File. S T A To Form any Number of Men into a Square Battle, asfuppofe, extract the nearest Square Root of, which is in Integers, and that will give the Number of Men for Rank and File. There will be a Remainder of Men, vvhomay be difpofedof as the Commander thinks best.

squarebattalionofground.c: SQUARE Battalion of Ground, is when the Ground of the Flanks is of the fame Extent, as the Ground of the Front and Rear. To make a Square Battalion of Ground; as suppose theNumr ber were, Multiply by, the number of Feet which every Man takes up in Front, the Pro - duct will be S; divide that by, which is the number of Feet each Man takes up in depth, or which is the distance of the Ranks, the Quotient without a Fraction will be,; whose Square Root is, which will give the number of Men in File. And if you divide the first given Number by this Root, you will quote, which is the Number of Men in each Rank.

stable.c: STABLE - STAND, is the Term for one of the Evidences or Prefumptions whereby a Man is Converted, to intend the Stealing the King ’ s Deer in the Forests. The other are Dog - draw, Back - bear, and Blcody - hand. This Stablc - Land, is when a Man is in Stabili St at lone, nihis Standing in the So - reft with a Cross - bow, or Long - bow, ready to sliort at a Deer; or else when he is standing close up by a Tree, &c - with Grey - hounds in a Leash ready to flip.

stake.c: STAKE, is the Name of a small Anvil, used by Smiths; sometimes it stands on a broad Iron - foot, on the Work Bench, to be moved up and down occasionally; and sometimes it hath a strong Iron Spike at the bottom, by which ’ tis fixed to some place on the Work - bench. Its use is to let small and cold Work Strait, by hammering it on the Stake, or to Cut or Punch upon with the cold ChiJ - sel, or cold Punch.

stallage.c: STALLAGE, was a Customary Rent paid in Fairs or Markets, for the Liberty of a Stall or Standing, by the Stallangers or the Creamers, i. e. thole Traders who exposed their Goods to Sale on the said Stalls. In Scotland they call it St allonge, the Romans called it Siliquaticum from Siliqua, which was their first and least Weight, a kind of CaraH of Grains.

stamping.c: STAMPING - MILL, called also a Knocking - Mill, is a Mill used in the Tin - works to bruise the Ore final. See the Description of it under Tin.

standardforgold.c: STANDARD for Gold - Coin in England is Caradts of fine Gold, and Caradts of Copper, and the French and Spanifto Gold are nearly of the fame Standard. See CaraH. For Silver - Coin, Ounces and Penny Weight of fine Silver, and Penny Weight of Copper, being melted together is the true Standard, and such Silver is called Sterling. When either Gold or Silver is finer than Standard, they call i t better, if courser, worse, and they reckon the Excess or Defedtby Caradts, and Grains of a Caradt in Gold, and by Penny - weights in Silver. And it is thus discovered: They take a small quantity and Af - fay it; that is, Weigh it very exactly, and then melt it in a Crucible with a strong Fire, fc long iJ till ST U till the Copper, or other Allay mix ’ d with it be burnt away. When cold, they weigh it aga. in ac - curately, and if it hath loft nothing of the air ft Weight, they call it fine Gold if it hath loft part of its Weight, they call it Gold of x Cara & s, or one Caradt better than Standard; if it have loft parts, then ’ tis Caradts dine, or Standard; if it hath loft parts, ’ tis called Caradfs fine, or i Caradt worje than Standard, &c And so they Assay Silver, only they compute its loss by Penny - weights, ( c.

stannaries.c: STANNARIES, are the Mines and Works where ( Stannum ) Tin is dug and Smelted, as in Cornwall, and other Places. There are several Laws about, and Liberties granted to the Stanna - ry Courts in several Ads of Parliament; as in the Time of Ed. i. and afterwards, as Abridg ’ d by Ed.. and in Car.. c.

staple.c: STAPLE, signifies this or that Town, City or Place where the Merchants of England were, by Ad of Parliament, to carry their Wool, Cloth Lead and Tin, ( c. and such like Staple or Stan ding Commodities of this Land, in order to their being Sold by the Great. These Places you wil And in several Statutes, appointed awTaLfered by the Kings of England, from th, e second Year of j Ed.. to the fifth of Ed.. and what Officers these Staples had belonging to them; you may fee an Anno E.. St at.. c. xi. The Staple Com - modities of this Land are, Wool, Leather, Wool; sells, Lead, Tin, Butter, Cheese and Cloth j a ! tho ‘ some will allow appears by i R so. c. only the first five.

star.c: STAR. All Deeds, Obligations, Contra & s, Releafes,. ( c. of the Jews were anciently called Stars, from the Hebrew Shetar, a Deed or Contrad. These were fomedmes written in Hebrew and La - tino, but usually in Hebrew alone.

STAR - CHAMBER,, was a Chamber at Weft - mingler, formerly so called, from its Roof being Tainted with Stars. Henry the Seventh and Eighth, order ’ d by several Statutes, that the Chancellor, a ( lifted by others there named ( vid. H.. c.. and xi H.. c. z. ) should have Powef to Punish Pouts, Riots, Forgeries, Embraceries, Perjuries, and such other Mifdemeanors, as were not fufficiendy provided for by the Common - law; and for which the Inferior Judges are not so proper to give Cor - aretftion. Bat this Court, by Car. u c.. was entirely dissolved and determined, and so conti - pnues to this day.

stellionate.c: STELLIONATE, in the Civil Law, is all kind of Cozenage, and Knavish Pra & ice in Bargaining, and all forts of Frauds that have no peculiar Names in the Law. And ’ tis so called from Stellio, a Li - zard with great variety of Spots, and very preju - dicial to Mankind.

sterlingmoney.c: STERLING Money, this word seems to come, as Mr. Somner hath derived it, from the Srfxow word Steore, that is, a Ride or Standard; and therefore it signifies that Coin or Money, which for Metal and Value, was to be a common Standard of all Current Money. And this is the more probable, because such Money at the comingdn of the Nor - mans, was called Sterilenfis. As Orderic. Vital. Sub. Anno. Porrigam quindecem Sterilenfi - um, Dr. Kennet's Glojfary. Efterling in Stow is used for a Penny - weight, signifying a Penny of fine Silver, such as we now call Standard. But the word Sterling, as being a piece of Money, gent - rally, if hot always, signifies a Penny. And as for a good while together there was no other Coin but Penny s; and that Denarius signifies in many Au - thors the fame as Nummus, all good Standard Sil - ver, eameto be called Sterling Silver, and good Mo - new, Sterling Money, as it is to this day.

stiles.c: STILES, the upright pieces which go from the bottom to the top in any Wainscot, are by the Workmen called Stiles.

stilobatum.c: STILOBATUM, is in Architecture the Boar of the Fedeftal of any Column. ’

stipuleation.c: STIPULE ATION, in the Civil Law, is a Con - trad; made by Words, and not in Writing, by as - king a Question, and receiving presently a proper ' Answer: And in this Contrad the Obligation is only upon one side, e. on the side of the Promi - fer, who was called Reus Debendi, or Promittendi j as the Stipulator or Creditor, to whom the Promise is made, was called Reus Credendi, or Stipulandi This was the old Sense, but now with us the Word Stipulation is commonly used for the Ad of the Per - foil obliged; and some fay that the word Stipula - tor is common both to Debtor and Creditor..

stomach.c: STOMACH, fee Ventriculus. Monsieur Chi - arc, Profelfcr of Medicine at Montpellier, hath bv an easie Experiment, shewn that the Force of the Stomach alone ( in Vomiting ) without taking into consideration the Muscles of the Diaphragm and Abdomen ( whose force together is more than that of Pound Weight ) is equal to that of xxooo Pound Weight.

strainsingunnery.c: STRAINS, in Gunnery, are Plates of Iron of the length and breadth of one of the Felloes which serve for the Round of the Wheel of a Gun - carriage, and fix ’ d on the Circumference of the Wheel with strong Nails, which are called the Strain - nails, these Strains cover the Joynts of the. ’ ' e Hoes and defend the Wheel.

strikesinarchitecture.c: STRIKES, in Architecture, are the hollow Chanels isi the Shaft of a Column, called by our Workmen Elutings and Grooves. They more pro - perly belong to the lonick Order, tho ’ they are found some times in the Dorick, and often in the Corinthian and Compoftte. They are generally at right Angles with the Plane of the Base, but are fomedmes - found winding about the Pillar. Some - times the Strigcs are filled up with a Swelling a third part from the Bale, lying in the hollow like a Stick foot of a round form: These Mr. Evelyn thinks we should - d call Staved or Cabled Columns.

stuccopaintinginstucco.c: STUCCO, Painting in Stucco was revived from the Ancients by Giovanni d ’ Vdine a Scholar of Raphael ’ s ', he found the true Matter which the Ancients made use of, which wasaCompofition of Lime and Marble Powder ’ d very fine.

strut.c: STRUT, is a Term used by some Builders for that Brace which is framed into the King - piece and the principal Rafters

studding.c: STUDDING - SAILS in a Ship are Bolts of Canvas, or any Cloth that will hold Wind, ex - tended in a fair Gale of Wind along the side of the Main - fail, and Boomed out with a Boom they are fomedmes also used to the Clew of the Main - fail, Fore - fail and Sprit - fail, when the Ship goes either before the Wind, or Quartering. subnormal.c: SUBNORMAL is a Line, determining in any Curve, the Interfedlion of the Perpendicular to the Tangent in the Point of Contadfc, with the Axis. And this Subnormal in the Common or Apollonian Parabola, is a Determinate Invaria - ble Quantity for ’ tis always equal to half the Parameter of the Axis,

subrogation.c: SUBROGATION in the Civil Law, is put - ting another Person into the Place and Right of him, that in any Case, is the proper Creditor. This is also called Cession.

substitution.c: SUBSTITUTION, is in Algebra or Fluxions, the putting in the room of any Quantity in an Equa - tion, some other Quantity which is really equal to it, but express ’ d after another manner; and this is done, in order to find at lead such a proper Ex - pression in the Equation, as shall Solve the Pro - blem, or Question proposed. And in the Knack of doing this readily, consists the chiefeft Bufineis of the Operations in Fluxions.

suburbscarleregiones.c: SUBURBS CARLE Regione's, called also Sub - urbane e, Vr vicar i st vicinct, were such Regions or Cities of the Roman Empire, as lay within an i oo Miles of Rome, and were under the Jurifdi - dion of the Praefed of that City: Wherefore they are sometimes called Regiones Solitx, because in these the Governor of Rome was wont to Ever - cifehis Solemn Jurisdiction. This also was the Ancient Extent of the Power and Charge of the Bishops of Rome, before the Papal Ufurpati - on. - SUCTION, there are many Effeds vulgarly attributed to SuBion, which in Reality have very different Causes. As when any one Sucks Water, or any other Liquor up thro ’ a Pipe; tis common - ly thought, that by that Adion the Person draws the Air up into his Mouth, and that the Water which is Contiguous to it, follows it by a kind of AttraBion, as if the Air and Water hung to - gether: And others fanfie that the Air moves in - to the Mouth of the Sucker, and the Water move's up after the Air, to prevent a Vacuum, which they fay. Nature abhors. Whereas the true Cause of this Phenomenon, is only that the Air and At - mosphere presses with its whole weight, uniformly on the Surface of the Liquor in the Vessel, and con - sequently prevents any one part of the Water to rife higher than the other there: And if a Pipe be put in of any tolerably large Bore, and be o pen at both ends, the Water will rife within the Pipe to the fame height as without, and indeed a little higher, because the Pressure of the Ait with - in the Pipe is a little taken off " by bearing again the sides of the Pipe. Now when ancone ap - plies his Mouth to the upper end of the Pipe and Sucks, his Lips so strongly enclose the Pipe, that no Air can get between them and it; and by the voluntary Motion of the Spirits in the Muscles, the Cavity of his Thorax, or Breast is opened and enlarged; by which means the Air included there, hath now a much larger Space to dilate its self in, and consequently cannot press so strongly against the upper end of the Pipe, as it did before the Cavity of the Thorax was so enlarged, and when the Weight of the whole Atmosphere kept its Spring bent. And that Weight or Pressure be - ing now taken off by the Lips of the Man that Sucks, ' the Equilibrium is destroyed, the Air Gra - vitates on the Surface of the Water, ' but cannot d so on the upper Orifice of the Pipe, because the Jun & ures the Lips takes it off; and the Spring of the Air included in the Thorax, -, being weakened W Wf by the Dilatation of its Cavity, it cannot press lb hard against the upper Orifice of the Pipe, as the Water will do against, the lower, and conse - quently the Water muff be forced up into the Pipe. ’ Tis much the fame thing in the Suction of a common Pump: The Sucker being tight, takes off entirely the Pressure of the Atmosphere on the Surface of the Water within the Barrel of the Pump, and consequently the Atmosphere by its Weight must force the Water up to make the. / Equi - librium. See Hydrofatickj.

suffragan.c: SUFFRAGAN, is a Titular Bishop, appointed to Aid and Assist the Bishop of the Diocese, and by H.. c.. every Bishop is Empowered to Elecft two Honest and Discreet Spiritual Paftois, which shall be called Bishops Suffragans.

sulphur.c: SULPHUR, Sir If. Newton, on very good Grounds, concludes, that the common Sulphur is Composed of Volatile and fixed Parts, strictly ad - hereinto one another by Mutual Attraction, so that they will both Sublime together; for by dis - solving Flowers of Sulphur in Oil of Turpentine, and then Distilling the Dissolution, Tis found that Sulphur consists of a thick, Volatile and Inflammable Oil, or of a. fat Bitumen, an Acid Salt, and. a very fix ’ d Earth with a little Metal. The three first of which are found there in nearly an equal Quantity; but there is - Only a very small Proportion of the last. The Acid Salt being dissolved in Water, is the fame with the Oleum Sulphuris per Campanam.

superiorplanets.c: SUPERIOR Planets, are Mars, Jupiter and & j - turn: They are so called, because they move in Orbits round the Sun, which are larger than that of our Earth, and so are above us with regard to the Sun, and never can come between the Earth and him. The Theory of the Motions of these Superior Planets, to an Eye placed on the Earth, are these; . That besides their apparent Motion from Eajl to Weft, which the Diurnal Rotation f the Earth occasions; they appear usually to move also slowly from Weft to East, and to make entire " Re - volutions this way; as in reality they do in their Orbits round the Sun. But Mars moves faster than Jupiter, and Jupiter than Saturn, in proper - tion to their several Distances from the Sun. . But sometimes they will also to an Eye at our Earth, appear to move the contrary way from East to Weft, which was a great Difficulty in the ola Astronomy; but may easily be Solved by the Consideration of the following Diagram; in which let A be the Sun, MGB the Orbit of the Earth, in which it moves annually from M by G towards B from S if P B from iVesl to Eafi let the Circle QRS be the Orbit of any Superior Planet moving the fame way as the Earth, Let the Circle TV rere - sent the Sphere of the six'd Stars supposed at an immense distance, and with rested to which the Retrogradation and Stations, &c. of the Planets are accounted. For tho ’ to an Eye placed in the Sun at A, the Planets would appear to move al - waysuniformly and equally forward intheirOrbs, as in reality they do j yet to an Eye placed on the Surface of our Earth, the Phasnomena will be ve - ry different, and the Planets will appear some - times to be Retrograde and Stationary in their Mo - tions, as well as at other times dire. For sup - pose the Earth at M, and Jupiter in G, while Ju - peter moves from C to R, and describes the Ark CR, a part of its Orbit round the Sun in A: The Earth, because its Angular Motion is much more Swift, will describe the Ark MG; so also while Jupiter describes the Ark RE, the Earth will move from G to B. Now while the Earth is de - serving the Ark M K, Jupiter will appear to be moving a little forward; but whilst the Earth moves thro ’ the Ark KG, Jupiter, tho ’ in reality till progressive ordiredt, will appear to be Retro - grade, and to move backward from F to O; Nor can it be otherwise while the Earth moves from G to D, and while Jupiter describes the Ark R E. But when the Earth comes towards B, then the Planet will appear a little dire again, and his ap - parent Progrefiive Motion will for a while conti - nually encrease. And when the Earth is near j or D, the Planet will appear to be Stationary in F or H. So that ’ tis obvious to fee that the app - rent Motion of the Planets will be very irregular and unequal, sometimes fwifcer, and sometimes flower, according to their Position, with respect to the Earth. The Progrefiive Motion of every Superior Planet will be swiftest in his Conjunction with the Sun, as his Retrograde Motion will be swiftest inhisOppofition. For the apparent direct Moti - on of the Planet in his Conjunction, arises from the Sum of the Motions of the Earth and Planet then moving directly contrary one to another; and the Retrograde Motion in the Opposition arises from the greatest Excess of all the Terrestrial Motions above the Planetary, both from there being then the least distance be - tween the Earth and the Planet, and from the Parallelism of their Motions at that time, as is clear from the Consideration of the Fi - gure.

supremacy.c: SUPREMACY of the Queen within her Do - minions, is declared by the th Article of the Church of England, by Can. i - and. by Stat. H.. c.,,. and by Stat.. to be Power of Soveraignty and Rule over all Persons born within her Majefties Dominiohs and Realms, of what Estate soever they be, whe - ther Ecclesiastical or Civil ( or Temporal ) so as no Foreign, nor other Power, shall or ought to bear any Superiority over them. This Su - primacy chiefly consists in the following Inftan - ces. . That the Archbilhops of either Pro - since cannot Summon their Bishops and Cler - gy to Convocation, nor exadfc any Canons without the Queen ’ s express Consent, by Hen.. c.. Whereas before that Adfc the Convocation was often called, and Laws were made by it for Governing the Church, without any Authority from the Grown. . In that there lies now an Appeal from the Archbishop to the Queen in Chancery, and on such an Appeal, a Commission under the Great Seal is to be dire & ed to certain Persons, whereof com - monly half are Lay - men, and half Clergy - men which is called the Court of Delegates; and which finally determines all Ecclesiastical Au - fes, by H., c.. tho ’ sometimes a Re - view is granted. Before this Statute, the Ap - peal from the Archbishop ’ s Court lay to the Peo - ple only. . The Queen can - grant Commiftions for vi - firing such Places as are exempt from the Jiirifr mistion of the Bishops and Archbilhops, and Ap - peal lies from thence to the Queen in Chan - very: Whereas before H.. the Pope could only visit them, and receive Appeals from those Courts. E. Pest S Y N S Y Z . Persons in Holy Orders are not, as formerly, exempt from the Queen ’ s Temporal Laws, any more than Laymen. And . Now the Bishops and Clergy neither Swear nor pay any Obedience to the Pope, but must take the. Oaths of Allegiance and Supremacy to the Qpeen, &c.
